STATEMENT OF QUALIFICATION
Q.PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.
A.My name is Dante Mugrace. My business address is 22 Brooks Avenue, Gaithersburg, MD 20877. 
Q.WHAT IS YOUR PRESENT OCCUPATION?
A.I am a Senior Consultant with the Economic and Management Consulting Firm of PCMG and Associates, LLC. (PCMG). In my capacity as a Senior Consultant, I am responsible for evaluating and examining rate and rate related proceedings before various governmental entities, preparing expert testimony recommending revenue requirement, as well as, offering opinions on economic policy, policy issues and methodologies used to set a value on a utility’s rate base and cost of service components of revenue requirement. 
Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE.
A.PCMG is an association of experts in utility regulation and policy, economics, accounting and finance.  PCMG’s members have over 75 years collective experience providing assistance to counsel and expert testimony regarding the regulation of electric, gas, water and wastewater utilities that operate under local, state and federal jurisdictions.  PCMG focuses on areas regarding revenue requirement, cost of service, rate design, cost of capital and rate of return. Prior to my association with PCMG, I was employed as a Senior Consultant with the consulting firm of Snavely King Majoros and Associates (SKM) from 2013 to 2015, in the same capacity as PCMG.  Prior to SKM I was employed by the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (NJBPU) from 1983 to my retirement in 2011.  During my tenure at the NJBPU, I held various Accounting, Rate Analyst, Supervisory and Management Positions.  My last position was Bureau Chief of Rates in the Agency’s Water Division (Bureau Chief of Rates).  I held this position for nearly 10 years.  My resume is attached as DM-1.
Q.WHAT EXPERIENCE DO YOU HAVE IN THE AREA OF UTILITY RATE SETTING PROCEEDINGS AND OTHER UTILITY MATTERS?
A.In my capacity as Bureau Chief of Rates at NJBPU, I was responsible for overseeing the rate process regarding administrative, financial, and managerial functions of the Rates Bureau.  My primary duties were to ensure that the jurisdictional utilities had sufficient revenues to cover their operating expenses, the ability to earn a reasonable rate of return on plant investments, and to ensure that the provision of safe, adequate and proper service at reasonable rates was met.  During my time at the NJBPU, I was involved in hundreds of rate and rate related proceedings. In my capacity as a Senior Consultant previously with SKM and now with PCMG, I have been and am currently involved in rate and rate related proceedings before the Commissions in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, and the States of Maine, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, and Ohio.  I was involved in the Generic Proceedings to Establish Parameters for the Next Generation Performance Based Rate Plans before the Alberta Utilities Commission.  I was involved in transmission formula rate plans before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) regarding the PECO Energy Company on behalf of the Pennsylvania OCA and the Rockland Electric Company on behalf of the NJ Division of Rate Counsel.  
Q.WHAT IS YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND?
A.I hold a Master of Business Administration (MBA) degree with a concentration in Strategic Management from Pace University-Lubin School of Business in New York, New York.  I hold a Master of Public Administration (MPA) degree from Kean University in Union, New Jersey.  I hold a Bachelor of Science (BS) degree in Accounting from Saint Peter’s University in Jersey City, New Jersey. 

II.PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY
Q.ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING?
A.I am testifying on behalf of the Georgia Public Service Commission Public Interest Advocacy Staff (“PIA Staff” or “Staff”). 
Q.WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?
A.The purpose of my testimony is to review and make recommendations with respect to the Georgia Power Company’s (GPC or Company) 2022 Rate Case’s Operation and Maintenance (O&M) Expenses for the test year ending July 31, 2023 and for the three Alternate Rate Plan (ARP) Years 2023, 2024 and 2025 with respect to just and reasonableness of the expenses and whether any of the expenses have been overestimated.  My testimony addresses the Company’s historical O&M Expenses that were used as a basis to set the test year O&M Expenses for the twelve months ending July 31, 2023.  My testimony addresses the setting of the prospective O&M Expenses related to the Company’s ARP for the periods 2023-2025.  
III.CASE OVERVIEW AND STRUCTURE OF TESTIMONY- PIA STAFF RECOMMENDATIONS 
Q.PLEASE PROVIDE A BRIEF OVERVIEW OF GPC’S RATE CASE FILING?
A.On June 24, 2022, GPC filed a base rate case proceeding with the Georgia Public Service Commission requesting recovery of a Levelized Revenue Deficiency applicable to traditional base rate tariffs of $738.661 million each year in 2023, 2024 and 2025. The Company is also requesting increases in Environmental Compliance Cost Recovery (ECCR), Demand Side Management (DSM) and Municipal Franchise Fee (MFF) tariffs’ revenue requirements to be recovered from customers.   The Company is proposing to recover an additional $312.245 million during the test year period ending July 31, 2023 and $426.415 million is proposed to be recovered during the 2023-2025 Levelized Adjustment periods ending December 31, 2023, December 31, 2024 and December 31, 2025 (Company Exhibit APA/SPA/ADH/MBR-1 Schedule 2 Traditional Base).   
Q.DID THE COMPANY UPDATE ITS FILING SUBSEQUENT TO THE JUNE 24, 2022 FILING?
A.Yes. On August 22, 2023, the Company updated its filing which contained revenue requirement impacts from various items included in the Final Order approved by the Commission in the 2022 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) and DSM Certification proceedings in Docket Nos. 44160 and 44161, respectively (August 22, 2022 petition). 
Q.WHAT O&M EXPENSE ADJUSTMENTS ARE YOU RECOMMENDING?
A.Based upon the use of the Company’s test year ending July 31, 2023, I have the following recommendations:
My recommended O&M Expenses for the test year ending July 31, 2023 is $886 million which is $192 million lower than the Company’s expense of $1,078 million. 
My recommended O&M Expenses for the rate year ending December 31, 2023 is $907 million which is $147 million lower than the Company’s expense of $1,053 million. 
My recommended O&M Expenses for the rate year ending December 31, 2024 is $906 million which is $147 million lower than the Company’s expense of $1,043 million.
My recommended O&M Expenses for the rate year ending December 31, 2025 is $886 million which is $169 million lower than the Company’s expense of $1,055 million.
I have accepted the Company’s Production Expenses for the test year period and for each of the rate year periods (2023-2025) as indicated below:
  
Test Year $3,303 million
Rate Year 2023$3,242 million
Rate Year 2024$3,147 million
Rate Year 2025$3,272 million

Q.WHAT APPROACH DID YOU USE IN DETERMINING YOUR ADJUSTMENTS TO THE COMPANY’S O&M EXPENSES?
A.In developing my adjustments to certain of the Company’s O&M Expenses, I determined whether the expenses were reasonable, prudent, known and measurable and realistic, and whether the Company should recover these expenses from ratepayers, and whether they were a necessary part of the Company’s operations.   I reviewed the Company’s historical expense data, as well as the Company’s forecasted data to determine my recommended O&M expense levels related to the Company’s category of expenses for the test year and for each of the rate year periods.  The more reliance on forecasted data the more subjectivity was used to determine the estimates proposed in the Company’s rate year periods.  My review and recommendation of the Company’s O&M Expense levels reflects cost that are recurring over time. My approach incorporates whether expenses should be normalized or averaged out based upon prior historical data and/or whether expenses should be recovered consistently over the rate year periods.  The ultimate goal in setting rates for service is to provide the ratepayers with safe and reliable service at reasonable rates with the Company being provided the opportunity to earn a reasonable rate of return on its funded plant investments, and to recovery all known and measurable expenses.  
Q.WHAT DID THE COMPANY STATE REGARDING O&M EXPENSES?
A.Mr. Womack stated that despite inflation and increased labor and healthcare costs over the last three years, the Company has worked hard to hold O&M cost escalation below the rate of historical inflation, budgeting about $1.7 billion in 2023 compared to about $2.0 billion of O&M expenses in current rates (Womack testimony at 12).  Included in the revenue requirement proposal are incremental inflation adjustments totaling $94 million and adjustments to its non-fuel O&M expenses that reflects a reduction of $163 million that are attributable to projected decreases in costs for employee benefits and effective cost management and reductions for outages and maintenance work on existing and retired coal units (Abramovitz, Adams, Houston and Robinson testimony (hereinafter as AAHR) at 18).   The Company stated that storm damage expenses have been reduced from $213 million per year to $65 million per year which reflects the average annual storm damage costs incurred over the past ten years (AAHR testimony at 19). 
Q.DO ANY OF THE COMPANY’S O&M EXPENSES INCLUDE COSTS RELATED TO SOUTHERN COMPANY AND SOUTHERN NUCLEAR OPERATING COMPANY?
A.Yes.  Southern Company services (SCS) expenses include various engineering costs, system costs, terminal processing charges, miscellaneous computer charges and other general charges to Georgia Power Company (STF-LA-2-6 page 18). With respect to Southern Nuclear Operating Company (SNOC) the Company is allocated costs related to Incentive Compensation and restricted stock awards (STF-LA-2-78 TRADE SECRET and STF-LA-2-81).

Q.PLEASE EXPLAIN YOUR APPROACH AND REASONING FOR EACH OF YOUR ADJUSTMENTS WITH RESPECT TO THE COMPANY’S TRANSMISSION EXPENSES FOR EACH OF THE YEARS SHOWN.
A.With respect to my averaging out of certain expenses in the Test Year 2023, I reviewed the Company’s prior three years of actual data as shown in response to STF-PIA-7-1.  I utilized the most recent three years of data (2019, 2020 and 2021) to perform my expense averaging.  The Accounts listed above (under the Test Year period) revealed variations and fluctuations over the 2019-2021 periods. Expenses under Account 566 are related to miscellaneous transmission expenses and typically fluctuate from year to year depending on the nature of the work involved.  Expenses under Account 569 are related to maintenance of structures including computer hardware, computer software, support services and regional transmission services.   These costs have fluctuated during the 2019-2021 periods, and I believe are appropriate and reasonable to use as a basis for the projections.  By averaging out these costs in the Test Year period, it smooths out any variations and provides for a steady recovery of incurred expenses over the life of the ARP.  Expenses under Account 570 are related to maintenance of station equipment and storage equipment.  These costs have fluctuated during the 2019-2021 periods, and I believe it is appropriate to average out these costs in the Test Year period, which smooth out any variations providing for a steady recovery of incurred expenses.  In calculating my adjustments, I removed the Labor costs that were included in each of these accounts as shown in response to STF-LA-2-72 and utilized the non-labor costs to average out these expenses for the 2019-2021 periods.   Regarding Account 571, these expenses are related to Tree Trimming Expenses – Transmission Forestry (STF-LA-2-65).  To calculate my adjustment to the Test Year period I averaged out the costs that were incurred in 2019-2021 and adjusted the sum of the average to the Company’s proposed Test Year period balance of $28,596,000.   Tree Trimming Expenses vary from year to year as the expenses show in response to STF-LA-2-65, and it is appropriate to average out these costs based upon actual historical balances during the 2019-2021 periods.  My adjustments are shown on my Schedule DM-3.
Q.HOW DID YOU ADJUST THESE SAME EXPENSES FOR THE RATE YEARS 2023-2025?
A.In reviewing these expenses for the Rate Years 2023-2025, only two accounts varied considerably from the Test Year period to the Rate Year periods.  These are Accounts are 570 and 571.  I removed the labor portion that was included in Account 570  and utilized the non-labor costs to average out this expense for the 2023-2025 periods. My reasoning for averaging out this expense is the same as indicated above for averaging out the expenses under the Test Year period.  For Account 571, I took the average of Tree Trimming Expenses for the actual historical balances in 2020, 2021 and budgeted 2022 and adjusted the sum of the averages to the Company’s proposed Rate Year 2023-2025 balances shown in response to SFT-LA-2-65.  The balance in Account 570 shows an annual recovery of $20.296 million (which includes the Tree Trimming- Transmission Forestry expenses) for each of the Rate Years 2023-2025.  My adjustments are shown on Schedule, DM-4, DM-5 and DM-6 for the Rate Year periods 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively.     A summary of my adjustments are as follows:

Q.PLEASE EXPLAIN EACH OF YOUR ADJUSTMENTS WITH RESPECT TO THE COMPANY’S DISTRIBUTION EXPENSES FOR EACH OF THE YEARS SHOWN.
A.With respect to my averaging out of certain expenses in the Test Year 2023, I reviewed the Company’s prior three years of actual data as shown in response to STF-PIA-7-1.  I utilized the most recent three years of data (2019, 2020 and 2021) to perform my expense averaging.   The Accounts listed above under the Test Year period, revealed variations and fluctuations over the 2019-2021 periods.   Expenses under Account 581 relate to expenses for load dispatching operations pertaining to the distribution of electricity.  These fluctuations occur depending on the year to year activities and any construction going on including emergency purposes.  Expenses under Account 583 and 584 relate to overhead line expenses and underground line expenses and do vary from year to year depending upon the annual activities for overhead and underground distribution lines and stations.   Expenses under Account 586 relate to meter expenses and do vary from year to year depending upon the installation, relocations, inspections, testing and other various supplies and materials.  Expenses under Account 587 relate to customer installation expenses and do vary from year to year depending upon inspection of premises, investigations, locations and installations of fuses, as well as testing and adjusting fixtures on customers’ properties.  Expenses under Account 588 relate to miscellaneous distribution expenses, include general materials and supplies not provided elsewhere and tend to fluctuate from year to year.  Expenses under Account 591 include structure maintenance and tend to vary from year to year.  Expenses under Account 592 relate to station equipment maintenance and also tend to vary from year to year depending on the activities incurred and needed to maintain electrical structures.  Regarding Account 593, these costs relate to Tree Trimming expenses – Distribution Forestry (STF-LA-2-65) Tree Trimming Expenses tend to vary from year to year as the expenses show in response to STF-LA-2-65, and it is appropriate to average out these costs based upon actual historical balances during the 2019-2021 periods.  Company actual costs for the 2019-2021 periods show varying fluctuations from $44.289 million in 2019, $37.548 million in 2020 and $73.656 million in 2021. The Company proposed a balance of $71.358 million for the Test Year period. Given the past actual and historical balances, it is appropriate to average out these costs providing for a steady and consistent recovery over the life of the ARP.  These costs have fluctuated during the 2019-2021 periods, and I believe it is an appropriate and reasonable to use them as a basis for the projections.  I removed the Labor costs that were included in each of these accounts as shown in response to STF-LA-2-72 and utilized the non-labor costs to average out these expenses for the 2019-2021 periods.   My adjustments are shown on my Schedule DM-3.
Q.HOW DID YOU ADJUST THESE SAME EXPENSES FOR THE RATE YEARS 2023-2025?
A.In reviewing these expenses for the Rate Years 2023-2025, only two accounts varied considerably from the Test Year period to the Rate Year period 2023 and three accounts for the Rate Year periods 2024 and 2025.  These are Accounts 586 and 593 in Rate Year 2023, and Accounts 586, 593 and 594 for Rate Years 2024 and 2025.  I removed the labor portion that was included in these Accounts and utilized the non-labor costs to average out this expense for the 2023-2025 periods.  My reasoning for averaging out this expense is the same as indicated above for averaging out the expenses under the Test Year period.  For Account 593, I reviewed the activities from the 2029-2021 and compared actual balances to the Company’s projected balances for 2022, the Test Year period 2023 and the projections for 2023-2025 Rate Year periods.  
I took the average of Tree Trimming Expenses – Distribution Forestry for the actual historical balances in 2020, 2021 and budgeted 2022 and adjusted the sum of the averages to the Company’s proposed Rate Year 2023-2025 balances shown in response to SFT-LA-2-65.  The Company’s Distribution Forestry expenses were $97.237 million for the 12-months ending May 31, 2022 and $99.040 million for the calendar year 2022.  The Company budgeted $52.016 million, $54.603 million and $57.320 million for the Rate Years 2023-2025, respectively.  I averaged out these expenses arriving at a yearly recovery of $54.646 million beginning in the Rate Year 2023 and through the Rate Year 2025, providing for a consistent and stable expense recovery.  The balance in Account 593 shows an annual recovery of $120.260 million (which includes the Tree Trimming- Distribution Forestry expenses) for each of the Rate Years 2023-2025.  My adjustments are shown on Schedule, DM-4, DM-5 and DM-6 for the Rate Year periods 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively.     A summary of my adjustments are as follows:

Q.WHAT HAS THE COMPANY PROPOSED WITH RESPECT TO CUSTOMER ACCOUNT EXPENSES IN THE TEST YEAR AND IN EACH OF THE RATE YEARS?

Q.DID YOU NOTICE ANY MAJOR INCREASES IN PRIOR YEARS 2019-2021 AND FOR THE TEST YEAR, AND FOR EACH OF THE RATE YEARS 2023-2025 RELATED TO ANY OF THE CUSTOMER ACCOUNTING EXPENSES?
A.Yes. In Accounts 902 (Meter Reading), and 903 (Customer Records and Collection), these expenses increased from a balance of $5.422 million (Account 902) in 2019 to $26.146 million in 2021; and for Account 903 from a balance of $90.235 million to $102.493 million in 2021.  For the Test Year 2023, Account 902 increased to $30.296 million and leveled off to $30.789 million for 2025.  For the Test Year 2023, Account 903 increases to $127.255 million and increased further to $142.368 million for 2025.  
Q.WHAT WERE THE REASONS THE COMPANY PROVIDED FOR THESE INCREASES IN THE CUSTOMER ACCOUNTING EXPENSES?
A.In response to STF-PIA-9-3, the Company stated that the increase in this category is primarily due to the Customer Information System (CIS) project of $15.1 million; labor costs of $5.8 million; incremental inflation of $4.6 million; customer payment transaction fees of $4.6 million; Southern Linc of $2.6 million; corporate IT billing of $2.5 million; customer billing administration of $2.2 million, Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) tower lease budget of $1.5 million; and Customer Service System (CSS) of $1.4 million.  In response to STF-PIA-9-4, the Company stated that these drivers were the reason for the increase in this category. The Company stated that its CIS is dated (1998) and need to be replaced, given the importance of investing in technology, applications and equipment that allow the Company to provide the best level of service to its customers. The Company stated that it delayed the implementation of a new CIS for as long as possible (STF-PIA-9-5) but Georgia Power, along with other Southern Company electric operating companies are the last major utilities utilizing the current platform and it is becoming increasingly challenging to support as the resources available to support the current system are diminishing. With respect to Transaction Fees, the Company’s updated platform will allow multiply payment options to the increasing number of customers who choose to utilize these options (PayPal, Venmo, Amazon Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay), as well as payment card autopay.  

Q.IN REVIEWING THE DOCUMENTS IN THE FILING AND EVIDENCE PROVIDED THROUGH DISCOVERY, WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION REGARDING THE COMPANY’S CUSTOMER ACCOUNTING EXPENSES FOR EACH OF THE YEARS SHOWN ABOVE?
A.Given that the Company’s current CIS has not been replaced in over 20 years, and the fact that current support services are dwindling as resources to support the current CIS system are currently diminishing, I am accepting the Company’s invested costs of $40 million which will continue over the ARP needed to upgrade and enhance its Customer Accounting System through the Test Year and the Rate Year periods,  however, I am recommending averaging out these costs over the life of the ARP (Rate Years 2023-2025).   In response to STF-PIA-9-3, the Company stated that the amount reflected with respect to the update to its CIS system are average increases or decreases over the three year (2023-2025) period.  Therefore, a three-year average would reflect incremental adjustments over the Test Year period and provide for a gradual recovery of costs over the life of the ARP.  In calculating my three-year average, I removed the labor portion that was included in this Account and utilized the non-labor costs to average out this expense for the 2023-2025 periods (STF-LA-2-72). What I am also recommending is that the Company should provide the implementation dates, actual costs by project (STF-PIA-9-3) and other relevant information and cost components, so that the Commission can track and verify that the costs the Company has included in this filing have actually been expensed and costs components have been implemented, with any differences identified in a separate filing.   A summary of my adjustments with respect to the Company’s CIS System which is included in Account 903 are as follows:

Q.WHAT HAS THE COMPANY PROPOSE WITH RESPECT TO ITS CUSTOMER SERVICE AND INFORMATION EXPENSES?

Q.WHAT WAS THE COMPANY’S CUSTOMER SERVICE AND INFORMATION EXPENSE FOR 2017 - 2021?
A.Customer service and information expense ranged from $79 million to $100 million per year with an average of $91 million per year over the five year period 2017 through 2021.
Q.WHY HAS CUSTOMER SERVICE AND INFORMATION EXPENSE INCREASED BY $46 MILLION PER YEAR OR 50 PERCENT?
A.The Company has included $23 million, $17 million, $18 million and $19 million of regulatory adjustment related to DSM tariff additional sum for the test year, 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively. The remainder of the increase is from the expansion of existing cost from an average $91 million per year 2017 thought 2021 to $112 million, $120 million, $121 million and $119 million in test year, 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively.
Q.DID THE COMPANY PROVIDE AN EXPLAINATION FOR THE LARGE INCREASE IN EXISTING CUSTOMER SERVICE AND INFORMATION EXPENSE FROM $91 MILLION PER YEAR TO $120 MILLION PER YEAR?
A.Yes.  With respect to data responses to STF-PCMG-3-1, the Company stated that the increase in this account is due to the DSM program expenses in the 2022 Base Rate Case Supplemental filing being recorded in FERC Account 908 and the regulatory adjustment associated with the DSM tariff additional sum, as approved by the Commission in the 2022 DSM Certification Docket No. 44161. In response to STF-PIA 9-8, the Company stated that the increase was due to the DSM returning to full activities in the test period when the pandemic greatly reduced DSM program activities.  
Q.WHAT IS STAFF’S RECOMMENDATION?
A.Staff believes that some increase in existing customer service and information expense is warranted but not 33 percent without support from the Company. Staff recommends that existing customer service and information expense grow by five percent per year and regulatory adjustment related to DSM tariff additional sum be recovered.

  Q.WHAT DID THE COMPANY PROPOSE WITH RESPECT TO SERP AND SERP-NON-SERVICE COSTS, SERVICE AWARDS AND RECREATION?
A.In response to STF-LA-2-71 the Company proposed the following costs related to SERP Expenses, Service Awards and Recreation:

As shown in response to STF-PCMG-2-12, the Company stated that the SERP and SERP-Non-Service Costs are related to Southern Company SERP and Supplemental Benefits Plan (SBP-Pension) which are non-qualified pension benefits for senior management level employees and represent the increase in the projected benefit obligation resulting from an additional year of service provided by the eligible employee.  The SERP-Non-Service Costs are related to the non-service cost portion of SERP and SBP-Pension and represents interest costs, amortization or prior service costs, and any gains or losses from prior years. Q.WHAT ADJUSTMENT DO YOU HAVE RELATED TO THE COMPANY’S VARIOUS SERP EXPENSES?
A.With respect to SERP and SERP-Non-Service Costs, I am recommending removing these costs from the Test Year period and for each of the Rate Year periods 2023-2025. I believe these types of costs do not benefit ratepayers in the provision of safe and reliable utility service, but rather benefit top executives by rewarding them to be retained by the Company. These types of SERP and related SERP costs are based upon certain agreements to obtain a certain amount of retirement income based upon various eligibility conditions that must be met. SERP costs are used by companies seeking to incentivize key executives in staying with the company.  Further, SERP and SERP related costs benefit the Company in that the Company gets the tax benefit because it pays the premiums on the insurance, and even if the employee quits or passes away, the Company still has access to the insurance cash value and is a beneficiary of the payout.  Given this scenario, I see no benefits going to ratepayers and therefore recommend these costs be removed from the Employee Pension and Benefits balance in the Test Year and in each of the Rate Years 2023-2025. 
Q.WHAT ADJUSTMENTS DO YOU HAVE WITH RESPECT TO SERVICE AWARDS AND FOR RECREATION COSTS?
A. I am recommending removing these costs from the Company’s Test Year period and for each of the Rate Year periods 2023-2025. For the Service Award costs, these costs represent premature anticipated costs in the event an employee reaches a certain number of years of service and are not a known and measurable cost. In the past, the Company has booked $331,000 in 2020, $535,000 in 2021 and $115,000 for the twelve months ending 5/31/2022.  In the Test Year the Company is proposing to recover $807,000 and $818,000, $836,000 and $856,000 in the Rate Years 2023-2025, respectively.  The Company has not provided any further information as to whether or not employees attained another year of service or whether any criteria was needed to be met in order to receive the bonus.  Given this lack of information, I am recommending these costs be removed from the Company’s Employee Pension and Benefits account.  With respect to Recreation costs, the Company has not booked any costs in 2020, 2021 or for the 12 months ending 5/31/2022.  The Company began booking these Recreation costs in the Test Year and for each of the Rate Years 2023-2025 (STF-LA-2-71).  The Company has not provided any further reasoning in recovering these costs but for representing it for meals and travel expenses (STF-PCMG-2-12).  I do not see these costs as benefitting ratepayers, in that the Company’s response does not fully explain the need for these costs (utility services related, customer services related, regulatory related etc.).  Therefore, I am recommending these costs be removed from the Company’s Employee Pension and Benefits account 926.

8.Inflation Adjustments
Q.WHAT DID THE COMPANY PROPOSE RELATED TO THE IMPACT ON INFLATION?
A.Company witness Womack stated that the recent levels of significant inflation are impacting the Company. This is due to the unprecedented economic environment, resulting in high uncertainty and increasing costs of goods and services, challenges related to geopolitical tensions, stressed supply chains, and historically high inflation and tight labor markets all exacerbated by a rising interest rate environment that resulted in a tightening federal monetary policy (Womack testimony at 10-11).  Mr. Womack stated that the current significant level of inflation, fueled by national and local economic forces, impacts the cost to serve customers and must be appropriately reflected in the Company’s rates (Womack testimony at 11).  In AAHR at 18, Company witnesses stated that the incremental inflation resulted in an increase of about $94 million in the Company’s revenue requirement. 
Q.HOW DID THE COMPANY DEVELOP ITS ADJUSTMENT RELATED TO INFLATION?
A.As indicated in response to STF-LA-2-10, the Company does not create a budget by applying an inflation rate to all the actual or historic year expense.  Expenses are reviewed and based upon known increases or decreases the budget amounts are adjusted accordingly.   Based upon the type of expenditure, inflation rates may be applied to derive projected expenses. The budget guidelines and assumptions for the 2022 budget process include escalation rates for both labor and non-labor costs.  The labor escalation rates are based upon data supplied by the Employment Cost Index (ECI) Private Sector Wage and Salaries and non-labor escalation rates are derived from the Bureau of Economic Analysis Gross Domestic product (GDP) index values as of April 2022.   The Company provided the following cost indexes for the ECI and for the GDP:
ECIGDP
20225.8%5.8%
20235.4%2.9%
20244.5%2.4%
20254.2%2.3%

Q.WHAT IS YOUR RESPONSE TO THE COMPANY’S PROPOSAL RELATED TO INFLATION ADJUSTMENTS?
A.In response to STF-PCMG-1-5, the Company provided a breakdown of its proposed Inflation adjustment of $94 million by FERC Account No. and by the test year and rate year periods. Q.WHAT ADJUSTMENTS DO YOU HAVE WITH RESPECT TO THE COMPANY’S INFLATION ADJUSTMENT IN THE AMOUNT OF $94 MILLION?
A.I am accepting the ECI index for labor wage increases, as there is no other way to calculate the adjustment of wages but for cost of living adjustments and bargaining unit agreements.   With respect to O&M Inflation, I am accepting the cost adjustments related to Production expenses as these costs adjustments result in a >1.00% increase with respect to the overall Production expenses in the Test Year and in each of the Rate Years 2023-2025.  Given that energy costs have been particularly high I have no issues with these expenses in what the Company has proposed.  With respect to the remaining expenses All Other O&M expenses, I did an analysis which computed the Company’s proposed Inflation Adjustments for All Other O&M Expenses in relation to the Test Year and Rate Years Inflation Adjustments as shown above. Q.PLEASE EXPLAIN YOUR OVERALL REASONING RELATED TO THE COMPANY’S PROPOSED INFLATION ADJUSTMENTS AS IT PERTAINS TO THE SETTING OF RATES.
A.It is my opinion that the use of inflation rates and factors to set rates for service in ratemaking are not a known and measurable cost, in that these types of cost increases do not reflect the actual costs the Company will incur, but rather estimates with no foundational reasoning.  These types of costs are essentially broad economic adjustments that do not particularly address any one individual expense category.  Inflation adjustments are overall blanket type adjustments that are applied to all goods and services that may or may not be related to costs incurred by the Company, especially if the GDP is used, which is a broad basket of consumer goods and services such as housing, clothing, food, etc.   While such inflation costs adjustments are typically used to develop economic data, they should not be used for ratemaking purposes in most cases.  In this case, under the Company’s ARP, inflation may not stay elevated during the term of the 3-year rate plan.  I believe that the Company’s inflation adjustment forecast is too high, and it may result in rates being set too high for utility service. Given this situation, I am recommending lowering the Company’s proposed Inflation Adjustments in the Rate Years as follows:

Q.WHAT WERE THE REASONS GIVEN BY THE COMPANY REGARDING THE VARIATIONS OF CONTRACT LABOR FROM THE TEST YEAR PERIOD THROUGH THE RATE YEARS 2023-2025?
A.As more specifically addressed in response to STF-LA-2-72, the Company stated the reasons for the variations of Contract Labor were due to outages schedules, maintenance activities, permanent reduction in maintenance expense on steam production, variations in yearly spending in both asset and vegetation management driven by workload and economic conditions, participation levels in DSM programs, DSM program evaluation, and growth in electric transportation programs, facility management, legal spend, rate case costs and advertising. In response to STF-LA-2-73, the Company stated that the decrease in employee headcount from prior years are the result from attrition, turnover and cost containment initiatives by the Company.  The Company stated that it continues to review business processes to enhance customer experience as well as focus on efficiency.  The actual headcount has been reduced by about 438 employees since 2019. In response to STF-PCMG-2-13, the Company further stated that the decrease in projected contract labor O&M from $448.492 million in 2022 to $363.444 million in 2025, was largely due by decreases in contract labor related to steam generation, transmission, and distribution functions.   The projected decrease in steam generation contract was driven by lower outage spend in 2024 and 2025 as well as projected steam unit retirements.  The reduction in distribution contract labor was driven by lower vegetation management spend and the completion of the distribution backlog in 2022.  The projected decrease in transmission contract labor was driven by lower asset management spend due to current and forecasted economic conditions.

Q.PLEASE DESCRIBE THE COMPANY’S PEFORMANCE PAY PROGRAM (PPP) 
A.As more fully described in the response to STF-LA-2-78 Attachment A (BEGIN TRADE SECRET), the Company’s Performance Pay Program rewards achievement of operational goals, earnings per share, and GPC net income.  A target percentage of base pay is established for each employee based on his/her classification and grade level for target-level performance.  All employees are eligible to participate.  (END TRADE SECRET). 
Q.HOW ARE PERFORMANCE GOALS WEIGHED?
A.As identified in response to STF-LA-2-79, the Company has weighed the components of the overall program by one-third operational goals, one-third business unit financial goals (net income for Georgia Power) and one-third earnings per share.    
Q.DID YOU ASK THE COMPANY WHAT THE ACTUAL RESULTS OF THE COMPANY’S PPP WERE IN PRIOR YEARS?
A.Yes, in response to STF-PCMG-2-18, I asked the Company to provide the actual results of the Company’s PPP for the years 2017-2021 and for the expected year 2022, including the dollar amount associated with each program component and the dates of payouts.  
Q.WHAT WERE THE RESULTS OF THE COMPANY’S PPP FOR THOSE YEARS?
A.The Company stated that results for the 2017-2021 years were in excess of 100% of the Performance Goal factors(STF-LA-2-79).  These included assumptions for directly incurred – GPC, allocated from SCS to GPC and allocated from SNC to GPC.   The 2022 actual results will not be available until the year is complete.  The PPP is funded at the total performance level and, therefore, the dollar amount associated with each program component are not available.  
Q.WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION?
A.Based upon the criteria of the PPP which allocates one-third of the overall annual Performance Based Compensation by operational goals, business unit financial goals and earnings per share, I am recommending that only the operational goals be allowed in the O&M Expenses.

Q.PLEASE EXPLAIN YOUR ADJUSTMENTS.
A.I am recommending that the Company not recover PPP compensation related to financial goals (Net Income for Georgia Power) and for earnings per share, but only for operational goals that related to ratepayer benefits in the area of safety, culture, customer satisfaction, major projects, availability, reliability and such goals that benefits the provision of safe and reliable utility service to customers (STF-LA-2-78 Attachment B page 6).  I do not believe that incentive compensation related to increasing  net income and financial performance goals that affect the Company’s, SCS’s and SNC’s earnings per share should be afforded recovery from ratepayers.  These types of incentive costs benefit the Shareholders of the Company, and of SCS and SNC, and do not directly benefit the ratepayers in the area of safe and reliable utility service.  My recommendation is shown on my Schedule DM-11 Performance Pay Plan.

Q.WHAT WERE THE REASONS THAT THE COMPANY CLAIMED TO EXPLAIN THE YEAR TO YEAR VARIANCES?
A.In response to STF-LA-2-73, the Company stated that the decrease in headcount from 2016 through 2021 was primarily due to attrition, turnover and cost containment initiatives by the Company. The Company has continued to review business processes to enhance customer experience as well as focus on efficiency. The actual headcount has been reduced by about 438 employees since 2019.  
Q.HAS THE COMPANY EXPLAINED THE NEED TO HIRE APPROXIMATELY 470 EMPLOYEES FROM THE MAY 2022 ACTUAL HEADCOUNT TO THE TEST YEAR AND RATE YEAR PERIODS?
A.In response to STF-PCMG-2-15, the Company stated that its staffing level at any point in time is dynamic and will fluctuate as hiring and attrition are a part of normal business operations.  Therefore, vacancies will occur throughout the rate year periods as part of normal business and will fluctuate accordingly.  The hiring and attrition process will also vary based upon the needs of the business at that time.  Because of the normal inflows and outflows of headcount throughout the year, it is difficult to project or develop a schedule of expected hirings.  During the interim when vacancies are not filled, labor cost continues to be incurred as the work is performed by overtime from existing workforce and contract labor. 
Q.WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION?
A.For the Test Year, I am recommending a vacancy ratio rate based upon the prior three years of historical data (2019, 2020 and 2021).  Averaging out the vacancy ratios for these periods results in an average vacancy ratio rate of 8.33%. (6%+9+10%)/3.  
Q.PLEASE EXPLAIN YOUR REASONING FOR A VACANCY RATE RATIO ADJUSTMENT.
A.As stated in response to STF-PMCG-2-14, the Company stated that vacancies occur throughout the year and will fluctuate from month to month.  Attrition rates are on the rise and replacing positions externally has been challenging with the current competitive labor market.  The Company’s historical vacancy rate ratio trend provides a good indicator of what is to be expected going forward, given the current labor market and based upon the Company’s staffing plans and individual business unit work plans.  Given that the  Company experiences vacancies throughout the year, it is appropriate to take these vacancies into consideration when setting labor costs. These vacancies are due to a number of factors -- employee stability, voluntary and involuntary leave by employees, increased / decreased work load, shifting of employees from one affiliated entity to another (business unit staffing), difficulty to fill vacancies due to the challenge of attracting and retaining employees and overall business strategy.   Using the Company’s projected Contract Labor of $428,467,945 minus my recommended reduction related to Performance Pay Incentive Compensation booked in the Test Year, my net Contract Labor for purposes of calculating my vacancy rate ratio is $322,291,871.  Using my  average vacancy rate ratio of 8.33%, I compute an adjustment of $29,286,360 for the Test Year period.  This is shown on my Schedule DM-11. 
Q.WHAT ADJUSTMENTS ARE YOUR RECOMMENDING RELATED TO THE COMPANY’S PROPOSED ADDITIONAL EMPLOYEES OF 470?
A.I am recommending phasing these employees over the Company’s three-year rate plan (2023-2025).  Using the Company’s proposed additional 470 employees and dividing that by the Company’s current employee staff level of 6,546 as of May 2022, this results in a ratio of 7.18%.  Dividing the 7.18% over the three-year rate plan an annual rate of 2.39% is computed.  I then reduced the employee additions in the Rate Year 2023 by taking the Company’s proposed Contract Labor in 2023 of $387,339,165 (minus my recommended adjustments related to Performance Pay - Incentive Compensation) and multiplying that amount by two-thirds of the overall 470 additional employees (2.39% times 2= 4.786%) to arrive at an adjustment of $14,737,684 for the Rate Year 2023.  For the Rate Year 2024 I reduced the employee additions by taking the Company’s proposed Contract Labor of $373,920,349 and multiplying that amount by one-third or 2.39% or $7,522,258.  Finally, in the Rate Year 2025, I assumed that the Company will have hired the remaining one-third of the employees, so there will be no reduction in the employee additions. My adjustments are shown on my Schedule DM-11 Additional Employees. Below is a summary of my recommended employee head count:

 4   Q.       HOW DID THE COMPANY PROPOSE TO RECOVER THE REVENUE

 5            DEFICIENCY FOR THE TEST YEAR ENDING JULY 31, 2023?

 6   A.       The rate filing indicates that the Company requests a revenue requirement increase of

 7            approximately $738.661 million rather than the $447.521 million revenue deficiency

 8            associated with the test year. The $738.661 million is based on a $426.415 million

 9            "levelized" revenue deficiency which the Company calculated based on calendar 2023

10            through 2025. This is shown on Company Exhibit__(APA/SPA/ADH/MBR-1, Schedule

11            2 Traditional Base), page 1 of 3. As shown there, Georgia Power first calculated a retail

12            jurisdictional revenue deficiency for the test year of approximately $312.245 million. To

13            that amount the Company added a "2023-2025 Levelization Adjustment" amount of

14            $426.415 million3, to derive its requested Levelized Revenue Deficiency Applicable to

15            Traditional Base Rate Tariffs of $738.661 million, as shown on Company

16            Exhibit__(APA/SPA/ADH/MBR-1, Schedule 2 Traditional Base), page 1, lines 1-3.

18   Q.       IS THE COMPANY'S PROPOSED RECOVERY OF A REVENUE DEFICIENCY

19            BASED ON THE TRADITIONAL TEST YEAR APPROACH?

20   A.       No. The Company’s rate request in this case is not based on the traditional ratemaking

21            approach. Rather, it is based on an Alternative Rate Plan that uses projected data from an

 4   Q.      WHAT TEST YEAR SHOULD BE USED TO DETERMINE THE COMPANY’S

 5           TRADITIONAL REVENUE REQUIREMENT IN THIS CASE?

 6   A.      Under the Commission’s February 6, 2020 Order Adopting Settlement Agreement as

 7           Modified in Docket No. 42516, the test period to be used in this case is from August 1,

 8           2022 to July 31, 2023. The February 6, 2020 Order Adopting Settlement Agreement as

 9           Modified also required the Company to file testimony and exhibits required in a general

10           rate case along with supporting schedules required by the Commission to support a

11           “traditional” rate case by July 1, 2022, so that the Commission may consider whether to

12           continue, modify, or discontinue the Alternative Rate Plan established in Georgia Power

13           Company's 2019 Rate Case, Docket No. 42516 ("2019 Rate Case").

14

15           Both the Company and Staff have presented revenue requirement calculations using the

16           test year ending July 31, 2023, as well as for calendar years 2023, 2024 and 2025, which

17           comprise the Company's Alternative Rate Plan presentation in the current rate case.

 4   Q.    DOES STAFF PROPOSE TO LEVELIZE THE ECCR REVENUE

 5         REQUIREMENTS?

 6   A.    No. Staff has not reflected a "levelization" of the 2023 through 2025 ECCR revenue

 7         requirements, similar to the Company's proposed $46.8 million decrease. Rather, Staff

 8         recommends that annual ECCR revenue deficiency (or excess) amounts for 2024 and

 9         2025 be established based on compliance filings to be made by the Company on October

10         1, 2023 and 2024, respectively. Because the ECCR is a separately identifiable tariff

11         component, annual adjustments can be made for the annual changes in the ECCR revenue

12         requirement. Thus, Staff proposes that the ECCR revenue requirement be reflected as

13         annual rate changes, rather than a levelized approach.

17         adjustments to reflect ratemaking treatments. In the current alternative rate plan, for

18         example, the Company reports its results for each year in an Annual Surveillance Report

19         ("ASR"), which is reviewed by Staff. The Company's earnings are reviewed to determine

20         if they were below, within or above an established earnings band. Staff's specific

 1                         VII.    MUNICIPAL FRANCHISE FEE TARIFF
 2

 3   Q.   PLEASE PROVIDE SOME BACKGROUND ON THE COMPANY’S MFF

 4        TARIFF.

 5   A.   In the 2007 Georgia Power Rate Case Order, the Commission ordered the establishment

 6        of the MFF tariff in accordance with the Commission’s Order in Docket No. 21112. The

 7        MFF tariff initially reflected 50 percent of MFF revenues being collected from customers

 8        located within municipal areas covered by a franchise agreement and 50 percent being

 9        collected from all customers, regardless of location. However, over the years, the

10        Company has experienced a shift with more of its total revenue coming from customers

11        within municipalities. Because the MFF tariff is a percentage rate and is calculated based

12        on each customer’s total bill before sales taxes are applied, the percentage rate does not

13        have to be changed even if revenues change.

14

15   Q.   WHAT CAUSES THE MFF TARIFFS TO CHANGE?

16   A.   As described on pages 30-31 of the Abramovitz/Adams//Houston/Robinson Direct

17        Testimony, the primary components of the MFF tariff that could change from year to

18        year are the amount of revenues collected relative to whether or not customers are

19        receiving service within a municipality’s boundaries. As customer demographics change,

20        so would the respective MFF tariff.

21

22   Q.   WHAT HAS THE COMPANY REQUESTED FOR AN MFF TARIFF REVENUE

23        REQUIREMENT?

1         VIII.   COAL COMBUSTION RESIDUALS ASSET RETIREMENT OBLIGATIONS
2                               REVENUE REQUIREMENT
3

4    Q.      HOW IS THE OBLIGATION FOR CCR COMPLIANCE RECORDED FOR

5            ACCOUNTING PURPOSES AND RECOVERED FROM CUSTOMERS IN

6            RATES?

7    A.      For accounting purposes, the Company's obligation for compliance with CCR regulations

8            is recorded as an Asset Retirement Obligation. A related liability is also recorded to

 9           recognize the legal obligation to incur such costs. Historically, costs related to the

10           remediation of ash ponds and landfills that have been used to store coal ash at plants that

11           were still operational would have generally been included in the cost of removal/negative

12           net salvage component of depreciation rates and would have been recovered over the

13           estimated remaining life of the coal-fired generating plants. CCR compliance costs for

14           coal-fired generating plants that have already been retired or are being retired before their

15           previously estimated useful lives are being addressed for cost recovery. Both the

16           Company and Staff have calculated revenue requirements related to the recovery of CCR

17           costs in the current rate case proceeding. On Exhibit __(RS/RT-6) we have replicated the

18           Company's calculated CCR ARO Compliance revenue deficiency amounts for the test

19           year and for each plan year, 2023 through 2025, and also present Staff's calculated

20           revenue deficiency amounts for each period for the CCR ARO Compliance. Staff’s

21           adjusted amounts differ from those calculated by the Company primarily because Staff

22           has used witness Gorman’s recommended cost of capital.

23


                      Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey
                                                   Page 42 of 140

                                                                                                     PUBLIC VERSION


 1   Q.         HOW DOES THE OBLIGATION FOR CCR COMPLIANCE IMPACT

 2              RATEPAYERS?

 3   A.         The Company’s expenditures for CCR compliance have consistently exceed revenues

 4              collected from ratepayers under ECCR. This creates unpaid balance that the Company

 5              earns a full return on including interest expense, return on equity (profit) and income

 6              taxes in addition to the direct cost for remediating coal ash ponds. The Company has

 7              projected to spend $320 million, $408 million and $510 million in 2023, 2024 and 2025,

 8              respectively, for CCR compliance. The revenues collected from ratepayers are estimated

 9              to be $237 million, $308 million and $345 million in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively.

10              The unpaid balance is projected to grow to $365 million, $465 million and $630 million

11              as of December 31, 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively.10 Georgia Power would collect

12              approximately $26 million, $34 million and $45 million for profit and income taxes on

13              the unpaid balance in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively.11 The profit and income tax

14              amounts are in addition to the interest expense on the portion of the unpaid CCR

15              compliance balance that has been financed with debt.12

16

18              APPROVED IN THE 2022 INTERATED RESOURCE PLAN (IRP)?

10   Q.         HAS THE COMPANY EXPLAINED WHY THE ENERGY DIRECT PREMIUM

11              PACKAGE REVENUE AND EXPENSES ARE UNREGULATED (I.E.,

12              RECORDED BELOW-THE-LINE) WHEN THE STANDARD PACKAGE

13              EXPENSES ARE REGULATED (I.E., RECORDED ABOVE-THE-LINE)?

14   A.         Yes. In response to an informal Staff inquiry regarding this issue, the Company stated:

15                      Energy Direct provides a management tool for Commercial and Industrial
16                      customers. The standard package is available at no cost and is a Regulated
17                      Above the Line (ATL) service. The premium packages provide customers
18                      with additional data and have a monthly cost to customers. All revenue for
19                      EnergyDirect is unregulated below-the-line (BTL) because it is associated
20                      with premium packages.
21                      When EnergyDirect was launched, the Company allocated expenses based
22                      on the initial development costs incurred to stand up the EnergyDirect
23                      Program. At that time, it was determined that 70% of the Program’s capital
24                      and O&M costs would have been incurred to develop the Regulated ATL
25                      Standard Package and 30% for the Unregulated BTL Premium Packages.
26                      This breakdown for program expenses continues. However, expenses that
27                      are incurred specifically to support the Unregulated offerings are charged
28                      100% Unregulated BTL.

                                                       Page 59 of 140

1    Q.   DO YOU AGREE WITH THE COMPANY’S ACCOUNTING TREATMENT

2         WHEREBY THE REVENUES AND EXPENSES ASSOCIATED WITH THE

3         ENERGY DIRECT PREMIUM PACKAGES ARE UNREGULATED (I.E.,

4         RECORDED BELOW-THE-LINE)?

5    A.   No. We do not agree with the Company’s accounting treatment whereby the revenues

6         and expenses associated with the energy direct premium packages are unregulated (i.e.,

7         below-the-line). Specifically, we do not see a valid distinction as to why the expenses

8         associated with the Energy Direct Standard Package should be recorded above-the-line

9         while the revenues and expenses associated with the Premium Packages should be

10        recorded below-the-line. This treatment would appear to allow the Company to retain the

11        pre-tax profits being earned on the Premium Packages.

12

5         E-8, Interest Synchronization Adjustment
6    Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE GEORGIA POWER’S PROPOSED INTEREST

7            SYNCHRONIZATION ADJUSTMENT SHOWN ON STAFF EXHIBIT__(RS/RT-

8            2), SCHEDULE E-8.

 9   A.      The Company is proposing that interest expenses to be used as a deduction in the

10           calculation of the test year pro forma adjusted income taxes be based on the interest

11           expenses that are implicit in its proposed overall rate of return. These pro forma interest

12           expenses (referred to as the so-called “synchronized” interest expenses) are determined

13           by multiplying the weighted cost of debt component of the overall rate of return times the

14           rate base used in this case.

2    Q.   WHAT IS STAFF’S RECOMMENDATION REGARDING ELECTRIC

3         TRANSPORTATION MAKE READY?

4    A.   The Make Ready program proposed by Georgia Power Company in this docket should be

5         denied and the associated costs be removed for ratemaking purposes. Investments

6         needed to provide an unregulated service to private groups should be paid for by the

7         business or organization wanting to provide that unregulated service. This is true whether

8         or not the unregulated charging service is private or available to the public. As with

9         investments associated with regulated public utilities, the costs should be recovered from

10        cost-causers. The general body of ratepayers should not be subjected to paying for private

11        assets that primarily benefit Make Ready participants. The program, if continued for the

12        next decade, will increase the revenue requirement by close to half a billion dollars.

13

14   Q.   WHY IS THE MAKE READY PROGRAM NOT IN THE PUBLIC INTEREST?

15   A.   The Make Ready program obligates captive electric service customers to subsidize the

16        provision an unregulated service, electric vehicle charging. The vast majority of retail

17        electric customers do not own electric vehicles and will not own EVs this decade.

18        Additionally, Make Ready equipment is only needed in order to provide unregulated

19        charging services to a small set of Georgia Power’s customers. The equipment is not used

20        and useful in providing regulated retail electric service to Georgia Power’s customers.

21        As noted in the response to STF-HR-1-2, “To date, nearly all of the total Make Ready

                   Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey
                                                Page 74 of 140

                                                                                         PUBLIC VERSION


 1        program spend (over 99%) is for the funding of equipment on the customer side of the

 2        meter.” Make Ready results in co-ownership of unregulated EV charging stations by the

 3        monopoly utility. The monopoly utility is allowed to profit now, not only on assets used

 4        and useful in the provision of retail electric service, but also on unregulated assets fully

 5        funded by customers who do not have a choice of providers.

 6

 7   Q.   WHAT MAKE READY SPENDING WAS APPROVED FOR GEORGIA POWER

 8        IN THE 2019 RATE CASE AND WHAT WAS APPROVED?

 9   A.   Georgia Power received approval of Make Ready spending in the 2019 Rate Case of $6

10        million per year. The issue was not litigated, and interveners did not have the opportunity

11        to submit positions into the record. The $6 million per year for Make Ready was added to

12        a settlement agreement reached between certain interveners. Item 30 from the 2019 Rate

13        Case Settlement, which was ultimately approved by the Commission, stated:

14        30.    The funds for electric vehicle infrastructure will be allowed as proposed by
15               the Company with an additional $6 million per year to be invested in support
16               of wire and transformer upgrades for customer sited charging stations.
17

18   Q.   WHAT SPENDING WAS AUTHORIZED BY THE APPROVED SETTLEMENT?

19   A.   The annual budget was specifically authorized to support “wire and transformer

20        upgrades”. The Company’s implementation of the program, however, has exceeded the

21        scope of uses specified in the stipulation agreement. Rather than limit the program to

22        wire and transformer upgrades, which would reasonably be expected to be on the

23        Company’s side of the meter, Georgia Power spent 99% of the authorized funds on

24        equipment on the customer’s side of the meter as noted above.

25

                   Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey

5    Q.   HOW LONG WILL RATEPAYERS BE OBLIGATED TO PAY FOR THE MAKE

14   Q.   ARE THERE OTHER REASONS TO NOT MANDATE THAT RATEPAYERS

15        SUBSIDIZE ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING VIA THE MAKE READY

16        PROGRAM?

17   A.   Yes. The long-term success of the electric vehicle charging market depends on making it

18        a competitive free market. Make Ready creates an uneven playing field for providers of

19        Electric Vehicle Charging services, and gives Georgia Power the ability to select winners

20        and losers in the charging station market. More importantly, GPC customers should have

21        the economic freedom to only pay for the retail electric service they need. Customers

22        who have no alternative for their electric service should not be required to also pay for

23        other Georgia Power customers to have private Electric Vehicle charging stations.


                   Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey

1    Q.   ARE THESE MAKE READY ASSETS OWNED AND MAINTAINED BY

3         IN THE PROVISION OF REGULATED RETAIL ELECTRIC SERVICE?

4    A.   No. The assets are only used to provide electric vehicle charging, which is currently not

5         regulated.

6

7    Q.   HAS THE COMPANY IDENTIFIED THE MAKE READY LOCATIONS?

8    A.   In data request STF-PIA-1-1, Staff requested that the Company identify the ET Make

9         Ready sites. In its response, the Company provided the “Premise Company” and

10        “Contact Address”. Make Ready assets are owned and maintained by Georgia Power.

11        As such, the location of these assets should not be designated as trade secret. With very

12        rare exception, the locations of Company-owned assets have not previously been

13        withheld from the public. Staff subsequently requested the Company provide the

14        addresses of the Make Ready projects as public disclosure information and without trade

15        secret designation. The Company responded by indicating that by virtue of being

16        collocated with participating Make Ready Customers, revealing the Make Ready sites

17        would disclose customer information (i.e. which of its customers are Make Ready

18        participants). Although Staff has recommended the Make Ready Program be

19        discontinued, if the Commission chooses to approve the program, it should do so with

20        full transparency required. The names and addresses of the participants should be

21        disclosed, and the Company should also be required to identify which locations are

22        available to the public for charging.

13   Q.         IN YOUR OPINION, SHOULD GEORGIA POWER BE AUTHORIZED TO

14              MAKE ADDITIONAL CAPITAL INVESTMENTS IN THE COMMUNITY

15              CHARGER PROGRAM?

16   A.         No, they should not. First, the table above clearly demonstrates the current and future

17              charging stations will not generate enough revenue to cover O&M expense and


     2828
            STF-LA-6-19


                          Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey
                                                       Page 83 of 140

                                                                                    PUBLIC VERSION


 1   depreciation, much less the return on capital and income taxes associated with the

 2   investment. The Community Charging stations are being subsidized by all ratepayers

 3   including the vast majority who do not own an electric vehicle, and are not expected to

 4   own an electric vehicle in the next decade. Continuation of the program, and increasing

 5   the annual capital expenditures to $3 million annually will result in additional costs to

 6   ratepayers that exceed the programs revenue.

 7

 8   Second, the competitive market is expected to provide, with assistance from federal

 9   funding and grants, a significant number of new charging stations throughout the state,

10   including those being installed by companies risking their own capital. It would be unfair

11   and inappropriate regulatory policy to allow Georgia Power to expand its monopoly to

12   build more EV charging facilities at the expense of ratepayers. To the extent that EV

13   charging stations being used for the purpose of fueling the Company's fleet of vehicles

14   that are used in the provision of providing service, such costs may be appropriate for

15   recovery from ratepayers assuming the investment was prudent and economic, as these

16   are used and useful. However, as discussed above, the Company's plan for the $9 million

17   investment in EV charging facilities over the term of plan years 2023-2023, is largely

18   centered on making such charging facilities available to portions of the general public

19   that have EVs. Also, the rates that the Company is charging for EV charging for the

20   service are insufficient to recover the costs, given the low utilization of the chargers. Staff

21   recommends that the costs associated with the Company’s Community Charging Stations

22   program should not approved. Staff has therefore made an adjustment to remove the

23   costs and revenues associated with the EV charging facilities.

 5        E-36, Depreciation Expense – Depreciation Rates Correction for Fort Benning and Fort
 6           Gordon
 7   Q.      PLEASE EXPLAIN YOUR ADJUSTMENT ON SCHEDULE E-36.

 8   A.      In the Company’s response to STF-LA-8-18, discrepancies were noted between the

 9           depreciation rates proposed by Georgia Power in Attachment A to the response to STF-

10           LA-8-18 and what was reflected in the Company’s depreciation study for its Fort

11           Benning and Fort Gordon solar facilities. Through an informal inquiry, Georgia Power

12           advised that due to a formula error in its depreciation rate calculations, the depreciation

13           rates reflected in its filing for Fort Benning and Fort Gordon were 2.584% and 0%,

14           respectively. However, Appendix A to the depreciation study reflects depreciation rates

15           of 2.835% and 2.820% for the Fort Benning and Fort Gordon solar facilities,

16           respectively, which the Company confirmed are the correct rates to apply. The Company

17           stated that it did not make this correction in its supplemental filing, thus their proposed

18           depreciation expense is understated. Therefore, we are making an adjustment to reflect

19           this correction.

20

21           As shown on Exhibit__(RS/RT-2), Schedule E-36, applying the correct depreciation rates

22           to the Fort Benning and Fort Gordon solar facilities increases retail electric depreciation

23           expense by $1.186 million for the test year and by $2.033 million for each plant year

24           2023, 2024 and 2025.

20           unprotected EADIT in 2022, and will continue to have amortization of protected EADIT

23   Q.      IS STAFF RECOMMENDING ANY ADJUSTMENT FOR EADIT

24           AMORTIZATION IN THE CURRENT RATE CASE?


                      Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey
                                                   Page 93 of 140

                                                                                         PUBLIC VERSION


1    A.   No. The amortization of the unprotected EADIT through December 2022 is consistent

2         with the treatment provided for in the Commission Order in Docket No. 42516, which

3         provided that the Company would amortize the benefit of unprotected EADIT for the

4         benefit of customers over the three-year period ending December 2022, as further

5         explained in the Company’s response to STF-LA-2-115.

6

 7        The amortization or protected EADIT is subject to certain normalization requirements,

 8        which include utilizing the average rate assumption method (“ARAM”) to amortize the

 9        protected EADIT. The use of the ARAM for protected EADIT results in that being

10        amortized in annual amounts that can differ from year to year in total such that the

11        protected EADIT gets amortized over a period that approximates the remaining useful

12        life of the utility plant to which the protected EADIT is attributable. The Company will

13        continue to be amortizing the protected EADIT using the average rate assumption method

14        which is required by the Internal Revenue Service. Accordingly, the Company has

15        projected protected EADIT amortization of approximately $66 million for the test year

16        and for 2023, and approximately $67 million for 2024 and approximately $69 million for

17        2025, which have been reflected in the Company’s filing as a reduction to income taxes.

18        Because the impacts of the continuing amortization of protected EADIT using the ARAM

19        appears to have been properly and reasonably reflected in the Company’s application,

20        Staff is not recommending any further adjustments related to protected EADIT

21        amortization in the current rate case.

 5                       with and charged by solar generation. The Company believes the 65 MW
 6                       Mossy Branch battery storage project, which is projected to be on-line in
 7                       2023, will qualify for a 30% ITC. The IRA also gives an “opt-out” from the
 8                       existing ITC normalization, which permits the Company to recognize the
 9                       full ITC benefit in the year the project goes into service, thereby providing
10                       a benefit to customers by lowering the levelized cost of electricity over the
11                       life of the project as compared to the cost under the existing ITC
12                       normalization option. In order to take advantage of this “opt out” option
13                       offered in the IRA, the Commission must specifically approve the “opt-out”
14                       option. The Company’s calculation above assumes that the full $31.7
15                       million of estimated credit resulting from the normalization opt-out option
16                       would be recognized in 2025.29
17
18                       Solar Credits: The IRA provides a PTC option, which may be utilized
19                       instead of the existing normalized ITC for solar investments. The Company
20                       estimates the PTC option will provide an approximate $0.4 million of
21                       additional benefits for customers in 2025 on projected self-build ash pond
22                       solar investments compared to the normalized ITC option.

10   Q.   WHAT ARE STAFF'S CONCERNS REGARDING THE COMPANY'S PHFFU?

11   A.   Staff is concerned that the "expected use" dates keep getting pushed off further and

12        further into the future, such that land acquired for future use is sitting in the PHFFU

13        account and being included in rate base to earn a return for investors for extended multi-

14        decade periods in some instances. A large portion of the Company's PHFFU at

15        December 31, 2021 for example has projected use dates of 2030 or beyond, and over

16        60% of the total PHFFU cost is for projects which have "expected use" dates of 2040.

17        Additionally, the PHFFU includes about $22.9 million for a future generating plant site in

18        Stewart County, Georgia; however, the Company has no plans to construct generation

19        there, nor has the Commission approved the construction of a new generating plant at that

20        site. To the extent that the Company does not have firm plans at this time to construct a

21        new generating plant on the Stewart County site within a reasonable planning period,

22        Staff recommends that the Company evaluate whether the costs of that site should be

23        transferred to a non-utility property account.

 4        Overview of Affiliate Charges from Southern Company Services and Southern Nuclear
 5          Operating Company to Georgia Power Company
 6   Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE THE COSTS THAT GEORGIA POWER INCURS

 7           INDIRECTLY THROUGH CHARGES FROM SOUTHERN COMPANY

 8           SERVICES AND SOUTHERN NUCLEAR OPERATING COMPANY.

 9   A.      In addition to the charges that it incurs directly, Georgia Power incurs costs from two

10           affiliated centralized service companies, SCS and SNOC. These two affiliates provide

11           management and technical services to both regulated and non-regulated Southern

12           Company affiliates. These two affiliates charge Georgia Power and the other Southern

13           Company affiliates directly for services provided specifically to each affiliate and then

14           allocate the remaining indirect costs incurred each year to all appropriate affiliates on the

15           basis of various allocation factors.

16

17           The SCS cost and allocation methodologies are detailed in the SCS Cost Control and

18           Accountability Manual (“SCS CAM”), which is revised each year to reflect more recent

19           data and changes in the Southern Company affiliate chart. The Company has designated

20           the SCS CAM as Trade Secret information.

21

22           The SNOC cost and allocation methodologies are detailed in the SNOC Classification of

23           Accounts Manual (“SNOC CAM”), which is also revised each year to reflect more recent

24           data and any other accounting or allocation changes. The Company does not consider the

25           SNOC CAM to be trade secret information.

 1

 2        Southern Company Services Charges to Georgia Power Company
 3   Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE THE SCS COST ALLOCATION METHODOLOGIES.

 4   A.      SCS provides services to numerous Southern Company affiliates pursuant to Service

 5           Agreement contracts entered into between SCS and each of those affiliates, including

 6           Georgia Power. The SCS Service Agreement with Georgia Power states that SCS will

 7           provide to Georgia Power the following services at direct or allocated cost: general and

 8           design engineering, purchasing, accounting and statistical analysis, finance and treasury,

 9           tax, information resources, marketing, auditing, insurance and pension administration,

10           human resources, systems and procedures, and other services with respect to business and

11           operations and power pool operations.

12

13           The costs incurred by SCS are tracked through work orders. Work orders are unique

14           accounts in which the costs for various SCS work activities are collected. The costs then

15           are charged from these work orders to the Southern Company affiliates that use those

16           specific services or cause those costs to be incurred by SCS. For those costs that are not

17           directly charged to the various affiliates for services provided specifically to an affiliate

18           or affiliates, SCS applies an allocation factor to each work order. These factors are used

19           to allocate the SCS work order costs to each affiliate that caused the costs to be incurred.

20           For calendar year 2021, SCS used 21 basic allocation factors to charge costs to the

21           various affiliates. We have attached a description of these allocation factors provided by

22           SCS in its Form 60 public filing with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

23           (“FERC”) as our Exhibit__(RS/RT-21). We do not propose any adjustments for the

24           allocation factors selected and applied by SCS as discussed below.

5    Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE THE SNOC COST ALLOCATION METHODOLOGIES.

7            of the Hatch, Vogtle and Farley nuclear generating facilities in Georgia and Alabama.

 6   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE METHODOLOGY EMPLOYED BY GEORGIA

 7        POWER TO DETERMINE THE COSTS OR PRICES CHARGED TO OTHER

 8        SOUTHERN COMPANY AFFILIATES FOR THE SERVICES IT PROVIDES.

 9   A.   The Company generally charges the cost it incurs to provide the services to the other

10        affiliates, although certain of its service agreement contracts with the other affiliates

11        include a test of that cost against market to guard against subsidization of its non-

12        regulated affiliates. For example, the Company’s service agreement with Southern

13        Power states that: “As compensation for such services or the market value thereof,

14        whichever is higher.”

15

16        Although the methodology for quantifying cost is not defined in the Company’s Service

17        Agreement contracts with the other affiliates, we have reviewed the methodology used by

18        the Company for charges to the other affiliates. The Company determines its “cost” on a

19        comprehensive basis. Cost includes the direct costs to provide the services, including a

20        return of and on all investment costs, and indirect costs, including labor payroll taxes,

21        benefits, and other corporate overheads. The overheads include an allocation of

22        administration and general expenses, which in turn include amounts initially charged to

23        Georgia Power by SCS.

 1          Georgia Power Company Charges to Southern Power
 2   Q.         DID YOU REVIEW THE COMPANY’S PROCEDURES FOR CHARGING

 3              COSTS TO SOUTHERN POWER COMPANY?

 4   A.         Yes. The previous agreement between Georgia Power and Southern Power was

 5              terminated in August 2007, and replaced with a new service contract. Under the service

 6              contract, the Company provides and bills Southern Power for specifically requested

 7              services.

 8

 9              The Georgia Power General Accounting Procedure (“GAP”) 58 describes accounting for

10              work performed by Georgia Power Company on behalf of other companies. The

11              methodology used by Georgia Power to charge Southern Power appears to be

12              comprehensive and includes Georgia Power overheads, both those incurred directly by

13              Georgia Power and those incurred indirectly through charges to Georgia Power from

14              SCS.

16              GAP 58 at pages 1 and 2 states in part that:

17                      Upon request, the Company may provide services to associated companies

11   Q.   DID GEORGIA POWER REMOVE STOCK-BASED COMPENSATION
