16

17   Q.   WHAT WAS THE REASON FOR GEORGIA POWER NOT REMOVING

18        STOCK-BASED COMPENSATION EXPENSE FROM ITS ANNUAL

19        SURVEILLANCE REPORTS IN 2020 AND 2021?

20   A.   The 2019 base rate case settlement in Docket No. 42516 that was approved by the

21        Commission provided for the inclusion of stock-based compensation within retail cost of

22        service under the 3-year alternate plan. However, Staff was not a party to the Company’s

23        2019 rate case settlement, and in fact had recommended the removal of the costs of stock-

24        based compensation from retail cost of service in Docket No. 42516. In its post-hearing

25        brief in Docket No. 42516, Staff stated that the Company incurs the costs of stock-based

26        compensation in an effort to improve Southern Company’s financial performance for the

27        benefit of shareholders rather than for the benefit of ratepayers. Specifically, Staff stated:


                   Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey
                                                Page 121 of 140

                                                                                        PUBLIC VERSION


 1               For instance, the purpose of these incentives is not to improve customer
 2               service or meet other regulated utility service requirements. To the
 3               contrary, the objectives of maximizing shareholder value on the one hand
 4               and minimizing costs to ratepayers on the other hand, are generally opposed
 5               to each other. And the fact that maximizing shareholder value frequently
 6               does not serve the ratepayer interest of lower rates for the service shows the
 7               fatal flaw in the argument that these financial incentives should be seen as
 8               merely part of a compensation package, and as such, should be recovered
 9               from ratepayers.
10

11   Q.   WHAT DOES STAFF RECOMMEND IN THE CURRENT GEORGIA POWER

12        RATE CASE?

13   A.   As is explained below, Staff recommends that the PSU expense and the RSU expense be

14        removed from retail jurisdictional operating expenses for purposes of establishing the

15        Company's revenue requirement in the current rate case. As a matter of regulatory

16        principle, ratepayers should not be required to pay executive or management

17        compensation that is based on the performance of Southern Company’s stock price, or

18        which has the primary purpose of benefitting shareholders and/or to align the interests of

19        participants in the stock-based compensation plans with those of such shareholders.

20

21   Q.   SHOULD THE COMMISSION INCLUDE THE PSU AND RSU EXPENSE IN

22        THE REVENUE REQUIREMENT?

23   A.   No. The stock-based incentive compensation expenses for these programs should not be

24        included in the revenue requirement. The cost of these incentive compensation programs

25        is incurred to improve the Southern Company financial performance for the benefit of

26        shareholders, not to improve customer service or meet other regulated utility service

27        requirements. In fact, the objectives of maximizing shareholder value on the one hand

28        and minimizing costs to ratepayers on the other hand, are generally opposed to each

                  Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey
                                               Page 122 of 140

                                                                                         PUBLIC VERSION


 1        other. In addition, the hypothetical stock performance pursuant to the PSU should not be

 2        considered expense for ratemaking purposes because dividends are considered in the

 3        determination of the required return on common equity and stock performance is a

 4        component of shareholder return.

 5

 6   Q.   HAVE YOU QUANTIFIED THE EFFECT OF YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS

 7        TO DISALLOW THE STOCK-BASED INCENTIVE COMPENSATION

 8        EXPENSE FOR THE PSU AND RSU?

 9   A.   Yes. The effect is to reduce Georgia Power’s forecasted test year retail operating

10        expenses by $29.172 million. This quantification includes the costs directly incurred by

11        the Company of $10.922 million and the affiliate charges of $13.033million from SCS

12        and $5.217 million from SNOC for these stock-based compensation programs. The

13        quantifications and the source of the data that we relied on for these quantifications are

14        detailed on Exhibit__(RS/RT-2), Schedule E-4.

15

16        In addition, as it relates to the Company’s alternative rate plan, the effect of removing the

17        expense for the PSU and RSU is to reduce retail operating expenses by $29.063 million,

18        $26.933 million, and $28.230 million for calendar years 2023, 2024 and 2025,

19        respectively. Of these amounts, $10.666 million, $9.641 million and $10.251 million

20        reflect costs directly incurred by Georgia Power. Likewise, $13.096 million, $12.206

21        million and $12.553 million reflect affiliate charges from SCS and $5.301 million, $5.085

22        million and $5.425 million reflect affiliate charges from SNOC.

1                   XIII. RATE PLAN PRINCIPLES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
2         Multi-Year Rate Plans Versus Traditional Test Year Based Ratemaking
3    Q.      HOW IS AN ALTERNATIVE RATE PLAN DIFFERENT FROM A

4            TRADITIONAL RATE CASE ORDER IN TERMS OF EARNINGS ABOVE THE

5            ROE BAND?

6    A.      Under a traditional rate case order, the Company could earn in excess of an authorized

7            ROE without the ratepayers receiving any rate reductions or any benefit from the

8            application of earnings above the top of the rate band. While the Commission would have

 9           the authority to bring the Company in under a Rule Nisi proceeding to reduce its rates,

10           such a proceeding would take a significant amount of time and any order reducing rates

11           would be prospective in nature.

12

13   Q.      HOW IS THE ALTERNATIVE RATE PLAN DIFFERENT FROM A

14           TRADITIONAL RATE CASE ORDER IN TERMS OF EARNINGS BELOW THE

15           AUTHORIZED ROE OR LOWER ROE BAND?

16   A.      Under a traditional rate case order, the Company could earn less than the authorized ROE

17           and would not have any recourse except to file a rate case. Any relief would be

18           prospective in nature.

19

20   Q.      HOW DOES TRADITIONAL RATEMAKING COMPARE WITH A MULTI-

21           YEAR RATE PLAN IN TERMS OF WHEN THE COMPANY FILES RATE

22           CASES?

23   A.      Under a traditional rate case order, the Company would be able to file another rate case

24           whenever it deemed appropriate, and the Commission would have the ability to bring

                      Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey
                                                   Page 127 of 140

                                                                                         PUBLIC VERSION


 1        Georgia Power in for a Rule Nisi to address any overearnings. Some such costs, such as

 2        projected increased costs for 2024 and 2025, did not fall within the test year period for

 3        this docket, and those costs could have fallen within the test year period of a subsequent

 4        rate case filing.

 5

 6   Q.   HOW CAN A MULTI-YEAR RATE PLAN PROVIDE FOR RATE STABILITY?

 7   A.   The accounting order/rate plan can provide ratepayers with rate stability and certain

 8        benefits depending on how it is structured. Unless the Company’s earnings are projected

 9        to drop below the bottom of the earnings band, the Staff proposed alternative rate plan for

10        the current case (similar to previous rate plans) would prohibit Georgia Power from filing

11        for a rate increase until a date provided for in the rate plan. However, the Company

12        would have the option to petition the Commission to increase rates up to lower band if its

13        projected earnings would fall below the lower band. Also, the plan may include step

14        increases which increase rates rather than stabilizing rates. While there are certain

15        advantages in step increases there are tradeoffs including only considering certain cost

16        that are increasing rather than all cost which may include some cost that are decreasing.

17        If a three-year rate plan were to be approved, the Company would be prohibited from

18        increasing rates (other than the two step increases) prior to January 1, 2026, unless it

19        were projected to earn below the bottom end of the allowed earnings band.

20

21   Q.   IS HAVING A THREE-YEAR RATE PLAN A BENEFIT TO THE COMPANY?

22   A.   Yes. Having a rate plan that is approved by the Commission and agreed to by the

23        Company benefits the Company. One benefit is that the first-year revenue requirement


                   Docket No. 44280 Direct Testimony of Ralph C. Smith and Robert L. Trokey
                                                Page 128 of 140

                                                                                                       PUBLIC VERSION


 1               could be based on calendar year 2023, rather than upon the statutory test year ending July

 2               31, 2023. The Company’s filing shows a traditional base rate revenue deficiency of

 3               approximately $312.2 million based on the July 31, 2023 test year,34 and a base rate

 4               revenue deficiency of approximately $431.4 million35 for calendar year 2023 as well as

5                revenue deficiencies of $718.0 million and $1.080 billion for 2024 and 2025. 36 Thus, the

6                time shifting of the revenue requirement basis for the first year of new rates has a

 7               monetary benefit to the Company.37

 8

 1   Q.      WHAT ARE THE REASONS FOR RECOMMENDING A STEP INCREASE

 2           APPROACH, RATHER THAN A LEVELIZED APPROACH TO THE THREE-

 3           YEAR RATE PLAN?

 4   A.      First, customers should not be required to pay for 2024 and 2025 revenue requirements

 5           starting January 1, 2023, i.e., before the related costs have been incurred, especially

 6           during a period when the economy could be entering into a recession. Also, the

 7           Company has projected that Plant Vogtle Unit 3 will be in commercial operation by

 8           March 2023 and Unit 4 by December 2023. Currently, the Company is collecting from

 9           ratepayers portions of the financing cost for those units while they are under construction.

10           The Company continues to incur construction costs and AFUDC. While those dates

11           might be delayed, the Vogtle Unit 3 and 4 rate impacts, once more fully recognized, are

12           anticipated to be substantial.40

13

14           Furthermore, Staff has concerns about some of the large items in the 2024 and 2025

15           revenue requirements. Under a levelized approach, ratepayers would incur the costs

16           related to these items beginning January 1, 2023. These items include recognition of cost

17           increases that are occurring in 2024 and 2025 beyond levels projected for 2023. These

18           concerns, coupled with the uncertainties about the timing of cost incurrence, warrant a

19           cautious approach to determining appropriate revenue requirements for the Company for

20           the 2024 and 2025 plan years.

 1        plan Staff recommends a band of 8.45% to 10.45% which would allow the Company to

 3

 4   Q.   HOW DOES STAFF RECOMMEND THAT EARNINGS ABOVE THE TOP END

 5        OF THE BAND BE APPLIED?

 6   A.   As noted above, Staff proposes an ROE band of 8.45% to 10.45% above which is 100

 7        basis points below and above the 9.45% ROE recommended by Staff witness Gorman.

 8        Any earnings above the band should be used to pay down Georgia Power’s regulatory

 9        assets. This band is symmetrical in terms thresholds unlike the previous band of 9.5% to

10        12.0% with a set point of 10.5%. This band strikes a more equitable balance between the

11        ratepayers and the Company. The consequences of breaching the band under Staff’s

12        proposal would also be more equitable. The lower band effectively places a floor

13        underneath the Company’s earnings – guaranteeing the Company a minimum return. It is

14        only fair that all earnings that exceed the upper band be retained to the benefit of

15        customers.

INTRODUCTIONS AND PREVIEW

Q.MR. ALVAREZ, PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.
A.My name is Paul J. Alvarez.  My business address is Wired Group, P.O. Box 620756, Littleton, Colorado 80162.

Q.WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION?
A.I lead the Wired Group, a small consultancy specializing in distribution utility planning, investment, regulation, and performance.

Q.HAVE YOU PROVIDED AN EXHIBIT SUMMARIZING YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND AND PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE?
A.Yes.  It is presented in Exhibit PA/DS-1. This exhibit summarizes my educational background, professional experience, and appearances before state utility regulators.

Q.MR. STEPHENS, PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.
A.My name is Dennis Stephens. My business address is 1153 Bergen Parkway, Suite 130, Evergreen, CO 80439.

Q.WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION?
A.I am an independent consultant specializing in utility distribution planning, investment, operations, asset management, reliability, and safety. I frequently work for the Wired Group in support of the firm’s clients. 

Q.HAVE YOU PROVIDED AN EXHIBIT SUMMARIZING YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND AND PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE?
A.Yes. It is presented in Exhibit PA/DS-2. This exhibit summarizes my educational background, professional experience, and appearances before state utility regulators.

Q.ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU APPEARING?
A.We are testifying in the public interest on behalf of the Georgia Public Service Commission Public Interest Advocacy Staff (Staff).  

Q.WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?
A.The purpose of our testimony is to provide recommendations for Commission consideration regarding Georgia Power Company’s (Georgia Power or Company) proposed continuation of the Grid Investment Plan (GIP). With the exception of transmission lines, we have completed detailed reviews of, and discovery into, all aspects of the GIP.  (Transmission lines are addressed in the testimony of Staff Witness Mr. Raj Rana, though many of the themes of our testimony are repeated in Mr. Rana’s testimony, and many observations made by Mr. Rana are relevant to the portions of the GIP we examined.)  

Q.PLEASE PREVIEW YOUR TESTIMONY
A.Our testimony begins in Section II with context regarding transmission and distribution investments related to reliability improvements, as well as perspectives on the associated timing and rate increases. (The Company claims the GIP is needed to maintain and improve service reliability.)  Later, our testimony presents analyses indicating that the largest components of GIP spending will not deliver reliability improvements sufficient to outweigh costs.  But in this Section we observe 1) that electric rates are already poised to rise substantially in Georgia over the next few years; 2) that there is no pending reliability emergency or customer demand for the reliability improvements Georgia Power proposes to pursue; and 3) that the results of various GIP investments to date will not be known for at least a few more years.  These observations strongly suggest a need to complete formal and rigorous (independent) study of the results of Georgia Power’s GIP spending so far before more such spending is authorized. 

In Section III, we explain why the GIP investments the Company plans for its transmission grid will not deliver reliability benefits of sufficient value to outweigh associated rate increases. Proposed at $1.0 billion from 2023-2025, and representing a 278% increase over annual transmission spending in years prior to the GIP, the transmission investment plan (TIP) benefits shareholders far more than it will customers or Georgia’s economy. Specifically, we challenge the Company’s practice, new to the GIP, of replacing substation (and transmission line) equipment that has passed periodic, objective tests and inspections that all utilities, including Georgia Power, conduct routinely. The practice, which we call premature equipment replacement, relies on the estimated useful lives – typically employed only to inform accounting depreciation periods -- rather than objective test and inspection results, to determine when equipment should be replaced. We will explain why premature equipment replacement is inappropriate, and recommend all proposed investments from this practice be rejected. We favor the objective approaches Georgia Power has successfully employed in the past, and continues to employ in this rate case, to identify equipment for replacement.   

In Section IV, we explain why some distribution investment packages in the Company’s GIP will not deliver reliability benefits of sufficient value to outweigh associated rate increases. Proposed at $1.3 billion from 2023-2025, and part of a total distribution capital spending request amounting to a 131% increase (more than double) over annual distribution spending prior to the GIP (2009-2019), the distribution investment plan (DIP) is rendered cost-ineffective by circuit hardening and undergrounding investment packages. Not only are these packages cost-ineffective due to their extremely high cost per premise, the DIP ignores vastly less expensive practices almost all utilities employ to improve reliability, namely, more aggressive vegetation management and a more formal worst-performing circuit program. In this section we will also describe multiple flaws with the Optimization Model the Company uses to select circuits to treat and investment packages to deploy, and which the Company uses to justify its distribution investment plan. Finally, we summarize what the Maryland Commission has done to cost-effectively improve reliability, and recommend that proposed spending on circuit hardening and undergrounding be eliminated while preserving a 55% increase in overall distribution capital spending over the average levels prior to the GIP.     

In Section V, we address the Company’s plan to invest $100 million in a distributed energy resource management system, or DERMS. The level of distributed energy resources needed to justify such a system is high, and will not be reached by the time the proposed DERMS is fully depreciated in 2030, let alone by the end of the upcoming rate planning period in 2025. Further, Georgia Power already maintains systems and processes to manage distributed energy resources. We recommend this proposed spending be postponed until a future rate case, when the level of distributed energy resources on Georgia Power’s grid provides sufficient justification for such a system.  

Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE SPENDING ADJUSTMENTS RECOMMENDED IN YOUR TESTIMONY
A.Table 1 below summarizes our recommended spending and cost recovery adjustments. These adjustments are translated into revenue requirement reductions in the testimony and exhibits of Staff Witnesses Mr. Ralph Smith and Mr. Robert Trokey (Smith-Trokey). It should be noted that the annual amount of transmission and distribution capital investment Staff does not recommend be rejected is still double the annual average for 2009 – 2021. This large increase that still remains is in contrast to the much smaller growth in number of customers, energy sales (MWhs), and peak demand (MW).

We did not include all responses to data requests cited in our testimony, as these are collectively, and in many cases individually, too voluminous to include as exhibits. For these data request responses, we trust the administrative record will serve as an accurate and accessible repository.


TRANSMISSION AND DISTRIBUTION RATE INCREASES ARE BAD FOR GEORGIA’S BUSINESSES, CONSUMERS, AND ECONOMY UNLESS ACCOMPANIED BY RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENT VALUE SUFFICIENT TO OUTWEIGH THEM

Q.PLEASE PREVIEW THIS SECTION OF TESTIMONY.
A.This section of testimony will begin with a review of Georgia Power’s Grid Investment Plan (GIP). It will provide context on transmission and distribution (T&D) rate increases for reliability improvements generally; present Georgia Power’s recent reliability performance in the context of its peers; discuss the lack of customer demand for, or willingness to pay for, better reliability; present imminent rate increases heading toward Georgia’s economy outside of the Company’s or the Commission’s control; and note that the results of over a billion dollars in GIP spending to date are not yet known.  All of these call the timing of continued GIP spending in the upcoming rate case period into question. 

Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE GEORGIA POWER’S GRID INVESTMENT PLAN.
A.In its 2019 rate case Georgia Power proposed a $7.5 billion Grid Investment Plan (GIP) to be completed over eleven years, from 2020 to 2031. The GIP consisted of $2.6 billion in transmission grid reliability investments (the Transmission Investment Plan, or TIP) and $4.9 billion in distribution grid reliability investments (the Distribution Investment Plan, or DIP). The GIP, combined with requested increases in more typical T&D capital spending, delivers extreme increases in T&D investments relative to historic investment levels. Figure 1 below indicates that the Company’s proposed T&D capital spending 2023-2025 is almost three times (296%) the historical levels of investment before the GIP. Even without the GIP, proposed T&D capital spending increase is almost two times (197%) the historical levels of investment before 2020. 
Figure 1: Total T&D Capital Spending Actual ’09-‘21/Projected ‘22/Requested ’23-’25.


Q.WHAT BENEFITS DID GEORGIA POWER PROJECT FROM THE GIP IN 2019 RATE CASE DOCKET 42516?
A.Georgia Power projected no reliability improvements at all from the TIP, and states that the TIP is designed only to maintain current transmission reliability levels. At the time the DIP was initially proposed, Georgia Power projected the DIP would deliver a 50% reduction in system average interruption duration (SAIDI), from approximately 130 minutes on average at the time to 65 minutes on average by 2031. The Commission approved the Company’s proposed GIP spending. By the end of this year, the Company anticipates completing $00.0 billion in TIP investments and $00.0 billion in DIP investments. 

Q.IS GEORGIA POWER PROPOSING TO CONTINUE GIP SPENDING IN THIS RATE CASE?
A.Yes, the Company proposes to continue its GIP in the amount of $2.3 billion from 2023 to 2025, including $1.0 billion in TIP spending and $1.3 billion in DIP spending. The Company is making some adjustments to the DIP from its initial 2019 proposal.  Based on the Company’s experience implementing the DIP 2020-2022, it is discontinuing some spending programs.  The total DIP capital requirement has thus fallen from $4.9 billion originally to about $4.6 billion in the current DIP, a reduction of 7.7%. It has also reduced expectations for DIP-related reliability improvements. Originally projected at a system SAIDI of 65 minutes by 2031, the revised system SAIDI target is 80 minutes by 2031, a 23.1% deterioration. This significant revision in target system SAIDI after only three years calls into question the Company’s projection of the actual performance improvement customers will receive for very large capital investment made by Georgia Power. The TIP appears to be unmodified from its original proposal.  

Q.DO GEORGIA POWER’S RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENT ESTIMATES AND CHANGES CAUSE YOU CONCERN?
A.Yes. We are concerned that the Company attributes no reliability improvements at all to its TIP spending.  But our biggest concern relates to the lack of performance accountability, a subject we will return to in Section IV, which is dedicated to the DIP. 
We also note the 23.1% deterioration in the SAIDI target from the 2020-2022 DIP to the current DIP. Such a significant change in just three years is consistent with our experience that reliability improvements from increased grid investment are not a given, and that reliability-related investment performance varies dramatically from utility to utility, and among various types of spending packages. As indicated in Figure 2, reliability performance by U.S. Investor-Owned Utilities (IOUs) over the last ten years has not improved, and in fact has deteriorated, despite dramatic increases in grid investment per customer. The lack of correlation between grid investment and grid performance has also been noted by other researchers. 
Figure 2: U.S. investor-owned utility reliability performance relative to distribution investment, 2013-2020.


Q.HOW DOES GEORGIA POWER’S RELIABILITY PERFORMANCE COMPARE WITH OTHER INVESTOR-OWNED UTILITIES?
A.As indicated in Figure 3, Georgia Power service interruption duration and frequency are about average for U.S. IOU peers over the last 5 years. There does not appear to be any grid reliability emergency at Georgia Power that must be addressed immediately, or that would justify the massive increase in the transmission and distribution capital investment proposed by the Company. 
Figure 3: 5-Year Reliability Performance Averages, Georgia Power vs. US IOUs


Q.WHAT ABOUT CUSTOMER DEMANDS? ARE CUSTOMERS DEMANDING RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENTS FROM GEORGIA POWER?
A.No. With but one exception, customer satisfaction surveys filed by the Company with the Commission in 2019, 2020, and 2021 indicate that both residential and business customers rate their satisfaction with Georgia Power reliability higher than they rate their satisfaction with Georgia Power overall.  (The lone exception is the residential customer class in 2021; this cohort reported reliability satisfaction slightly lower than overall satisfaction.)  Further, the Company’s most recent “willingness to pay” research on reliability indicates that customers in all classes are willing to pay less than a 1.7% rate increase on average for significant (50%) improvements in reliability.  We estimate that the revenue requirement increase for the $7.5 billion GIP at the time Georgia Power first presented it in 2019 will be 10%, or almost six times greater than what customers reported they were willing to spend, and for a reliability improvement which is projected to be much less than the 50% customers indicated they would be willing to pay a 1.7% rate increase to secure.      

Q.YOU MENTIONED THAT RATE INCREASES FOR REASONS OTHER THAN THE GIP ARE IMMINENT. WHAT ARE THE SOURCES OF THESE RATE INCREASES AND HOW LARGE WILL THEY BE?
A.Multiple sources of large electric rate increases will be hitting Georgia businesses and consumers simultaneously in the next few years. We believe the Commission should consider the impact of these rate increases on Georgia’s economy as it reviews Georgia Power’s request to continue GIP spending. At least two sources of significant rate increases are imminent beyond the Company’s request in this rate case, including 1) The full impact of Plant Vogtle has yet to hit rates; and 2) higher fuel rates to recover higher fuel cost and unpaid fuel balance.  Staff estimates the combined impact of these factors with the rate increase Georgia Power requests in this rate case to be in excess of 40%.

Q.WHAT IS THE RELEVANCE OF THESE RATE INCREASE PRESSURES?
A.These rate increase pressures are relevant because some of them, particularly fuel, are outside of the Commission’s control. When likely rate increases outside the Commission’s control are clearly apparent, it becomes more critical to scrutinize closely capital investment and expenses that are discretionary. GIP spending is clearly a source of rate increase under the Commission’s control. Given that there is no reliability emergency, and that customer demand for, and willingness to pay for, reliability improvements is almost zero, we consider GIP capital spending to be discretionary. Further, the results of GIP spending to date are not yet known, and our analysis of the two largest DIP programs, circuit hardening and undergrounding, indicate that rate increases exceed benefits by a wide margin. We note that other researchers examining circuit hardening and undergrounding come to the same conclusions, and we will provide details in Section IV. 

Rate increases negatively impact Georgia’s businesses and economy. Research indicates that employment falls as energy costs rise. We consider rate increases to be a precious resource; a tool to be drawn upon only when necessary. Accommodating all types of Georgia Power spending requests simultaneously leaves less gas in the Georgia economy’s tank for unexpected emergencies outside of Commission or Georgia Power control (like rising costs for capital or natural gas).   

Q.YOU MENTIONED THAT THE RESULTS OF GIP SPENDING TO DATE ARE NOT YET KNOWN. PLEASE EXPLAIN.
A.  All we have so far are the Company’s projected reliability improvements from DIP spending “packages”. As noted above, Georgia Power provides no projected reliability improvements from TIP spending; there is little evidence that increasing grid investment delivers improved grid performance nationally; and we have significant concerns regarding DIP performance improvement accountability. Further, circuit-specific reliability is inherently variable year-to-year, with weather being the largest of many sources of variation. Finally, despite the massive amount of money spent to date, the numbers of circuits rebuilt (hardened) to date, and the number of customers undergrounded to date, are extremely small. Further, and significantly, vegetation management the Company completed on circuits that were hardened or partially undergrounded makes it impossible to isolate the level of improvement secured by new investment from the level of improvement secured by vegetation management, a dramatically lower-cost option. (We will return to these subjects in Section IV.) In short, it is impossible to reach any conclusions regarding the reliability improvements if any from Georgia Power’s DIP spending so far.

We recommend a minimum of three years’ post-deployment experience be used to determine actual reliability improvement delivered relative to cost for each of the Company’s reliability improvement initiatives, including premature transmission equipment replacement (more on that in the transmission section of this testimony) and each of the distribution investment plan “packages”.  Further, controls for various performance impacts are needed. For example, vegetation management is typically conducted on circuits as they are rebuilt (circuit hardening in the Company’s parlance); we ask, to what degree was any performance improvement the result of vegetation management and not circuit hardening? All of this increases the need to complete formal and rigorous (independent) study of the results of Georgia Power’s GIP spending so far before more such spending is authorized. Given the lack of a reliability emergency, and the impending perfect storm of rate increases, the prudent thing to do now is to measure results to date before doubling down on the GIP. 

Q.YOU SEEM TO BE QUESTIONING GEORGIA POWER’S INTEREST IN IMPROVING RELIABILITY. WHY WOULDN’T GEORGIA POWER WANT TO IMPROVE SERVICE RELIABILITY?
A.We are not questioning Georgia Power’s interest in improving reliability. Certainly, Georgia Power wants to provide reliable service to its customers. What we do question are the Company’s methods. As the Commission is well-aware, the Company has a fiduciary responsibility to uphold and advance shareholder interests. Shareholder interests are advanced when share prices grow. Share prices grow when earnings grow, and earnings grow when the rate base grows (all else being equal). Thus, as illustrated by the Company’s GIP, capital bias looms large in IOU reliability improvement initiatives. Any utility can spend billions on its grid and improve reliability. The goal should be to improve reliability to as great an extent possible for the least possible cost to customers. As the rest of this testimony will indicate, Georgia Power’s GIP is not only intended to improve reliability; it is intended to improve reliability while massively and unnecessarily growing the rate base.

Further, we are concerned that advance approval of the GIP virtually eliminates the risk of penalties (cost disallowances) associated with excess grid investment. Before multi-year rate plans, Georgia Power would make the grid investments it considered necessary for safe and reliable service, and bore the responsibility for proving that its spending was prudent after the fact. The cost-disallowance risk presented a potential price shareholders might pay if the Company over-invested. However, if a grid investment plan is approved with unnecessary investments, the potential penalty for overspending is significantly lessened, as the regulator is unlikely to reverse a previous decision. This creates a moral hazard situation in which there is little to discourage a utility from proposing extreme or even cost-ineffective investments.  (In 1996 this Commission was only the second state utility regulator in the U.S., after the California Public Utilities Commission, to authorize the use of multi-year rate plans in ratemaking.) It is certainly plausible that Georgia Power considered capital bias and moral hazard as it developed its GIP. 
THE TRANSMISSION INVESTMENT PLAN (TIP) WILL NOT DELIVER RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENTS SUFFICIENT TO OUTWEIGH ASSOCIATED RATE INCREASES 

Q.PLEASE PREVIEW THIS SECTION OF TESTIMONY.
A.This section of testimony examines Georgia Power’s $2.6 billion Transmission Investment Plan (TIP) over the period 2020 -2031. The Company describes its TIP as the replacement of aging transmission infrastructure, which laypersons are likely to perceive as reasonable and necessary. However experts like Mr. Stephens, who have held the responsibility for maximizing reliability performance for the least amount of capital spending at a utility, would not describe the replacement of transmission assets based primarily on age as a cost-effective way to improve reliability, nor would such experts describe replacements based primarily on age as reasonable or necessary. We will describe why the practice of replacing transmission assets based primarily on age, which we call premature equipment replacement, is vastly more costly for customers than the value of the tiny reliability improvements it will deliver to customers, and why premature equipment replacement is both unreasonable and unnecessary. 

Q.WHAT IS PREMATURE EQUIPMENT REPLACEMENT?
A.Georgia Power defines aging transmission assets as those that have exceeded their “expected life”. The Company’s TIP selects transmission line and T&D substation equipment for replacement based on asset age relative to expected life. It is inappropriate to use expected life and asset age as the basis for transmission line and T&D substation equipment replacement. The actual operating condition of T&D equipment as measured by periodic, objective testing and inspection programs should be the primary drivers of replacement, not age.
   
Q.WHY IS IT INAPPROPRIATE TO USE THE AGE OF A PIECE OF EQUIPMENT, RELATIVE TO THE EXPECTED LIFE FOR EQUIPMENT OF THAT TYPE, AS THE BASIS FOR REPLACING THAT PIECE OF EQUIPMENT?
A.As the reader might imagine, there is significant variation between any individual piece of equipment’s actual age at failure and the expected life for that type on average. If the expected life for a particular equipment type is 40 years on average, it means a few units of that type are likely to fail immediately, a few units of that type will likely still be operating safely and reliably after 80 years, and all the other units of that type will fail at some age between zero years and 80 years. For illustrative purposes, a representative chart depicting failure rates for a hypothetical equipment type with an expected life of 40 years is presented in Figure 4 below. Most units of a particular equipment type will either fail very early in their lives (“infant mortality”, due to manufacturing defects, design errors, or unobserved damage caused during installation, as examples) or very late in their lives. This failure rate characteristic gives a failure rate chart a “bathtub curve” shape (because it resembles the cross-section of a bathtub). Hearing attendees may recall Georgia Power Witness Mr. Robinson mentioning the bathtub curve.

Figure 4: Illustrative "Bathtub" Curve for a hypothetical equipment type with an average expected or estimated life of 40 years.

The illustrative bathtub failure rate curve can be plotted by percent of units of a particular equipment type in service by age, as depicted in Figure 5 below. As Figure 5 indicates, replacing a piece of equipment simply because it has reached its expected useful life is inappropriate because it deprives customers of decades of useful life from transmission equipment that has passed its tests or inspections, that has therefore been deemed capable of providing safe and reliable service, and for which customers have already paid in rates. Premature equipment replacement thus increases rate base by “churning” assets unnecessarily, a practice which violates established regulatory precedent. Investor-owned utilities are motivated to replace assets once they are fully depreciated, as fully depreciated assets have no book value and earn no rate of return.
Figure 5: Application of illustrative Bathtub failure rate curve to percent of units in use by age.


Q.DOES PREMATURE REPLACEMENT IMPROVE RELIABILITY?
A.By the tiniest of amounts, yes, but almost imperceptibly. The degree of improvement is certainly not enough to justify the massive cost increases premature equipment replacements incur, for two reasons. First, all utilities, including Georgia Power, perform objective tests and inspections of transmission lines and critical T&D substation equipment on a routine, periodic basis. Any equipment which does not pass its tests or inspections is scheduled for repair or replacement, typically within a few months or a year. These objective tests are much more accurate predictors of equipment failure than age, which is precisely why utilities, including Georgia Power, have been using them for decades. Second, transmission systems are designed and operated based on the “N-1” criterion, explained in detail below. As a result of the N-1 criterion, in the already rare instance of a transmission line or T&D substation equipment failure, it is extremely unlikely such a failure will cause a service interruption for customers. Objective testing and inspection practices combined with the inherent redundancy in the transmission grid results in excellent transmission system reliability without premature equipment replacement. The opportunity to improve transmission line and T&D substation reliability through premature equipment replacement is therefore almost zero to begin with, as will be demonstrated with the Company’s own data later in this Section. 

Q.PLEASE DESCRIBE THESE OBJECTIVE TESTS AND INSPECTIONS.
A.Unlike distribution circuit equipment, for which any one asset may only serve a handful of customers, transmission lines and T&D substations can serve thousands of customers. The increased consequences of failure for transmission line and T&D substation equipment have motivated utilities to establish comprehensive testing and inspection programs for various pieces of equipment and lines. For example, utilities test T&D substation power transformers every three years or so through “dissolved gas analysis”, or DGA. Increases in certain types of gasses in transformer oil indicate deterioration that should be monitored closely and addressed. Utilities thus use DGA test results to indicate when a substation power transformer needs to be replaced. Construction planning to replace a power transformer that fails its DGA tests typically begins immediately and is scheduled and completed on a reasonably prompt basis. With an objective test like DGA available, there is no need to replace assets prematurely based on age relative to an estimated or expected useful life.

Similarly, T&D substation circuit breakers, switches, relays, and load tap changers are the subject of routine, periodic (typically every three to five years) functional testing programs at all utilities. In these programs, devices are taken out of service (power is temporarily rerouted to nearby equipment during testing) and forced to operate under simulated severe disturbance scenarios. Equipment that does not respond in an expected manner within parameters specified by the manufacturer are scheduled for prompt repair or replacement. Transmission lines, equipment, and towers are the subject of formal inspections conducted periodically, complete with checklists and objective scoring mechanisms. Conductor, equipment, or towers that fail inspections are immediately scheduled for repairs or replacements in a controlled manner. Further, there is nothing prohibiting Georgia Power from increasing the frequency of testing and inspections for older equipment if it chooses. 

To summarize, transmission line and substation equipment testing and inspection programs make the likelihood of equipment failures in service extremely rare.  Moreover, the practice of prematurely replacing equipment based on age means that Georgia Power is replacing equipment that has passed its most recent tests and inspections, and was therefore operating safely and reliably at the time it was replaced. On this measure alone, premature equipment replacement is unreasonable and unnecessary, and a strong case could be made that the practice is imprudent. Furthermore, utilities maintain spare stocks of critical substation equipment, as well as power line structures and conductors, which helps to reduce repair/replacement time. 
          
Q.PLEASE EXPLAIN N-1 CRITERION AND ASSOCIATED REDUNDANCY
A.Electric utilities are required to plan and operate their power systems using the N-1 criterion to comply with the NERC reliability standards. This means that the power system will operate safely and reliably following an outage of a single critical facility without causing thermal overloads or voltage problems on the facilities that remain in service. This also means that there is inherent redundancy in the system available to accommodate failures of critical network elements and equipment with no service interruptions for customers. Furthermore, the power system can operate reliably even with two network elements out due to options available to system operators such as temporary generation redispatch or network reconfiguration. Known as N-1-1 criteria, these additional options means that the power system can operate reliably in the event a critical network element fails and is followed by a second critical element failure. Once repairs/replacements are completed, the system is restored to a normal state of operation. Such built-in redundancy further reduces the likelihood that an equipment failure – already made rare through equipment testing and inspection practices – results in a service interruption for customers or causes any reliability problems. 

Based on transmission outage and equipment failure data provided by the Company in discovery from 2012 to 2021 (10 years), we have calculated the likelihood that various types of T&D substation equipment will both fail in service and result in a service interruption for customers. Further, we have applied the cost of premature equipment replacements to these likelihoods, arriving at the system-wide investment required to avoid one service interruption per year over the expected life of the new equipment by equipment type. Table 2 presents these results of these calculations, and is an accurate representation of the size (tiny) of the reliability improvement opportunity available from premature equipment replacement, as well as its extremely high cost. (See Exhibit PA/DS-6 for more calculation details.) As Table 2 indicates, the opportunity to improve reliability through premature equipment replacement is incredibly small to begin with, and certainly not worth the $2.6 billion cost of the Transmission Investment Plan. (Staff Witness Mr. Rana completes a similar analysis for premature Transmission Line replacements.)

Q.BUT WHAT ABOUT INCREMENTAL REPLACEMENT COSTS? GEORGIA POWER CLAIMS THAT EMERGENCY REPLACEMENT COSTS ARE TWO TO THIRTEEN TIMES HIGHER THAN PLANNED REPLACEMENT COSTS.
A.It is true that the costs to replace equipment in an emergency are higher than planned equipment replacements. But in our experience, replacements of equipment identified through equipment testing and inspection practices are planned, and do not constitute emergencies. These planned replacements are typically completed within reasonable timeframes of six to eighteen months, and do not incur incremental costs. Only replacements of equipment that fails in service and causes a service interruption constitute replacements so emergent as to incur such large incremental cost multiples. As Table 2 Column B indicates, such failures are incredibly rare. Thus while some amount of incremental emergency replacement cost can be avoided through premature replacement, the infrequency of emergency replacements makes these incremental replacement costs  very low relative to the extreme incremental cost of premature replacement.  

As an example, the rate of failure resulting in a service outage for substation circuit breakers is about five in one thousand per year, and Georgia Power reports having 1,868 circuit breakers. Thus, in an average year, about nine circuit breakers will need to be replaced on an emergency basis across the Company’s entire system. The incremental emergency replacement cost associated with replacing nine circuit breakers annually, even when combined with the reliability benefits of avoiding nine outages annually for 219 customers each outage, simply does not justify the $0.0 billion capital cost of prematurely replacing 1,868 circuit breakers before a test indicates such replacements are necessary.   
    
Further, like most large utilities, Georgia Power maintains an inventory of T&D substation equipment of various types and sizes, and this significantly reduces the cost of emergency replacement in many instances. The Edison Electric Institute, of which Georgia Power is a member, also maintains and/or participates in multiple T&D substation and transmission equipment access programs to reduce transmission and substation equipment procurement times and costs, including the Spare Transformer Equipment Program, SpareConnect, Grid Assurance, and RESTORE.

Q.HOW DO YOU KNOW THAT PREMATURE REPLACEMENT OF TRANSMISSION LINE AND T&D SUBSTATION EQUIPMENT DOES NOT DELIVER BENEFITS TO CUSTOMERS IN EXCESS OF COSTS TO CUSTOMERS?
A.Georgia Power bears the burden to prove that premature equipment replacement is cost-effective for customers. Georgia Power has not prepared any cost-benefit analyses of its TIP, or its premature equipment replacement program, or its distribution investment plan packages (a subject to which we will return in Section IV). Indeed, Georgia Power Witness Mr. Robinson claimed that it is not possible to complete such cost-benefit analyses. We do not agree, and Table 2 indicates the extreme costs of premature replacement relative to benefits, as informed by historical outage data. Further, neither we nor Georgia Power are aware of any industry studies or research indicating that premature equipment replacement is cost-effective. Furthermore, there is no industry standard that transmission equipment should be replaced when it reaches its expected useful life, nor any industry standards for the expected useful lives (in years) of various types of transmission equipment.,  

Q.HOW DO YOUR RESPOND TO MR. ROBINSON’S TESTIMONY THAT GEORGIA POWER WOULD NOT WAIT FOR EQUIPMENT FAILURE?
A.Mr. Robinson stated that “We don't want to be the utility to wait to failure. We have seen what happens across the United States when companies wait to failure, whether it is transmission lines or substation assets.”  “Waiting for failure,” is not an accurate description of Georgia Power’s historical approach to transmission reliability. Georgia Power has never simply waited for assets to fail. Through its equipment testing and inspections programs, Georgia Power has historically followed, and continues to follow, utility best practices for identifying equipment in need of repair or replacement in advance of failure. Through redundant design, Georgia Power has historically followed, and continues to follow, utility best practices for eliminating the consequences (service interruptions) associated with rare instances of transmission equipment failures in service.  In our estimation, Georgia Power should continue to rely on the best practices it has followed in the past to continue to provide customers with exceptional transmission system reliability in the future. 

Finally, we are not sure to which utilities Mr. Robinson was referring when he discussed what Georgia Power has seen “across the United States,” but we have a few observations to share. If Mr. Robinson was referring to the wildfires caused by Pacific Gas and Electric equipment failures, subsequent investigations blame those wildfires on a lack of inspections and maintenance (most commonly, vegetation management), not a lack of equipment replacement.  If he is referring to the lengthy service interruptions in Louisiana following Hurricane IDA, damage to transmission lines serving New Orleans was caused by a hurricane, not by a lack of Entergy equipment replacement or transmission investment. 

Georgia Power’s attempt to support its request through a vague reference to the experiences of other utilities is misplaced given how Georgia Power’s proposed increases compare to the transmission investments of other utilities. Even if the Commission rejects the Company’s entire $1 billion proposal to continue TIP spending 2023-2025, the remaining transmission investments proposed still represent a 171% increase (almost triple, from $313 million per year to $849 million per year) over average annual transmission investment from 2009 to 2021 (before the TIP commenced in earnest).  Thus, the Commission should rest assured that such a rejection would not deprive the Company of an ample increase in capital spending to improve transmission reliability, assuming the Company operates in an efficient and economic manner. Figure 6 illustrates the situation clearly. Given that energy sales (MWhs), peak demand (MW), and number of customers are expected to grow less than 2%, a 171% increase in capital spending should be more than enough to maintain and improve reliability under efficient and economic management.
Figure 6: Total Transmission Capital Spending, Actual 2009-2021/Projected 2022/Requested 2023-2025

A.We recommend the Commission reject Georgia Power’s $1.0 billion request to continue TIP implementation in its entirety, as summarized in the table below. The 171% increase over historical spending levels that remains after such a rejection (almost triple) will be more than sufficient to allow Georgia Power to make the investments required to maintain and improve transmission reliability. GEORGIA POWER’S DISTRIBUTION INVESTMENT PLAN (DIP) WILL NOT DELIVER RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENTS SUFFICIENT TO OUTWEIGH RATE INCREASES

Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE THIS SECTION OF TESTIMONY.
A.This section of testimony is organized as follows, as further introduced immediately below.
Summary of Georgia Power’s Distribution Investment Plan
Circuit hardening is not a cost-effective way to improve reliability
Undergrounding is not a cost-effective way to improve reliability
The DIP applies costly DIP investment packages to too many circuits which do not need them

This section of testimony begins with a summary of Georgia Power’s Distribution Investment Plan (DIP). We then critique the DIP, focusing on four problems: 1) The largest DIP investment packages by far, circuit hardening and undergrounding of overhead lines, are not remotely cost-effective approaches to improving reliability; 2) The Company applies costly DIP investment packages to too many circuits which already demonstrate reasonably good reliability performance, further damaging the cost-effectiveness of the DIP; 3) The DIP ignores dramatically more cost-effective approaches to improving reliability, including vegetation management and worst-performing circuit programs; and 4) The DIP appears to be causing premature retirement of reliable equipment customers continue to pay for in rates, as evidenced by $000 million in projected write-offs of equipment with book value remaining 2023-2025. (This is not only wasteful, but violates established legal and regulatory precedents). 

This Section also explains why the Commission should assign little or no weight to the Company’s Customer Benefit Study. (The Customer Benefit Study is not a cost-effectiveness test or cost-benefit analysis, but rather an optimization of capital-intensive options and constraints designed specifically to justify large capital investments.) We will also describe our concerns regarding Georgia Power’s accountability for securing DIP-related reliability improvements, and summarize the Maryland Public Service Commission’s efforts to secure reliability improvements from utilities in a cost-effective manner, along with associated results. We will conclude with recommendations for Commission consideration, including a recommendation that the Commission reject Georgia Power’s requests for the circuit hardening and undergrounding capital components of the DIP in their entirety. We note that if the Commission follows this recommendation, the remaining distribution capital budgets still represent an increase of 131% of historical distribution capital spending 2009-2019 (more than double). This increase should be more than enough to help Georgia Power improve the reliability of its distribution grid in a cost effective manner for customers. 
1.  Summary of Georgia Power’s Distribution Investment Plan (DIP)
Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE COMPANY’S DIP
A.Georgia Power’s DIP consists of six investment “packages” the Company has defined to be applied to circuits to improve their performance. (Note that the packages do not include low-cost options, or options involving operations and maintenance spending, a subject we revisit later in this Section.) The Company uses an Optimization Model to determine which of the packages to apply to circuits in the third and fourth reliability performance quartiles (meaning, the circuits performing below the median circuit’s performance), and in what priority. (Note that “median” is a much different measure than “average”, and that the calculation and use of the median value determines the universe of circuits to which packages can be applied; we will return to both observations later in this Section.) Of circuits performing below the median, additional criteria are applied to develop package lists per circuit. The packages are then implemented by a dedicated GIP project implementation department over time (meaning, the twelve years and four rate cases from 2020 through 2031). 

The Company defined each investment “package” to include a discrete set of actions and investments, along with implementation costs, resulting in both rate increases and reliability improvements for customers. These are the same definitions used in the Optimization Model. In that Model, “Rate Increases” reflect changes in O&M expenses and revenue requirements from capital investment, while reliability improvements are valued as customers might value them (meaning, as a reduction in the costs customers incur from service interruptions).  The Optimization Model varies all of these as investment levels change; discrete investment levels, described as “scenarios”, are associated with projected reliability improvements (system average interruption duration in minutes) by the end of the DIP period (2032) for each investment level. The cost of service outages to customers falls as the count of package applications increases (up to a point, called the point of diminishing returns, at which the incremental implementation costs become higher than the fall in customer service outage costs). The Company’s DIP capital requests thus represent the cost to implement the count of packages the Optimization Model determines to be optimum given the packages and their attributes as the Company has defined them. (We note this is not the same as the lowest-cost way to improve reliability, a subject to which we return later in this Section.)

Using its Optimization Model, the Company employed its 2017 reliability performance to place circuits into quartiles, thereby qualifying certain circuits (those below the performance of the median circuit in 2017) to receive DIP packages. These placements of circuits into quartiles, thus qualifying them to receive DIP packages, using 2017 data, remain static through to today. 

Brief descriptions of the six packages the Company has defined and proposed for 2023-2025 spending are presented in Table 4 below. As indicated earlier, Georgia Power spent $0.00 billion implementing DIP packages 2020-2022, and proposes $1.3 billion 2023-2025. As the chart indicates, packages “circuit hardening” and “undergrounding” are by far the largest categories of spending in the DIP, representing 85% of total DIP spending from 2020-2025 (39% and 46% respectively).
