Q.WHAT RESULTS DOES THE COMPANY EXPECT FROM ITS DIP?
A.In its initial DIP in the 2019 rate case, the Company projected that a system-wide improvement in average interruption duration (SAIDI), currently 132.6 minutes on average over the last five years as reported in Figure 3 earlier, to 65 minutes by 2031. (We note that the Company’s five-year average SAIDI is within 1% of the five-year average for U.S. investor-owned utilities.) In the current DIP, as noted earlier, the Company revises its projection to a SAIDI target of 80 minutes. In just three years, the Company’s projected reliability improvement has already deteriorated 23.1% from initial projections. In a discovery conference, the Company specified that Staff should not consider an 80-minute SAIDI as a goal (or as we prefer to say, an expectation), but rather as nothing more than a projection from its Optimization Model. The low likelihood that the Company can be held responsible for securing projected reliability improvements is a significant DIP deficiency, and is yet another subject we will revisit later in this Section.

Q.WHAT RESULTS HAS THE COMPANY SECURED TO DATE FROM DIP INVESTMENTS?
A.As indicated in Section II of this testimony, it is far too early to determine results from DIP investments.  Not only have relatively few of the most questionable packages implemented on circuits to date been completed (meaning, circuit hardening and undergrounding), there are insufficient years of experience (we recommend three years minimum) to make any conclusions. Significantly, packages have been deployed together, often in conjunction with vegetation management, making it impossible to determine if an investment package, or if simple and inexpensive vegetation management, was responsible for any improvements secured. We will return to this topic later in this Section.

 2.  Circuit Hardening Is Not a Cost-Effective Way to Improve Reliability
Q.WHAT IS CIRCUIT HARDENING?
A.The Company uses circuit hardening to describe a number of investments intended to reduce the frequency of service interruptions. Primary activities including replacing poles, replacing pole crossarms, installing animal guards, and replacing fuses with TripSaver® devices. The Company also claims circuit hardening investments will reduce operations and maintenance costs.

Q.PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY CIRCUIT HARDENING IS NOT A COST-EFFECTIVE WAY TO IMPROVE RELIABILITY.
A.Examining the cost-effectiveness of any grid investment involves comparing the benefits to customers from the investment (in this case, the value of reliability improvements) to the costs to customers of those investments (rate increases/revenue requirements). As the circuit hardening package includes multiple activities, it is difficult to parse these out individually. However, the analysis described below indicates that even if the Company secures the reliability improvements it projects from circuit hardening, the program is so costly on a per premises basis that it cannot deliver benefits to customers in excess of costs to customers.

Q.HOW EXPENSIVE IS CIRCUIT HARDENING?
A.Georgia Power reports that it will harden 000 circuits at a cost of $000 million between 2020 and 2025, for an average cost per circuit of $6.45 million. Including carrying charges (costs of capital, taxes on Company income, sales and property taxes, etc.) the cost per circuit to customers grows to $0.00 million (the present value of the revenue requirement on $6.45 million assuming the Company’s “k-factor” of 0.00). Given that the average Georgia Power circuit serves 1,109 customers, this works out to $0,000 in present value of revenue requirements per average customer served by a hardened circuit. We consider this to be quite expensive relative to the potential benefits available.

Q.HOW EFFECTIVE IS CIRCUIT HARDENING?
A.It is difficult to say. The Company projects a reduction in outage duration of 00% from circuit hardening. In discovery, the Company provided reliability data on 30 circuit hardening projects completed from 2012 to 2016. For these circuits, outage duration fell an average of 25% from pre-hardening performance, which seems to validate the Company’s projections. Unfortunately, vegetation management was completed concurrently on 50% of these circuits. While concurrent completion of vegetation management on circuits being hardened is common and appropriate (to make room for the work being done), concurrent vegetation management makes it impossible to determine how much of the reliability improvement realized on hardened circuits is due to vegetation management, and how much is due to hardening investment. 

Q.GIVEN THESE COSTS AND THE COMPANY’S EFFECTIVENESS PROJECTIONS, HOW DOES THE CUSTOMER VALUE OF RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENTS COMPARE TO CUSTOMER COSTS?
A.Unfortunately, not favorably. Our analysis finds that customers receive only $0.46 in reliability improvement value per dollar of rate increase. An explanation of our analysis follows.

We applied the Company’s current reliability improvement assumptions for the circuit hardening package to the average reliability 2017-2021 of the 25 circuits the Company selected for this package 2020-2022. (Remember, according to the Company’s Optimization Model, these first circuits prioritized for hardening should represent the worst circuits in the Company’s distribution system.) From a starting average SAIDI of 261.4 minutes on these circuits, the Company’s projected average improvement of 00% results in a reduction to 000.0 minutes. From a starting SAIFI on these circuits of 2.33 interruptions per year, the Company’s projected average improvement of 00% results in a reduction to 0.00 interruptions per year. As an initial observation, we note that the customer “willingness to pay” research cited earlier indicates customers would be unwilling to incur costs amounting to $0,000 each for such reliability improvement levels.  But we continued our analysis through an additional step: utilizing the US Department of Energy’s Interruption Cost Estimator (ICE) tool to quantify the dollar value to customers of reliability improvements from circuit hardening projected by Georgia Power. We can then compare this value to the average customer cost of $0.00 million per circuit to determine the cost-effectiveness of circuit hardening (or lack thereof). 

Q.WHAT IS THE DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY’S ICE TOOL?
A.The ICE tool is an internet-based software application designed specifically by the Department of Energy to help utilities estimate the value to customers of reliability improvements. Georgia Power employed the ICE tool to estimate the cost of outages to customers as a reality check against its Customer Benefits Study results using the Company’s own “cost of outage” estimates, secured from customer research conducted in 2011. (Customer Benefits Study results using the ICE tool estimates and using the Company’s own estimates were very similar.) A different option the ICE tool offers, based on the same underlying “cost of outages to customers” research data, estimates the value to customers of reliability improvements.

Q.HOW DID YOU USE THE ICE TOOL TO ESTIMATE THE PRESENT VALUE OF RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENTS FROM CIRCUIT HARDENING?
A.We used the ICE tool’s “value of reliability improvements” option to estimate the value to customers of the reliability improvements the Company projects from the circuit hardening package.  We input the starting and improved SAIDI and SAIFI levels for the first 25 circuits described above into the ICE tool, as well as all other inputs the tool required specific to Georgia Power (customer counts by class for these circuits; inflation rate =0.0%; discount rate = 0.00%; expected lifetime of benefits in years = 40; etc.). Using all this Company-specific and circuit-specific data, the ICE tool calculates the present value of projected reliability improvements from hardening the first 25 circuits to be $94.9 million, or $3.8 million per circuit. Compared to the present value of the average cost to customers to harden a circuit ($0.00 million per circuit, per above), the ICE tool valuation of reliability improvements indicates that circuit hardening delivers just $0.46 in reliability improvement value for every $1 in customer rate increase. 

Thus, the circuit hardening package is cost-ineffective by a wide margin, and not in the interest of customers or the public. Recall that our analysis employed Georgia Power’s own projections for costs and reliability improvements from circuit hardening; it is entirely possible Georgia Power will not be able to deliver the reliability improvements it projects within the costs it estimates. (Further, our finding is consistent with one of the most thorough studies of circuit hardening ever completed, on behalf of the Public Utilities Commission of Texas. The study, which focused on hardening for hurricanes, determined that cost-effectiveness for circuit hardening was only indicated for about 1% of distribution structures, including only those within 50 miles of the Gulf of Mexico. 

3.  Undergrounding of Overhead Lines Is Not a Cost-Effective Way to Improve Reliability 
Q.PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY UNDERGROUNDING IS NOT A COST-EFFECTIVE WAY TO IMPROVE RELIABILITY.  
A.As with circuit hardening, we cite undergrounding’s extreme cost as the primary reason why undergrounding cannot possibly deliver reliability improvements sufficient to deliver value to customers in excess of rate increases. While our circuit hardening analysis identified a cost per circuit of $0.00 million, and a cost per customer served by a hardened circuit of $0,000, the customer cost to underground overhead lines (present value of the revenue requirement) is 3.6 times more costly than circuit hardening on a per circuit basis ($00.0 million), and more than twice as costly as circuit hardening on a customer-specific basis, at $15,241. This customer-specific amount is far less than we have seen in the industry, at about $1 million in utility cost per overhead mile undergrounded, divided by the U.S. average of customers per distribution line mile of 40 ($25,000 per customer), which indicates that our customer-specific cost estimate (based on Georgia Power data) is likely understated by a significant amount. Recently, Pacific Gas & Electric Company reported an undergrounding cost of over $4 million per overhead line mile, though admittedly through rough terrain (steep, rocky, and heavily forested). In a discovery conference, Georgia Power admitted that one of the lessons learned from DIP implementation so far is that undergrounding costs more than original estimates due to the rocky nature of Georgia soil. 

Q.HOW EFFECTIVE IS UNDERGROUNDING AT IMPROVING RELIABILITY?
A.Undergrounding is quite effective at improving reliability. But high cost, not the level of effectiveness, is the problem. The Company reports using the reliability of circuits that are already undergrounded as the basis for its undergrounding reliability improvement projections (though it admits it has never implemented a massive undergrounding program in the past). While this is a reasonable approach in the absence of actual undergrounding program data, the cost of undergrounding is so high as to render the undergrounding effectiveness question meaningless. 

We know this because we applied a 100% SAIDI and SAIFI reduction to the eight circuits for which undergrounding was the only package the Company applied 2020-2022. In our analysis, using ICE tool values by customer class for the cost to customers of service interruptions, and the Company’s cost projections and other Company-specific assumptions, we found that the Company’s costs (not even including profits and taxes customers must pay) exceeded the customer value of reliability improvements for every single one of the eight circuits, and for most of them, by a very wide margin. This finding bears repeating: even at a 100% reliability improvement assumption (perfect reliability), the customer value of reliability improvements from undergrounding did not exceed the Company’s undergrounding costs.

Our contention that the extremely high cost of undergrounding overhead lines makes the practice a cost-ineffective way to improve reliability is well-supported by extensive amounts of research and state regulator evaluation. A study completed in follow-up to the aforementioned PUC Texas study (on circuit hardening) that focused exclusively on undergrounding found only $0.30 in benefits for every $1 spent to underground overhead lines. Multiple other state utility regulators have studied the undergrounding question, including Florida, Maine, Maryland, North Carolina, and Virginia. In every instance but one, no state utility regulator has endorsed undergrounding of its own accord. In the lone exception, the Virginia State Corporation Commission severely limited a utility’s undergrounding application, though that Commission fully rejected two other undergrounding applications by the same utility. 

Q.WHAT OTHER EVIDENCE DO YOU HAVE THAT UNDERGROUNDING IS NOT A COST-EFFECTIVE WAY TO IMPROVE RELIABILITY?
A.As with Georgia Power’s circuit hardening package, we used the ICE tool to estimate the reliability improvement value of the undergrounding package. We employed the same method for undergrounding as we did for circuit hardening, using the average SAIDI (270 minutes) and SAIFI (2.4 interruptions) 2017-2021 of the 16 circuits the Company selected for undergrounding 2020-2022 as the ICE tool starting point. We then input the reliability improvements the Company’s Optimization Model assumes for the undergrounding package, along with all other variables specific to Georgia Power and these 16 circuits, just as we did for circuit hardening. Using the Company’s own reliability improvement projections (SAIDI down to 00 minutes and SAIFI down to 0.0 interruptions) and all other circuit-specific and Company-specific inputs, the ICE tool calculated a reliability improvement value of $170 million, or $10.6 million per circuit. Compared to the average cost per circuit of $00.0 million, our analysis indicates that customers will receive only $0.36 in value per $1 of undergrounding rate increase – not significantly different than the $0.30 per $1 found by the Texas undergrounding study cited above.

Q.HAVE YOU INCLUDED THE OPERATIONS AND MAINTENANCE (O&M) SAVINGS ASSOCIATED WITH CIRCUIT HARDENING OR UNDERGROUNDING IN YOUR COST-EFFECTIVENESS CALCULATIONS?
A.No. But as the Company’s Customer Benefits Study indicates, avoided customer outage costs represent the greatest single value proposition of the Company’s DIP by far. Based on our finding that customer reliability value is dramatically insufficient to justify the cost of circuit hardening or undergrounding, it is not possible for the relatively small reduction in O&M costs associated with undergrounding (stemming largely from reductions in vegetation management) or circuit hardening to remotely make up the shortfall in customer reliability value relative to customer costs. 


4.  The DIP applies costly DIP investment packages to too many circuits which do not need them.
Q.IN THE INTRODUCTION TO THIS DIP INVESTMENT SECTION YOU STATED “The Company applies costly DIP investment packages to too many circuits which already demonstrate reasonably good reliability performance, further damaging the cost-effectiveness of the DIP.” PLEASE EXPLAIN THIS.
A.In our summary of the Company’s DIP we related that the Company’s DIP Optimization Model applies investment packages to circuits performing below the median (meaning, circuits performing in the third or fourth quartile) as measured in 2017. This criteria identifies half of all circuits as the best candidates for capital investment rather just the very worst performers. As the reader can imagine, one-half of the Company’s circuits exhibit a very wide range of reliability performance, with many circuits performance close to the system average performance. Indeed, our examination of circuits with “below the median” reliability 2017 to 2021 identifies circuits with SAIDI as low as 99 minutes (the circuit ranked immediately below the median circuit) in the third quartile. Given that the Company’s 5-year average SAIDI 2017-2021 is 131, this means that the Company’s DIP will eventually apply investment packages to circuits with above-average reliability. 

Clearly, the application of costly investment packages to circuits with above-average reliability does not make sense. To be sure, focusing investment packages on the worst-performing circuits, and not those above the average, nor even those near the average, makes the most sense. Figure 7 below illustrates the problem with applying investment packages to circuits “below the median”: it does not sufficiently focus DIP attention and investment on the worst-performing circuits.


Figure 7: Circuit Counts and SAIDI performance by quartile using the most-recent 5-year averages.


Figure 7 indicates that investing in so many circuits does not sufficiently concentrate spending to optimize package assignments. Unconcentrated spending increases the cost of the DIP and reduces the average reliability improvement per DIP capital dollar. This is because the very worst-performing circuits present a much larger performance improvement opportunity than circuits performing at, near, or above the average. For example, attention focused on circuits with SAIDI 2.5 times higher than average would address just 126 circuits at Georgia Power, not the 800 or so circuits that the Company’s DIP targets for package deployment. 

Q.WHY DOES A FOCUS ON FEWER CIRCUITS DELIVER A BIGGER BANG FOR THE BUCK?
A.As the reader can appreciate, the starting point reliability for a circuit makes a big difference in the percentage of reliability improvement that might be expected from the application of a package. For the sake of argument, assume that the average circuit’s SAIDI after hardening will average about 99 (the median circuit at Georgia Power in 2017). For a circuit with a SAIDI of 131 before hardening, the resulting SAIDI improvement would be 24% (131 to 99).  For circuit with a SAIDI of 400 before hardening, the resulting SAIDI improvement would be three times greater, at 75% (400 to 99). This illustrates why the performance improvement opportunity for a circuit with a SAIDI of 400 is much larger than the performance improvement opportunity for a circuit with a SAIDI of 131, and why a focus on 126 circuits with really poor reliability delivers much better “bang for the buck” than a focus on 800 circuits.  

Neither the Company’s DIP nor its Optimization Model account for this difference in performance reliability opportunity.  For all packages but undergrounding, the reliability improvement percentages the Optimization Model applies for a given package remain the same for all circuits receiving that package regardless of reliability starting point. This Optimization Model flaw guarantees that the DIP applies packages to circuits that do not need them, resulting in more capital investment than necessary to achieve a given reliability performance target.

Q.BUT EARLIER YOU SAID THAT THE COMPANY’S OPTIMIZATION MODEL DOES PRIORITIZE CIRCUITS BASED ON RELIAIBILITY.
A.Yes, this is true. But focusing on circuits with reliability in the third quartile does not sufficiently focus attention and investment on the very worst circuits where the most benefit could be achieved for each dollar of capital investment. Indeed, we know of no utility that focuses reliability improvement attention on circuits even in the fourth quartile, or the bottom 25% of circuits. Instead, our experience is that most utilities operate “worst performing circuit” programs focused on circuits with reliability that is three times worse than the average circuit. The most aggressive of such programs focus on circuits with reliability that is 2.5 times worse than the average circuit.  Such programs focus reliability improvement attention on far fewer than 25% or 50% of a utility’s circuits, as Georgia Power’s DIP does. 

In Georgia Power’s case, using 2017-2021 reliability data, a circuit with reliability performance 2.5 times worse than the 2017-2021 average of 131 minutes would be circuits with a SAIDI worse than 327.5 minutes. According to that definition, only 126 of Georgia Power’s circuits, or 5.8% of the 2,162 circuits on which the Company provided 5-year SAIDI data, merit attention.  Attention and investment in the 5.8% of circuits with the worst performance is much more targeted than attention and investments in the bottom 50% of circuits (third quartile and below, about 1080 circuits), and more targeted even than investments in the bottom 25% of circuits (fourth quartile, about 540 circuits). Focusing attention and investment on the bottom 5.8% of circuits would provide much greater reliability improvement per dollar than focusing on circuits in the third or fourth quartiles (50% of the Company’s circuits). This explains how the Company’s DIP applies too many packages to circuits which do not need them, constituting a significant problem with the Company’s DIP.

Q.EARLIER, YOU SAID THAT THE COMPANY USED 2017 RELIABILITY PERFORMANCE TO PLACE CIRCUITS INTO QUARTILES, AND THAT THE PLACEMENT OF CIRCUITS INTO QUARTILES USING 2017 DATA REMAINS STATIC THROUGH TO TODAY. IS THIS SIGNIFICANT? IF SO, HOW?
A.The static use of 2017 reliability performance to place circuits into quartiles is extremely significant, and extremely problematic. Georgia Power’s reliability performance in 2017 was strong. In fact, reliability performance in 2017 was the best of any year from 2015 to 2021. The Company reports that a SAIDI of 00.00 was the median in 2017, and that this value was used to qualify circuits for receipt of DIP packages. Applying such a SAIDI to actual reliability data 2017-2021, we found that a SAIDI of 00.00 is low enough to qualify about 75% of the Company’s circuits for investment packages. If the Commission allows the Company’s DIP to continue as is, the reliability investment packages will eventually be applied to all but 25% of the Company’s circuits. Applying packages and investments to 75% of circuits is the exact opposite of “focused” spending. Figure 8 indicates the severely unfocused and inappropriate nature of DIP spending permitted through the use of a SAIDI of 00.00 to qualify a circuit for costly DIP packages.  
Figure 8: Counts of circuits qualifying for DIP packages using 2017 median performance as criteria

As we see it, the DIP Optimization Model and the Company’s application of it are designed specifically to justify the greatest possible amount of rate base growth that also happens to improve reliability by some amount. It succeeds in this by including only high-cost, capital-intensive package options in its Optimization Model, and by employing parameters which result in the application of those packages to far too many circuits. It is not difficult to improve reliability with capital; any utility can throw billions of dollars at its distribution grid and improve reliability. The real challenge is to identify the actions that improve reliability at a cost which is less than the value to customer of those reliability improvements. But as we shall explain, this is not what the Company’s DIP or Optimization Model set out to do, because the DIP and Model ignore two extremely common and cost-effective approaches to improving reliability: more aggressive vegetation management and a more formalized approach to addressing worst-performing circuits.

5.  The DIP ignores dramatically more cost-effective approaches to improving reliability.
Q.WHAT ARE THE DRAMATICALLY MORE COST-EFFECTIVE APPROACHES TO IMPROVING RELIABILITY THAT THE COMPANY’S DIP IGNORES?
A.The two dramatically more cost-effective approaches to improving reliability that almost all utilities employ are more aggressive vegetation management programs and more rigorous worst-performing circuit programs.  The Company’s Optimization Model and its resulting DIP do not consider such programs.

Q.DOESN’T GEORGIA POWER ALREADY HAVE SUCH PROGRAMS?
A.Yes, but our discovery indicates these programs are less formal and rigorous than we would have expected from a utility of Georgia Power’s size and sophistication. Critically, we note that neither more aggressive vegetation management nor a more rigorous worst-performing circuit program have been evaluated as alternatives to DIP packages.  

Q.WHY DO YOU DESCRIBE THE COMPANY’S VEGETATION MANAGEMENT PROGRAM AS LESS FORMAL AND RIGOROUS THAN YOU WOULD HAVE EXPECTED?
A.Early in discovery, Georgia Power reported that its program completes vegetation management on circuits at a frequency of between every 24 and 60 months, with an average of 42 months (3.5 years). Our examination of detailed historical “line miles cleared” data obtained through subsequent discovery revealed a different picture. From 2012 through 2021, assuming 55,188 overhead distribution line miles, Georgia Power actually completed vegetation management on circuits at a frequency of between two years and nine years, with an average of 4.4 years.  We also noted that budgets for vegetation management varied widely from year to year, with a low of $44 million reported in 2017 to a high of $124 million reported in the twelve months ending May 31, 2022. 

Given Georgia’s extended growing season, a more aggressive, formal, and consistent vegetation management program is the first place we would concentrate to secure cost-effective improvements in reliability. Indeed, an examination of outage cause data 2017-2021 indicates that vegetation contact was one of the most common causes of service interruptions, amounting to one-fifth of all service interruptions 2017-2021. This is consistent with our experience across utilities.

Q.HOW INEXPENSIVE IS VEGETATION MANAGEMENT RELATIVE TO UNDERGROUNDING?
A.Georgia Power’s vegetation management (O&M) costs averaged $0,000 per line mile from 2016-2021.  As noted earlier, an industry rule of thumb for undergrounding is $1 million capital cost per line mile. Granted, vegetation management costs must be incurred every four years or so. But at these price differentials, over the 40-year depreciation period typically applied to underground cable, no sophisticated analysis needs to be completed to recognize that vegetation management is tens of multiples less costly than undergrounding. 

Q.WHAT CHANGES TO GEORGIA POWER’S VEGETATION MANAGEMENT PROGRAM WOULD YOU RECOMMEND?
A.At a minimum, we would recommend strict compliance with a four-year vegetation management cycle. By “strict compliance”, we mean that no section of any circuit should go more than four years without vegetation management. Further, reductions in vegetation management cycles to 3.5 years or even 3.0 years should not be ruled out. Indeed, we note the Company plans to increase its average annual vegetation management budget by more than 58% over recent years, from $63 million (2016-2020) to $100 million, in this rate case test period. An increase of this magnitude could be expected to enable a reduction in the average vegetation management cycle from 4.5 years to 3.5 or even 3.0 years. We also recommend the Commission order an annual vegetation management report detailing miles cleared relative to the level required to maintain the Commission-approved vegetation management cycle, and to track resulting reliability improvements.  

If the Commission wishes to focus on improving reliability in a cost-effective manner, more innovative vegetation management ideas can be considered. For example, California recently increased utility rights-of-way radii from 18 inches to as much as four feet. A legislated expansion of utility rights-of-way in Georgia certainly represents one potential approach to improving reliability in a cost-effective manner. In Washington, Avista Utilities is developing a program to pay rebates to customers to trim (and possibly to remove) trees outside the right-of-way that pose a threat to distribution lines in windy conditions. Indeed, the Company agrees that purchasing additional rights-of-way is an option. But none of these approaches appear to have been evaluated on an economic or effectiveness basis as alternatives to capital-intensive circuit hardening or undergrounding packages the Company has defined.

Q.MOVING ON TO WORST-PERFORMING CIRCUIT PROGRAMS, CAN YOU PROVIDE A DESCRIPTION OF A TYPICAL UTILITY PROGRAM?
A.A typical worst-performing circuit program consists of several steps. The first step, completed annually, is to compute one or more reliability metrics for each circuit to enable the identification of poor performers.  While SAIDI and SAIFI (interruption duration and frequency) are the most common reliability metrics employed for this purpose, we have seen others used. Another popular metric is the count or percentage of customers on a circuit experiencing over a certain number of interruptions (for example five, six, or seven) in a year. Other metrics we have seen include identifying circuits that have appeared on the worst-performing circuit list (however defined, see next) for two or more years in a row, or to use two-year averages to measure circuit reliability. (Year-to-year variation can cause too many “false positive” worst-performing circuit identifications when a single year’s reliability is measured. Georgia Power’s program appropriately uses two-year averages to measure circuit reliability.)

Once the reliability of all circuits is calculated, the next step is to identify those that warrant additional investigation as “worst-performing”. As indicated earlier, most utilities establish an annual list of circuits performing at worse than three times the average circuit’s interruption duration or frequency, though we have seen definitions using 2.5 times worse than the average circuit at some utilities. As indicated earlier, about 6% of Georgia Power’s circuits would currently qualify for attention using a 2.5x definition.

For circuits identified as worst-performers, the next step is to complete root-cause analyses. Typically, the engineer responsible for the circuit’s performance will examine outage cause data as the first step towards identifying any recurring outage root causes. The inability to identify a root cause of poor reliability is common; random variability due to weather or accidents often encourage root cause analysts to recommend no remediation, or to simply put such circuits on a watch list for future consideration.  In summary, the challenge with identifying circuits in such programs is to avoid excluding circuits from the list that merit attention, nor to include on the list circuits that do not merit attention. To optimize spending, the ideal process for circuit identification/list creation is fairly sophisticated. Georgia Power’s approach – to identify every circuit below the median for potential application of packages – is not sophisticated at all and results in unnecessary capital investment.

When a recurring root cause is found, the next step is to develop and schedule remediation actions. In our experience the most common remediation activity is spot vegetation management, though sometimes a problematic piece of equipment is identified for replacement. Other common, and inexpensive, remediation actions include the installation of animal guards, or adjusting the settings of protective devices (such as reclosers) on a circuit. Root causes and associated remediation plans rarely involve large capital expenditures, though installation of additional reclosers, sectionalizing devices (to reduce the number of customers who are impacted by a fault), and distribution automation schemes are called for on occasion. (All of these latter options require capital spending.)   

Q.WHY DO YOU DESCRIBE THE COMPANY’S WORST-PERFORMING CIRCUIT PROGRAM AS LESS FORMAL AND RIGOROUS THAN YOU WOULD HAVE EXPECTED?
A.First, the Company has no standard criteria for identifying circuits as “worst,” thereby qualifying for additional attention. Instead, the Company seems to take actions commensurate with the level of spare capital budgets that might be available from year-to-year. The Company seems to have no written policies to formalize its worst-performing circuit program, nor do any dedicated capital or O&M budgets appear to exist for the program. Indeed, program spending has varied widely from year to year over the past 12 years, from a low of $000,000 in 2010 to a high of over $0.0 million in 2018.  

Q.ARE WORST-PERFORMING CIRCUIT PROGRAMS COST-EFFECTIVE?
A.Judging by their popularity among utilities, we believe so. Anecdotal data from Georgia Power’s program also appears to indicate that they might be, particularly relative to extremely costly DIP investment packages such as circuit hardening and undergrounding.  Table 5 below provides the pre- and post-investment results for worst-performing circuit projects completed in 2017 and 2018, along with average project costs per circuit.  Note the dramatically lower capital costs per circuit of this program compared to the radical capital spending per circuit associated with Georgia Power’s circuit hardening package.

Q. WHAT CHANGES TO GEORGIA POWER’S WORST-PERFORMING CIRCUIT PROGRAM WOULD YOU RECOMMEND?
A.We would recommend that the Company develop written policies to formalize its program, including clear criteria for identifying circuits for additional attention annually; standards for completing root-cause analyses; standards for developing remediation plans; and standards for reviewing plans and authorizing spending, as well as standards for tracking spending, projects, and results. We would also recommend that specific budgets for the program be established, and that personnel/organizational accountabilities for program administration, root cause analyses, and remediation plan development and implementation be established. The Commission may also wish to consider establishing annual reporting requirements for the program. The Maryland PSC has established a strong reliability performance improvement program, including both vegetation management and worst-performing circuit reporting features, that merits the Commission’s attention.  We will describe this program in more detail later in this Section.

6.  The DIP is prompting premature retirement of reliable assets for which customers are paying.
Q.DOES THE DIP PRESENT OTHER PROBLEMS FOR CUSTOMERS?
A.Yes. It appears that the DIP consists in large part of wholesale and indiscriminate equipment replacement, essentially constituting rebuilding or undergrounding entire circuits or sections of circuits, as examples.  We believe the new equipment installed via the DIP is inadvertently displacing a great deal of existing equipment that is perfectly sound and is operating safely and reliably (in the same way that the transmission investment plan’s premature replacement practice does). Replacing poles and cross-arms that have passed their most recent inspections, whether through circuit hardening or undergrounding packages, deprives customers of many years, or even decades, of useful life from equipment for which they have paid, or for which they continue to pay, in rates. This obviously represents a significant opportunity cost that should also be included in the Commission’s evaluation of the Company’s proposed DIP.

Q.WHAT IS YOUR EVIDENCE THAT THIS IS HAPPENING?
A.We can see from accounting details provided in discovery that the Company is retiring distribution assets with book value remaining at an alarming rate. A piece of equipment with book value means that it is still being depreciated. If a piece of equipment is still being depreciated, that means it has not yet reached the end of its estimated life, let alone the end of its operating life (meaning, fully depreciated but passing its inspections). To summarize, the opportunity costs to customers of the DIP makes the already negative cost-benefit ratio of packages like circuit hardening or undergrounding even more negative.

Q.WHY DO YOU CHARACTERIZE THE RETIREMENT OF DISTRIBUTION ASSETS WITH BOOK VALUE REMAINING AS “ALARMING”?
A.From 2023 to 2025, the Company projects that it will retire distribution equipment with a net book value of $000 million. Given that Company’s entire distribution capital request 2023-2025 (including the DIP) is $0.000 billion, our interpretation is that almost one quarter of the distribution capital the Company is requesting replaces assets that have not reached their estimated life. The replacement of equipment that is operating safely and reliably despite being fully depreciated comes on top of this amount. While a small amount of retirement is unavoidable (for example, government-requested facility relocations or accidents or storms that destroy equipment), we believe the DIP, and particularly its application to too many circuits not performing poorly enough to justify investment, is to blame for the extremely high level of equipment retirements Georgia Power projects.

The significant retirement of equipment with book value remaining is evidence of asset churn, or replacing assets with low (or no) book value simply to increase rate base and profits. There is legal and regulatory precedent against this practice, and we encourage the Commission to consider the waste and opportunity cost caused by circuit hardening and undergrounding as just one more reason to reject capital requests for these DIP packages.   

7.  Why the Commission should afford little to no weight to the Company’s Customer Benefits Study.
Q.YOU HAVE MADE SOME COMPELLING POINTS, BUT THE COMPANY’S CUSTOMER BENEFITS STUDY INDICATES ITS DIP IS COST-EFFECTIVE. HOW COULD THE COMPANY’S STUDY RESULTS BE SO DIFFERENT FROM YOUR FINDINGS?
A.Actually, the Company’s Customer Benefits Study provides no indication that the DIP is cost-effective (meaning, that it delivers economic benefits to customers in excess of associated rate increases). The Customer Benefits Study is not a cost-effectiveness test, nor is it a cost-benefit analysis, though the Company undoubtedly wants the Commission to consider it as such. Instead, the optimization modeling the Company presents in its DIP is a hypothetical exercise to optimize outcomes within a set of constraints self-imposed and designed by the Company. Neither the DIP nor the Optimization Model is designed to answer the question, “What are the most cost-effective ways to improve reliability?” Instead, the DIP consists of the following components:
A set of capital-intensive grid investment packages;
A set of implementation cost and customer cost reduction assumptions (from reliability improvements) for each package;
The application of constrained optimization modeling techniques to identify the mix and level of package implementation that results in the lowest total cost to customers given the limited set of capital-intensive grid investment packages specified.

The DIP provides the optimum results or plan given a limited set of solutions which exclude more cost-effective solutions such as more aggressive vegetation management, a more formalized worst performing circuit program, and a focus on fewer circuits with the most abject reliability performance. This is absolutely not the way to develop a cost-effective plan to improve reliability. 

Q.HOW DO YOU BELIEVE A UTILITY SHOULD DEVELOP A COST-EFFECTIVE PLAN TO IMPROVE GRID RELIABLITY?
A.Instead of modeling a constrained set of options designed and limited by Georgia Power, the Company should have identified all commonly-employed approaches to improve reliability, including approaches that are not capital-intensive, such as more aggressive vegetation management and a more formalized worst-performing circuit program. For each approach identified – including vegetation management and worst-performing circuit approaches – the Company should have used historical cost and results data from previous applications to project the costs and benefits (a cost-benefit analysis) for each approach.  Armed with a cost-benefit analysis for each approach, the Company could have selected those delivering the biggest reliability improvements per dollar, and applied them only to the circuits with the most dramatically poor reliability performance (rather than up to 75% of circuits, as the use of 2017 median circuit performance enables). The Company did not complete a cost-benefit analysis for any of the capital-intensive packages it defined, let alone for any of the myriad, lower-cost alternatives to the six capital-intensive packages that exist. Nor did the Company consider limiting spending to a smaller number of circuits.    

The Commission should give little or no weight to the Company’s Customer Benefits Study because it answers an irrelevant question. The irrelevant question the Study answers is “Of the capital-intensive packages we have defined, what mix delivers the lowest total cost to customers?” The relevant question the DIP should answer is “What are the most cost-effective ways to improve reliability?” Until and unless the Company provides cost-benefit analyses for all commonly-employed approaches to improving reliability, thus enabling an answer to this relevant question, we recommend the Commission afford no weight to the Company’s Customer Benefits Study and reject the Company’s requests for capital to continue the most outrageously expensive and cost-ineffective DIP packages: circuit hardening and undergrounding. 

Q.BUT SHOULDN’T THE COMMISSION ENCOURAGE GEORGIA POWER TO IMPROVE ITS SERVICE RELIAIBLITY?
A.Of course it should, but not at any cost. There are many more cost-effective ways to improve reliability than those the Company chose for its DIP that can be, and should have been, considered.  Figure 9 indicates that if the Commission follows our recommendation to reject continued investments in the circuit hardening and undergrounding packages 2023-2025 entirely, the remaining distribution investments proposed still represent a 55% increase (from $473 million per year to $732 million per year) over average annual distribution investment from 2009 to 2019 (before the DIP commenced). If the Commission follows our recommendations there is little to no risk that an authorized 55% increase could be perceived as disdainful of reliability improvement goals. Given such an increase, and assuming efficient and economic management, the Company should be able to maintain and improve service reliability without the circuit hardening and undergrounding components of the DIP. 
Figure 9: Total Distribution Capital Actual ’09-‘21/Projected ‘22/Requested ‘23’-25


8.  The DIP offers no performance accountability.
Q.DO YOU HAVE OTHER CONCERNS ABOUT GEORGIA POWER’S DIP?
A.Yes. Packages other than circuit hardening and undergrounding may also fail to deliver benefits to customers in excess of associated rate increases. The Company’s spending on moving distribution lines from back lots to front lots falls in this category. As with circuit hardening and undergrounding, this package entails an extremely high cost per premise. The “add circuit ties” package becomes cost-ineffective when applied to increasingly rural circuits. While circuit ties in urban and suburban areas are relatively short, circuit ties in rural areas, where circuits are far apart, are much longer, and therefore much more costly to build. At the same time, low customer density on rural circuits means that dramatically fewer customers will benefit per dollar spent adding ties. Thus, at some point, adding more circuit ties will cross into the point of diminishing returns. (Though of course, less costly ways to improve rural circuit reliability are available, and those should be pursued as appropriate.) Even distribution automation and sectionalization, an approach to improving reliability we generally favor, has its limits. At some point, the cost to add more sections and distribution automation schemes exceeds the resulting reliability improvements. None of these packages should be approved without cost-benefit tests to determine cost-effectiveness and the point of diminishing returns. 

But the period for discovery is limited, and the Company’s permitted response times are long. We simply did not have sufficient opportunity to investigate all DIP packages to the extent we would have preferred. Regarding other DIP concerns, the largest by far is our concern that the DIP offers no opportunities for holding Georgia Power accountable for securing the reliability improvements the Company projects from DIP spending. 

Q.WHY IS ACCOUNTABILITY A CONCERN?  THE COMPANY’S CUSTOMER BENEFITS STUDY CLEARLY INDICATES AN EXPECTATION THAT ITS DIP WILL ACHIEVE A SYSTEM-WIDE SAIDI GOAL OF 80 MINUTES.
A.An expectation does not constitute actual performance by the Company, nor an actual benefit from capital investment. Georgia Power’s Customer Benefits Study states “The revised plan . . . is expected to invest ~$3.4B over the remaining 8 years and achieve an end-state overall company SAIDI of ~80 by 2031.”  However in a discovery conference to review the Optimization Model the Company used to develop the DIP, the Company corrected our characterization of the system wide SAIDI of 80 minutes as a “target”. The Company explained that the 80-minute SAIDI cited was nothing more than the Optimization Model’s projected improvement from the level of spending the Company proposes in its DIP, and should not be considered a target. The Company also rejected any notion that its cost recovery vary with the actual reliability performance delivered. (There is an emerging trend in the US towards performance-based ratemaking, particularly in jurisdictions employing a forward-looking/multi-year rate plan approach to ratemaking, which Georgia Power has enjoyed since the mid-1990s). 

We also note that if reliability fails to improve by 2032, or improves only modestly, the Company’s shareholders will win, while the Company’s customers will lose. Shareholders will benefit from earnings and share price growth associated with billions of dollars in rate base growth. Customers will lose, saddled with decades of rate increases with little or no reliability improvement to show for it. Customers, not shareholders, bear the risk that GIP rate increases will not be offset by reliability improvements. This is what we mean when we say the DIP includes no performance accountability for Georgia Power.

Finally, we assume the Commission relied heavily on the reliability projection the Company provided with its first DIP, in 2019, which indicated a system-wide SAIDI of 65 minutes. We imagine the Commission is interested to know that the Company has not only relaxed its original SAIDI projection to 80 minutes, but also corrected our characterization of the SAIDI projection as a reliability performance target. These are not encouraging signs that the Company can deliver the reliability improvements it projects from its DIP.

Q.DO YOU HAVE ANY OTHER CONCERNS ABOUT THE COMMISSION’S ABILITY TO HOLD THE COMPANY ACCOUNTABLE FOR DIP RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENTS?
A.Yes. We note that all the DIP packages but one (package #5, “Bring Feeder to Road”, which is designed primarily to reduce outage duration by speeding repairs) are designed primarily to reduce the frequency of service interruptions (defined as those lasting longer than five minutes). Yet the Customer Benefits Study only publicly identifies a system-wide SAIDI (interruption duration) projection, and no system-wide SAIFI projection (interruption frequency). While a system-wide SAIFI projection for 2032 can be found in a trade secret response to an informal data request (0.00), the Company’s hesitation to publicly provide a system-wide interruption frequency projection is concerning. 

Interruption frequency and interruption duration are two vastly different measures of reliability, and both are important. We are concerned that the discrepancy between investment intentions (to reduce interruption frequency) and investment performance measurement (interruption duration) will make it difficult if not impossible for future Commissions to hold the Company accountable for delivering actual reliability improvements from the DIP.

9.  Summary of the Maryland Commission’s efforts to cost-effectively improve reliability, and associated results.
Q.HAVE YOU SEEN OTHER STATE UTILITY COMMISSIONS SUCCESSFULLY SECURE RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENTS IN A COST-EFFECTIVE MANNER?
A.Yes. We have become particularly familiar with the Maryland Commission’s efforts to improve distribution reliability in a cost-effective manner through our work on behalf of the Maryland Office of People’s Counsel. We are encouraged by the results of the Commission’s efforts, which are focused largely on annual performance reporting requirements.

Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE MARYLAND COMMISSION’S EFFORTS.
A.After a series of storms in 2010 and 2011 involving prolonged (1-2 week) service interruptions for many thousands of customers, the Maryland legislature tasked the Public Service Commission with implementing service quality and reliability standards for electric distribution utilities. After a series of stakeholder working groups led by the Maryland Staff, the Commission approved the addition of Chapter 20.50.12 to the utility section of the Code of Maryland Regulations, “Service Quality and Reliability Standards”. The Chapter specified minimum annual performance reporting requirements as well as the minimum reliability statistics (SAIDI and SAIFI, along with multiple variations) the utilities must measure. The initial Chapter included minimum SAIDI and SAIFI values the regulated utilities were required to achieve by year for the first few years. 

Subsequent workshops refined the reporting requirements, and periodic updates to the minimum SAIDI and SAIFI values have slowly required more stringent performance expectations over the years.  An example of an annual performance report from a Maryland utility is provided as Exhibit PA/DS-10.  As the reader can observe, there is a significant focus on vegetation management and worst-performing circuit programs, along with a focus on documented remediation action plans for failures to meet various performance expectations. In summary, the old adage “what gets measured, gets managed” applies.     

Q.HOW HAVE THE MARYLAND UTILITIES’ RELIABILITY PERFORMANCE LEVELS IMPROVED?
A.Maryland utility reliability has held constant or improved since the standards and reporting requirements were implemented, as presented in Figure 10. Maryland utility reliability has bucked the trend of deteriorating reliability exhibited by U.S. investor-owned utilities in recent years (See Figure 2), and at a reasonable cost. (No significant reliability improvement investment plans were implemented by Maryland utilities from 2013 to 2020.) If the Georgia Commission wishes to focus on improving reliability in a cost-effective manner, it might want to consider a similar type of effort. However, such efforts will not reduce the requirement to complete cost-benefit analyses on any reliability-related investments Georgia Power might propose.
Figure 10: Maryland reliability performance of investor-owned utilities 2013-2020.

THE LEVEL OF DISTRIBUTED ENERGY RESOURCES GEORGIA POWER MUST MANAGE DOES NOT WARRANT A $100 MILLION DERMS 

Q.WHAT IS A DISTRIBUTED ENERGY RESOURCE MANAGMENT SYSTEM?
A.A distributed energy resource management system (DERMS) is a software package which can, when combined with data from and remote control of customer and field equipment, help a utility meet the challenges of increasing levels of distributed energy resources on its grid. Distributed energy resources (DERs) can consist of synchronous generators (meaning a spinning turbine, such as an industrial customer might own), or inverter-based generators and energy storage devices (PV solar panels and batteries, also known as asynchronous). 

Q.WHAT “CHALLENGES” DO SYNCHRONOUS AND INVERTER-BASED DERS PRESENT TO UTILITIES?
A.Utilities typically describe four challenges DERs may present to grid operations. First, they are concerned that DER generation can “confuse” circuit breakers and other protective equipment, causing them not to operate when they should (leading to equipment damage), or causing them to operate when they should not (leading to service interruptions).  Second, they are concerned that DERs will continue to put power onto the grid during a power outage (unintentional islanding), presenting a safety issue. Third, they are concerned that DERs can increase grid voltage levels above prescribed limits in localized areas. Fourth, they are concerned that DERs “mask” loads that utilities must be prepared to serve if the DERs on a circuit discontinue power delivery unexpectedly.

Q.ARE THESE CONCERNS WARRANTED?
A.To some extent, but every situation is different, and we believe utility concerns regarding DERs to be overblown generally. For example, synchronous (spinning turbine) DER are known to confuse circuit breakers and other protective equipment. However, inverter-based (asynchronous, meaning PV solar and battery) DER are not known to cause such confusion. Further, Georgia Power’s interconnection standards require all DERs to follow IEEE 1547. IEEE 1547 requires all interconnected DERs be installed with a switch which disconnects the DER from the grid within seconds of a loss of grid power. This helps address unintentional islanding concerns. Switches also disconnect DER when voltage rises above prescribed limits, and switch “ride through” settings (which permit DER to remain connected until prescribed ranges of voltage or frequency disturbance are exceeded) can help ensure DERs do not disconnect unexpectedly. Finally, simply tracking the types and capacities of DER installed on a circuit can help a utility understand masked load levels. 

One study modeled various combinations of PV Solar locations and penetration levels (the peak DER capacity on a circuit relative to the circuit’s peak load) to determine PV Solar “tolerance” on 16 representative circuits. The model indicated that in more than two-thirds of cases, circuits tolerated PV Solar penetration of 90% or more relative to peak loads. The same study indicated that only 16% of circuits could not tolerate PV Solar penetration levels of 15% (a limit commonly applied to DER penetration by utilities with little DER accommodation experience).  All of these observations indicate that utility concerns over DER penetration generally, and PV Solar/battery penetration specifically, are overblown. 

Q.DOES GEORGIA POWER HAVE SYSTEMS IN PLACE TODAY TO MANAGE DER ON ITS TRANSMISSION AND DISTRIBUTION GRIDS?
A.Yes. Georgia Power reports that it uses SCADA systems (supervisory control and data acquisition) to manage DER connected to its transmission and distribution grids today. 

Q.HAVE OTHER UTILITIES INSTALLED DERMS TO MANAGE DERS?
A.Very few utilities have installed DERMS, due largely to the low penetration of DER on most utilities’ grids. Southern California Edison has installed a DERMS, but its overall DER penetration is somewhat high at over 17% of system peak load. Of note, Hawaiian Electric Company has not yet installed a DERMS despite overall DER penetration on Oahu Island of almost 50% of system peak load. 

Q.WHAT IS THE DER PENETRATION AT GEORGIA POWER? 
The Company reports having 000 MW of peak DER relative to 15,831 MW of system peak load, for a system-wide DER penetration of 0.0%. In addition, the 2022 Integrated Resource Plan approved by the Commission calls for as much as 200 MW of DER to be procured and up to 250 MW of DER to be installed under the Company’s new DER Customer Program. Even if these efforts are 100% subscribed, and even if all of this DER capacity is connected to the distribution grid (much will likely be connected to the transmission grid), it is highly unlikely DER capacity will exceed 000 MW, for a DER penetration of only 0.0% at most, by 2025. 

Q.WHAT INCREMENTAL CAPABILITIES WILL DERMS OFFER THAT GEORGIA POWER DOES NOT HAVE TODAY?
A.The principal value propositions of a DERMS are 1) Tracking types and capacities of (large) DER installed on each circuit; and 2) Monitoring and controlling large customer DERs and relevant field equipment settings remotely.

Q.ARE THESE CAPABILITIES REQUIRED DURING THE RATE CASE PERIOD?
A.No. First, tracking the types and capacities of (large) DERs on each circuit is not a demanding task, particularly given the relatively small number of (large) DERs connected to the Company’s distribution grid. Hawaiian Electric Company tracks these DER attributes through the use of an inexpensive Demand Response Management System.  Second, the SCADA systems the Company currently uses to manage DERs on the Company’s transmission and distribution grids already offer the ability to monitor customer DERs and to disconnect them in an emergency. (Emergency situations are the only ones in which we believe the Company should be able to exert control over customer DER absent written customer permission. Please see the testimony of Staff Witness Ms. Barber for more on Company control over customer-owned DER.) Third, while there is some merit to a capability to control field equipment settings remotely, we believe few field devices with remote communication and control capabilities have been installed, and note that linemen can be dispatched to modify equipment settings in any event. In short, the small incremental benefits and the low DER penetration likely during the rate case period simply do not justify the extremely high DERMS price tag.   
 
Q.HOW MUCH CAPITAL INVESTMENT IS THE COMPANY REQUESTING TO INSTALL DERMS IN THIS RATE CASE?
A.Georgia Power is requesting $100 million to install DERMS in this rate case. This amounts to at least $120,000 per MW of installed DER capacity (000 at most) we expect will be installed on the Company’s distribution grid by the end of the rate case period. Given that the cost to install DER capacity is likely around $1.8 million per MW, the cost to implement DERMS is roughly equivalent to a minimum 6.7% cost premium on top of the costs the Company or its customers incur to install DERs. This represents a high level of overhead for very little benefit. 

Q.DO YOU HAVE ANY OTHER CONCERNS REGARDING THE COMPANY’S PROPOSAL TO INSTALL DERMS?
A. Yes. If approved by the Commission, the Company proposes to depreciate its DERMS investment over five years.  For such an extensive system with significant capabilities, we believe DERMS constitutes a major software package. Any DERMS spending the Commission authorizes should be depreciated over 10 years, not five, consistent with a major software classification. 

Q.WHAT IS YOUR RECOMMENDATION TO THE COMMISSION REGARDING THE COMPANY’S $100 MILLION REQUEST TO INSTALL A DERMS?
A.We recommend the Commission reject the Company’s capital request to install DERMS in its entirety due to the small incremental benefits and relatively low DER penetration the Company expects on its grids by the end of the rate case period. The fact that the Company is successfully managing large DERs connected to the Company’s grids today figures prominently into this recommendation. The Commission can always reconsider any capital requests to install DERMS the Company might make in the future as the number and capacity of large DERs on Company’s grid increases. This recommendation is reflected in the revenue requirement reductions addressed in the Smith-Trokey testimony.   
SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTMONY PROVIDING PERSPECTIVES ON T&D RATE INCREASES, RELIABILITY, AND INVESTMENTS/TIMING.
A.In the perspectives section we relayed that rate increases are bad for Georgia’s businesses, consumers, and economy unless accompanied by reliability improvements of sufficient value to outweigh them. We characterized Georgia Power’s Grid Investment Plan (GIP) as discretionary, citing as evidence 1) Georgia Power’s reliability is about average relative to other investor-owned utilities; 2) customers are satisfied with current levels of reliability; and 3) customers are unwilling to pay much for reliability improvements. We described the exceptional electricity bill increases (estimated by Staff at over 40%) that are heading toward Georgia in the next rate case period, stemming largely from sources outside of Commission control. We also noted that the results of over $1 billion in GIP spending to date will not be known or measurable for a few more years. Finally, we observe that even if the Commission rejects the Company’s proposed continuation of the GIP in its entirety (which we do not recommend), the proposed transmission and distribution capital spending that remains still constitutes a doubling of Georgia Power’s average annual investment from 2009 to 2019 (pre-GIP). We conclude this section of testimony by calling into question the timing, necessity, and wisdom of continued GIP spending in the upcoming rate case period. 

Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY AND RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING GEORGIA POWER’S TRANSMISSION INVESTMENT PLAN.
A.The transmission portion of the Company’s GIP (which we call the Transmission Investment Plan, or TIP) consists entirely of premature equipment replacement, or what the Company calls “the replacement of aging transmission infrastructure”. While laypersons are likely to perceive aging equipment replacement as reasonable and necessary, we exposed the replacement of equipment based on age as the wasteful and cost-ineffective practice that it is. We described the objective testing and inspection practices all utilities use to determine the appropriate times for equipment replacement, and how these practices plus “N-1” criterion (redundant design and operation) make service interruptions resulting from transmission equipment failure exceedingly rare. For example, using Georgia Power’s own data, we calculated the likelihood that a substation power transformer will both fail and result in a service interruption at 45 in 10,000 per year. To summarize, the opportunity to improve reliability through preemptive equipment replacement is almost zero to begin with, making the extremely costly and wasteful practice unnecessary and unreasonable. We recommend the Commission reject the transmission portion of the GIP in its entirety as a result, which still leaves a 171% increase over historical spending levels in place. 

Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY AND RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING GEORGIA POWER’S PROPOSED DISTRIBUTION INVESTMENT PLAN.
A.We began with a summary of the distribution portion of Georgia Power’s GIP, which we refer to as the Distribution Investment Plan (DIP). We then critiqued the DIP, focusing on three problems: 1) The largest DIP investment packages by far, circuit hardening and undergrounding of overhead lines, are not cost-effective approaches to improving reliability; 2) The Company applies costly DIP investment packages to too many circuits which already demonstrate reasonably good reliability performance, further damaging the cost-effectiveness of the DIP; 3) The DIP ignores dramatically more cost-effective approaches to improving reliability, including vegetation management and worst-performing circuit programs; and 4) The DIP is causing premature retirements of distribution equipment operating safely and reliably, incurring large customer opportunity costs not otherwise being considered or accounted for. 

We also explained that the Commission should ignore the Company’s Customer Benefit Study, because that study is not a cost-benefit analysis of DIP packages, and therefore irrelevant to the task at hand (identifying the most cost-effective ways to improve reliability). We described our concern that the DIP is leading to premature equipment retirement, and our concerns regarding Georgia Power accountability for securing DIP-related reliability improvements. Finally, we summarized the Maryland Public Service Commission’s efforts to secure reliability improvements from utilities in a cost-effective manner, and concluded with a recommendation that the Commission reject Georgia Power’s requests for the circuit hardening and undergrounding capital components of the GIP in their entirety. We noted that the distribution capital budgets that remain still represent an increase of 55% over historical distribution capital spending pre-GIP, which should be more than enough to maintain and improve distribution reliability.   

Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY AND RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING GEORGIA POWER’S $100 MILLION PROPOSAL TO IMPLEMENT A DISTRIBUTED ENERGY RESOURCE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM.
In this section of testimony we described the challenges of managing high levels of distributed energy resources. But we also explained why utility claims that these challenges are imminent are generally overblown. We described how utilities with high levels of DER are managing the challenges, in at least one case (Hawaiian Electric Co., with extremely high levels of DER) with no DERMS at all. We identify the systems Georgia Power has been using to manage DER to date, and can continue to use in the future. Finally, we supported our belief that even under the most aggressive growth scenarios, Georgia Power DER levels will remain relatively low through 2025 as compared to other utilities. We recommend this proposed spending be postponed until some future rate case, when the level of distributed energy resources on Georgia Power’s grid provides sufficient justification for such a system.  

Q.DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCLUDING REMARKS FOR COMMISSION CONSIDERATION?
A.Yes. As indicated in our perspectives Section of testimony, the Company’s GIP spending is discretionary. However, the electric bill increases heading toward Georgia are unavoidable. Given our testimony on the cost-ineffectiveness of the transmission, circuit hardening, and undergrounding portions of the GIP, we are convinced these investments are not in the public interest. What’s more, there is no reliability emergency, and no harm in measuring the results of $1 billion in GIP spending to date, before approving more of the same. 

Finally, we believe the Commission should consider the positives of limiting T&D capital spending to “only” a doubling of pre-GIP levels. All businesses in Georgia other than regulated monopolies are required by market forces to restrain capital spending. The managers of these business face a constant challenge: how to deliver products and services the market wants for the least possible amount of capital. This forces them to restrict capital spending to only the most critical and immediate needs, and as a result, these businesses are putting their limited capital to its highest and best possible use. By rejecting some of the Company’s proposed capital spending through the recommendations we suggest, the Commission will simply be requiring the same type of discipline from the Company’s managers as other Georgia businesses must maintain. That is a very good thing. After all, utility regulation evolved as a way to replace the market forces lacking in authorized monopoly businesses.  

Q.DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR TESTIMONY?
A.Yes, it does.

Profile

After 15 years in Fortune 500 product development and product management, including P&L responsibility, Mr. Alvarez entered the utility industry by way of demand-side management rate and program development, marketing, and impact measurement for Xcel Energy in 2001. He has since designed renewable portfolio standard compliance and distributed generation rates and incentive programs. These experiences led to unique projects involving the measurement of grid modernization costs and benefits (energy, capacity, operating savings, revenue capture, reliability, environmental, and customer experience), which revealed conflicts between ratemaking and benefit maximization.  Since 2012 Mr. Alvarez has led the Wired Group, a boutique consultancy serving consumer, business, and environmental advocates, and regulators in matters of distribution planning, investment, and performance measurement.

Profile

Mr. Stephens has over 40 years’ experience in electric and gas distribution grid planning, design, operations management, and asset management, and the innovative use of technology to assist with these functions. He spent his entire career at Xcel Energy and its subsidiary Public Service Company of Colorado, a distribution utility serving 1.5 million electric customers and 1.4 million gas customers.  After a series of electrical and gas engineering and management roles of increasing responsibility, Mr. Stephens retired as the Director of Innovation and Smart Grid Investments for all of Xcel Energy’s electric and gas distribution businesses in 2011.  He now works for the Wired Group and its clients on a part-time basis.

A Customer Benefit Study of Distribution Investment for the Georgia Power Company System


August 2022
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Electric utility customers expect and depend on high levels of service reliability at a reasonable cost.  As such, when developing a reliability improvement plan, a diligent utility must carefully evaluate the costs and benefits that accrue to customers under such a plan.  The purpose of this Distribution Investment Study for the Georgia Power Company (“GPC”) system is to determine the range of investment in GPC’s distribution system that is optimal from a customer perspective. 

This study is an updated version of the Economic Benefit Analysis completed in 2019 and reviews a revised Distribution Investment Plan that reflects lessons learned over the last 3 years. This study analyzes the best set of investments to be made under the Grid Investment Plan starting in 2023. This study concludes that the revised 8-year investment plan in the amount of ~$3.4B is within the optimal range of investment. 

As background, GPC conducted an Economic Benefit Analysis on its original Distribution Investment Plan in 2019 to ensure that the plan was within the optimal range of investment from a customer perspective. The original plan was a ~$4.9B, 11-year plan that sought to improve approximately 800 of GPC’s worst-performing distribution feeder circuits (also referred to as “circuits”) with a target end-state SAIDI of ~65 by 2031 (also referred to as “Original Plan”). 

GPC has updated the Original Plan based on lessons learned through the execution of the plan over the last 3 years. Changes from the Original Plan are primarily driven by:
(1) Revised investment criteria, which select circuits with sustained poor performance. 
(2) Increased capital requirements by investment package due to increases in the scope and cost of work required to achieve expected reliability improvements. 
(3) A refined optimization methodology which relaxes the investment package hierarchy used in 2019 and allows for a larger set of possible investments to be evaluated when determining the optimal set of investments for a given scenario.

The revised plan (also referred to as “Distribution Investment Plan” or “the Plan”) is expected to invest ~$3.4B over the remaining 8 years and achieve an end-state overall company SAIDI of ~80 by 2031. By targeting GPC’s worst-performing circuits, the plan strives to equalize the customer experience and improve overall company reliability.

To create the Distribution Investment Plan, 15 alternate investment plans were constructed targeting end-state system reliability scores ranging from ~155 SAIDI to ~30 SAIDI. The plan that resulted in the lowest total cost to the customer under the most sensible set of assumptions was selected as the go-forward Distribution Investment Plan (also referred to as the “Base Case”).    

Plans targeting end-state SAIDIs lower than ~80 represent higher levels of investment than the Base Case. Plans targeting end-state SAIDIs higher than ~80 represent lower levels of investment than the Base Case.  The “No Incremental-Investment” plan represents a scenario in which GPC does not invest any incremental capital in its distribution system above historical levels, leading to a forecasted decline in GPC reliability and an end-state SAIDI of ~155 by 2031.  See III.A for further discussion of investment scenarios.

Consistent with findings from the Original Plan, the Base Case shows that higher levels of investment result in diminishing reliability improvement (see Figure 1). This is because circuits with the poorest reliability that represent the highest improvement opportunities are invested in first. Increasing capital investment means investing in circuits with relatively better reliability that represent lower improvement opportunities.  


Figure 1. Diminishing Reliability Improvement

As illustrated in Figure 1, incremental customer benefit from distribution investment levels off after a certain amount of spending.  The Base Case plan corresponds to the level of investment that includes the highest opportunity investments but excludes investments that produce diminishing returns. See III.B for further discussion of diminishing reliability improvement. 

To evaluate the Distribution Investment Plan from the customers’ perspective, the present values of three types of costs were evaluated for each scenario.  These include:
Capital Revenue Requirement: Capital revenue requirement refers to the direct monetary cost customers incur as a result of GPC’s capital investment. On a present value basis this is equal to the amount of capital GPC is required to spend under each scenario multiplied by GPC’s distribution capital k-factor of 0.00. See I.N for further discussion of capital revenue requirement assumptions and calculations.
Economic Cost:  Economic cost refers to the implicit costs customers incur as a result of outages. For the purposes of this study, economic cost strictly refers to the costs customers incur as a result of distribution outages in each scenario. See I.O for further discussion of economic cost assumptions and calculations.
Operations and Maintenance Expense (“O&M”):  In this study, O&M refers to outage repair-related and vegetation management O&M. Only these pieces of O&M are included, as investment in GPC’s distribution system will not impact other components of O&M.  See I.P for further discussion of O&M assumptions and calculations.

Because all of these costs are explicitly or implicitly borne by customers, an investment plan that minimizes the sum of these costs is considered to be within the optimal range of investment.

Figure 2. Present Value of Total Cost

Figure 2 demonstrates the total of these three costs (capital revenue requirement, economic cost, O&M) for each scenario. Moving from left to right along the chart’s x-axis, capital revenue requirements increase as more aggressive reliability targets are achieved, while both economic costs and O&M costs decrease. Of the 15 scenarios evaluated, the Base Case scenario results in the minimum present value of costs and should thus be seen as the preferred option for customers. 

Minimizing the present value of total customer cost is equivalent to maximizing the net present value of investment.  

Figure 3. Net Present Value

Figure 3 shows the net present value (“NPV”) of customer costs for each scenario.  The NPV for any given scenario (for example, scenario “S”) is calculated by taking the difference between the No Incremental-Investment scenario’s present value of costs and scenario S’s present value of costs. The Base Case scenario has the highest associated NPV of all scenarios and therefore creates more customer value than any other scenario analyzed.  See Section III for a further discussion of scenario cost calculation.

In addition, seven sensitivity analyses on key inputs to the model were conducted. While these sensitivities result in increases or decreases to the overall costs incurred by customers under each scenario, the Base Case plan remains in the optimal range of investment across all sensitivities.  As an example, Figure 4 shows a sensitivity on this study’s capital investment cost assumptions. To capture potential deviations from current investment cost estimates, cost assumptions were flexed up and down 10% to determine the impact on the optimal investment range. As shown in figure 4, the Base Case has the lowest total cost using both the 90% and 110% assumptions and therefore remains in the optimal range of investment under both assumptions. See Section IV for a further discussion of sensitivity analyses.

Figure 4. Investment Cost Sensitivity

Because the Distribution Investment Plan remains in the optimal range across all sensitivities, the Base Case investment plan should be considered the preferred option for GPC customers.

I.  ASSUMPTIONS
The following sections of this report provide detailed discussions related to the input assumptions associated with the 2022 Distribution Investment Plan.

Explanation of Investment Packages
The Distribution Investment Plan assumes that GPC distribution circuits can receive any one (or multiple) of 6 different “investment packages.” The menu of circuit investment packages was developed by GPC distribution engineers based on prior investments that GPC has successfully implemented in its distribution system. Packages are listed in Table I.1 below:

Table I. 1. Description of Investment Packages

Number
Name
Description
1
Add sectionalizing, DA devices
Install additional intelligent line devices on overhead line to achieve segmentation
2
Add / strengthen ties
For circuits without a tie:
Add new tie(s) to other circuit(s)
For circuits with existing tie(s):
Increase capacity of tie points that offer increased ability to restore load
In some cases, create a new tie on a radial branch of the circuit
3
Circuit hardening (BIL)
Replace wooden and steel pole arms with fiberglass brackets
Add wildlife protective equipment
4
Break feeder
Introduce a new source (e.g., new breaker at existing substation) to split an existing circuit into two smaller circuits while applying segmentation 
5
Relocate feeder; bring to road
Identify inaccessible lines and rebuild on private property along accessible roadway
6
Underground the feeder
Underground 100% of multiphase overhead lines

Criteria for each package are chosen to tailor package choice to each circuit based on that circuit’s specific characteristics.
