As shown in Table 4, the likelihood of a transmission outage while in service is very small based on the Company’s outage data history for the past ten years. This is because the Company is already maintaining transmission lines and associated station equipment under the Capital Maintenance and Reliability improvement programs. 
Q.IS THE COMPANY TAKING AN AGGRESSIVE APPROACH TOWARD TRANSMISSION INFRASTRUCTURE REPLACEMENT UNDER GIP?
A.Yes, the Company is taking an extremely aggressive approach to replacing transmission infrastructure under the GIP, which is unnecessary and results in steep rate increases for customers. The Company already has a replacement program under the Capital Maintenance and Reliability categories which is increasing further in 2023 - 2025.  Under these categories, the Company identifies and replaces assets requiring immediate replacement/repair based on objective inspections, tests, and other information.  The Company has relied on it in the past. It continues by using the industry-wide accepted, highly effective best practice of testing and inspecting each facility to identify the need for replacement. Such assets were repaired/rebuilt using informed decisions based on each facility's inspections, tests, and monitoring results rather than the age of the assets. As part of the GIP, the Company is clustering or grouping facilities to prioritize replacement by targeting the age of assets that exceeds the expected Company-defined useful life by 2031, irrespective of their actual operating performance.
Q.IS THE COMPANY’S APPROACH HARMFUL TO RATEPAYERS? 
A.Yes. This approach, from a financial perspective, is problematic in two ways : 1) the Company prematurely replacing assets that are performing safely and reliably with new ones that advance expenditures, and 2) unnecessarily resulting in a rate increase for the customers.
Q.HOW SHOULD THE COMPANY’S APPROACH TO GIP BE MODIFIED TO PROTECT RATEPAYERS? 
A.Transmission and distribution assets replacement prioritization must be based on objective testing and inspection results not just the age of the asset. This can be achieved by replacing assets using ongoing corrective maintenance (i.e., replacing/repairing an asset that has been damaged or has failed its tests or inspections or those rarely failed in service) as part of the Capital Maintenance and Reliability categories/plans. 
Q.DOES THE GIP DIVERT INVESTMENTS AWAY FROM WHERE THEY ARE MOST NEEDED?
A.All electric utilities are facing regulatory and public pressure to upgrade existing infrastructure while holding down costs and rates to customers and using the approved dollars wisely. The Company is requesting about $335 million per year for the next three years to proactively replace transmission assets based solely on age. The proposed GIP will dispose of some healthy, functional transmission assets and replace them with new ones, thus diverting investments from where they are most needed. On the other hand, if the Company continues to monitor and maintain its infrastructure transmission assets under the Capital Maintenance and Reliability categories and determines which assets are at the most significant risk of failure based on operating data and testing and where those failures would have the most significant impact, will result in transmission assets at risk receiving the full attention and priority they merit. This approach will prevent resources from being diverted away from more critical areas. It will also make the most efficient use of the Company’s transmission investment dollars while ensuring the system operation is safe and reliable. The Company’s ongoing routine-based Capital Maintenance program for maintenance, repair, and replacement is simple to implement, and highly predictable, which helps with planning spending and investments.
Q.WILL THE COMPANY’S MAINTENANCE COST BE REDUCED SIGNIFICANTLY WITH THE PROPOSED GIP?
A.No. The Company’s maintenance cost will not be reduced significantly with the proposed GIP. In most industries, such as manufacturing, revenue-generating assets are replaced due to increased maintenance costs or because newer assets have dramatic productivity improvements. The situation is different with the transmission asset management in electric utilities. There are no significant improvements in productivity, and maintenance cost is only slightly reduced with the new assets. The company’s primary focus is replacing the  infrastructure, and Operations and Maintenance (O&M) expense reduction is not the primary driver. The O&M expense reduction savings by replacing the transmission assets with newer ones is only expected to be about $6 million annually. 
  Q.DID THE COMPANY CONDUCT A COST-BENEFIT ANALYSIS TO EVALUATE THE DIRECT BENEFITS TO THE RATEPAYERS IN TERMS OF REDUCTIONS IN CUSTOMER OUTAGES AND DURATIONS OR RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENTS?
A.No.  In this Rate Case filing and discovery, the Company indicated that a cost/benefit study was not conducted for the proposed transmission investments. Furthermore, the Company did not perform the risk failure analysis using the historical failure data to justify the transmission assets replacements offered under the GIP. 
Q. DID THE COMPANY EXPLAIN WHY NOT?
A.Yes, in discovery, the Company indicated that such a cost/benefit study for transmission is unnecessary because the investment is needed to replace aging infrastructure. 
Q.DO YOU HAVE ANY THEORIES AS TO WHY THE COMPANY IS PROPOSING SUCH A MASSIVE TRANSMISSION INVESTMENT PLAN THAT WILL NOT RESULT IN ANY RELIABILITY IMPROVEMENT?
A.One theory is that the Company is interested in unnecessarily growing the rate base., The Company is front-loading transmission investments under the pretext of GIP.
CONCLUSIONS - SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS
Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY
A.As part of the Company's GIP, the Company will replace transmission lines prematurely. The practice of replacing equipment solely based on its age is not cost-justified and inefficient. This is because the GIP plan will:
Replace transmission assets that are healthy and functioning safely and reliably and have some life left in them. This practice will increase the replacement cost unnecessarily,
Not deliver customer reliability improvements sufficient to outweigh corresponding rate increases,
Not reduce O&M expenditures significantly,
Divert investment dollars away from funds needed in other important areas.

Instead, the replacement of transmission lines must continue based on the objective testing and inspection practices the Company is already using. These preventive, corrective, and condition-based maintenance practices allow the Company to determine the appropriate times for transmission line replacement. The Company’s ongoing Capital Maintenance program and associated corrective maintenance for transmission replacement are simple to implement and highly predictable, which will result in transmission assets at risk receiving the full attention and priority they merit. Furthermore, this approach will make the most efficient use of the transmission investment dollars while ensuring the system operation is safe and reliable and will prevent resources from being diverted away from more critical areas.
Q.WHAT RECOMMENDATIONS DO YOU MAKE? 
A. I recommend that the Commission require the Company to ensure that transmission assets replacement and rebuild projects are selected based on current health assessments and performance using physical inspections and objective tests under the ongoing Capital Maintenance and Reliability improvement plans, and not just based on the Company-defined age criterion. 
I recommend that the Commission enhance the oversight of approved transmission investment to ensure confidence that reasonable project implementation cost estimates are being made, ensure estimates are reasonable, and ensure that transmission builds are appropriately managed and completed within the 2023-2025 timeframe to contain costs consistent with initial cost estimates (i.e., avoid cost overruns during replacements).
Furthermore, I recommend that the Commission consider limiting the transmission costs exceeding estimates by a certain percentage to ensure that the Company's capital expenditures on transmission infrastructure are cost-effective and prevent cost escalation.
Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE SPENDING ADJUSTMENTS RECOMMENDED IN YOUR TESTIMONY
A.Table 5 below summarizes my recommended spending adjustments associated with the GIP. The details of these adjustments along with the other spending adjustments to the distribution lines and the transmission and distribution (T&D) station equipment spending are addressed in the companion testimony of Staff Witnesses Messrs. Paul J. Alvarez and Dennis Stephen. These adjustments are translated into revenue requirement reductions in the testimony and exhibits of Staff Witnesses Mr. Ralph Smith and Mr. Robert Trokey.

Q. WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS TO THE COMPANY’S RATEPAYERS IF THE COMMISSION FOLLOWS YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS?
A.In the short term, the ratepayers will benefit by avoiding unnecessary rate increases. This is very important for ratepayers because multiple sources of significant rate increases will be coming in the next few years. Furthermore, continuing the transmission assets replacement under the Capital Maintenance and Reliability categories based on objective tests and monitoring will ensure that the transmission assets at the highest risk for failure and where those failures would have the most significant impact will make the best use of the transmission investment dollars in ensuring safe and reliable transmission system.  Also, the unnecessary replacement of healthy and performing transmission assets could be prevented, thereby not diverting the resources and investments from where they are most needed.

 1          2023-2025 on behalf of the customers. This represents a significant increase of 360% of
 2          over the annual transmission expenditure for the 2009-2021 period. The Company proposes
 3          to invest about $1.2 billion per year in transmission under the GIP over 2023 – 2025 as part
 4          of these massive transmission investments. Under the Grid Investment Plan (GIP) for 2023-
 5          2025, the Company is proposing to use the Company-defined age criteria solely to replace
 6          transmission lines and associated station equipment prematurely irrespective of their actual
 7          operating performance. Furthermore, the assets slated for replacement have passed periodic,
 8          objective tests and inspections and performing reliably. The industry standard and most
 9          economical way to replace transmission lines and the associated equipment is based on the
10          approaches that the Company is successfully applying now under the Capital Maintenance

12          on the results of the objective tests, monitoring, and data analysis to identify equipment for
13          replacement. The GIP will not improve reliability for customers and will only reduce O&M

15          as the rates will increase.    I will explain why premature equipment replacement is

 6              $1.2 billion and distribution is about $1.1 billion per year. The Company has defined six

 7              types of investments as part of this proposed transmission grid expenditure plan. These

 8              categories (types) include 5:

 9              - New Business: Facilities required to provide service to new customers and new load.

10              - Growth/Load Flow: facilities required to address customer load growth and changing

11              generation impacts. This includes new distribution feeders, new transmission lines and

12              substations, and land for future use.

14              relocations.

15              - Reliability: Facility upgrades that include substation relay modifications, replacement of

16              obsolete equipment, insulation and grounding improvements, and grid modernization

17              projects.

18              - Capital Maintenance: Includes replacement of broken poles, replacement of

19              deteriorating conductor with an equivalent conductor, and replacing damaged or failed

21   Q.        THE COMPANY HAS FOCUSED ON THE AGE OF INFRASTRUCTURE AS A

22             DETERMINING FACTOR TO JUSTIFY THE REPLACEMENT OF

23             TRANSMISSION LINES AND THE ASSOCIATED EQUIPMENT THAT HAVE

24             EXCEEDED THEIR COMPANY-DEFINED USEFUL LIFE UNDER THE GIP


     10
          Company Exhibit APA/SPA/ADH/MBR-8

                                                  Page 11 of 12

     DOCKET NO. 44280                                                 TESTIMONY OF RAJ RANA
                                                                   PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION
 1        CATEGORY. IS THIS A REASONABLE APPROACH TO JUSTIFY THE

 2        REPLACEMENT OF AGING TRANSMISSION ASSETS?

 3   A.   No. Using the Company-defined expected useful life is not a reasonable and cost-effective

 4        approach to determining the replacement of the transmission infrastructure. The

 5        Company’s primary focus is on the age of the assets to develop the transmission

 6        replacement plan and uses a Companywide grouping method to identify the highest

 7        priority replacement based on age. The Company is employing a practice of proactively

 8        rounding up (grouping or clustering) the transmission assets for replacement based on age,

 9        not whether such assets are operating reliably and safely, and simply because they have

10        exceeded their Company-defined expected useful life. The useful life can be used as a

11        starting point for screening. Still, it must not be used solely in decision-making to target a

12        transmission infrastructure for replacement. Replacement of aging infrastructure can

13        reduce operations and maintenance expenses slightly, but prematurely replacing

14        infrastructure before it shows signs of reduced performance or failure results in

15        accelerated and unnecessary capital spending, which is not cost-effective. Identifying the

16        highest priority replacements must be based on monitoring, inspections, and objective test

17        data and analytics, not just because such facilities meet or exceed the Company-defined

18        useful life criterion.

19   Q.   WHAT CRITERIA DOES THE COMPANY USE TO JUSTIFY FACILITY

20        REPLACEMENT UNDER THE GIP?


                                              Page 12 of 13

     DOCKET NO. 44280                                                     TESTIMONY OF RAJ RANA
                                                                       PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION
 1   A.        The criteria used for the transmission asset replacement by the Company are shown in

 2             Table 3 11. The age of the transmission line (conductor or structure or both) is compared to

 3             the Company’s thresholds for expected useful life to determine when a transmission line

 4             has exceeded the Company’s criteria for expected useful life. As noted above expected

 5             useful life is a reasonable screen to determine which transmission lines may be best

 6             candidates for replacement but actual performance metrics should be the deciding factor.

 7             The expected useful life for conductors and structures of transmission lines is developed

 8             by Company’s internal subject matter experts based on operational experience. The

 9             transmission line is a replacement candidate if the age of the transmission line under

10             evaluation exceeds the Company’s criteria for expected useful life. However, the cut-off

11             percentages used in these criteria are also developed by Company’s internal subject matter

12             experts based on operational experience not supported by formal analysis. As part of the

13             $10 billion grid reliability and resiliency initiative, the Company has installed new

14             technologies, such as modern sensors, communications devices, and other hardware that

15             allow transmission assets to be tracked and controlled remotely and collect health data

16             remotely. New technologies also include analytical tools for processing, interpreting, and

17             responding to data from transmission assets that use real-time performance data to guide

18             asset replacement decisions rather than relying solely on the Company-defined useful life

19             and aged-based asset replacement criteria without considering actual operating

20             performance.

 1   Q.   HOW SHOULD THE COMPANY’S APPROACH TO GIP BE MODIFIED TO

 2        PROTECT RATEPAYERS?

 3   A.   Transmission and distribution assets replacement prioritization must be based on objective

 4        testing and inspection results not just the age of the asset. This can be achieved by

 5        replacing assets using ongoing corrective maintenance (i.e., replacing/repairing an asset

 6        that has been damaged or has failed its tests or inspections or those rarely failed in service)

 7        as part of the Capital Maintenance and Reliability categories/plans.

 8   Q.   DOES THE GIP DIVERT INVESTMENTS AWAY FROM WHERE THEY ARE

 9        MOST NEEDED?


10   A.   All electric utilities are facing regulatory and public pressure to upgrade existing

11        infrastructure while holding down costs and rates to customers and using the approved

12        dollars wisely. The Company is requesting about $335 million per year for the next three

13        years to proactively replace transmission assets based solely on age. The proposed GIP

14        will dispose of some healthy, functional transmission assets and replace them with new

15        ones, thus diverting investments from where they are most needed. On the other hand, if

16        the Company continues to monitor and maintain its infrastructure transmission assets

17        under the Capital Maintenance and Reliability categories and determines which assets are

18        at the most significant risk of failure based on operating data and testing and where those

19        failures would have the most significant impact, will result in transmission assets at risk

20        receiving the full attention and priority they merit. This approach will prevent resources

21        from being diverted away from more critical areas. It will also make the most efficient use

22        of the Company’s transmission investment dollars while ensuring the system operation is


                                              Page 17 of 18

     DOCKET NO. 44280                                                      TESTIMONY OF RAJ RANA
                                                                        PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION
 1           safe and reliable. The Company’s ongoing routine-based Capital Maintenance program for

 2           maintenance, repair, and replacement is simple to implement, and highly predictable,

 3           which helps with planning spending and investments.


 4   Q.      WILL THE COMPANY’S MAINTENANCE COST BE REDUCED

 5           SIGNIFICANTLY WITH THE PROPOSED GIP?

 6   A.      No. The Company’s maintenance cost will not be reduced significantly with the proposed

 7           GIP. In most industries, such as manufacturing, revenue-generating assets are replaced

 8           due to increased maintenance costs or because newer assets have dramatic productivity

 9           improvements. The situation is different with the transmission asset management in

10           electric utilities. There are no significant improvements in productivity, and maintenance

11           cost is only slightly reduced with the new assets. The company’s primary focus is

12           replacing the infrastructure, and Operations and Maintenance (O&M) expense reduction

13           is not the primary driver 19. The O&M expense reduction savings by replacing the

14           transmission assets with newer ones is only expected to be about $6 million annually. 20

     distribution systems, which brings higher reliability for customers. We will get to a more aggressive modernization of
     the generating fleet overtime. But in the near term,

     DOCKET NO. 44280                                                  TESTIMONY OF RAJ RANA
                                                                    PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION
 1        IV. CONCLUSIONS - SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS


 2   Q.     PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY

 3   A.     As part of the Company's GIP, the Company will replace transmission lines prematurely.

 4          The practice of replacing equipment solely based on its age is not cost-justified and

 5          inefficient. This is because the GIP plan will:


 6             •     Replace transmission assets that are healthy and functioning safely and reliably
 7                   and have some life left in them. This practice will increase the replacement cost
 8                   unnecessarily,
 9             •     Not deliver customer reliability improvements sufficient to outweigh
10                   corresponding rate increases,
11             •     Not reduce O&M expenditures significantly,
12             •     Divert investment dollars away from funds needed in other important areas.
13
14          Instead, the replacement of transmission lines must continue based on the objective testing

15          and inspection practices the Company is already using. These preventive, corrective, and

16          condition-based maintenance practices allow the Company to determine the appropriate

17          times for transmission line replacement. The Company’s ongoing Capital Maintenance

18          program and associated corrective maintenance for transmission replacement are simple to

19          implement and highly predictable, which will result in transmission assets at risk receiving

20          the full attention and priority they merit. Furthermore, this approach will make the most

21          efficient use of the transmission investment dollars while ensuring the system operation is

22          safe and reliable and will prevent resources from being diverted away from more critical

23          areas.


24   Q.     WHAT RECOMMENDATIONS DO YOU MAKE?


                                                Page 20 of 21

     DOCKET NO. 44280                                                TESTIMONY OF RAJ RANA
                                                                  PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION
 1   A.   I recommend that the Commission require the Company to ensure that transmission assets

 2        replacement and rebuild projects are selected based on current health assessments and

 3        performance using physical inspections and objective tests under the ongoing Capital

 4        Maintenance and Reliability improvement plans, and not just based on the Company-

 5        defined age criterion.

 6        I recommend that the Commission enhance the oversight of approved transmission

 7        investment to ensure confidence that reasonable project implementation cost estimates are

 8        being made, ensure estimates are reasonable, and ensure that transmission builds are

 9        appropriately managed and completed within the 2023-2025 timeframe to contain costs

10        consistent with initial cost estimates (i.e., avoid cost overruns during replacements).


11        Furthermore, I recommend that the Commission consider limiting the transmission costs

12        exceeding estimates by a certain percentage to ensure that the Company's capital

13        expenditures on transmission infrastructure are cost-effective and prevent cost escalation.

19        are addressed in the companion testimony of Staff Witnesses Messrs. Paul J. Alvarez and

 3   Q.      WHAT ARE THE BENEFITS TO THE COMPANY’S RATEPAYERS IF THE

 4           COMMISSION FOLLOWS YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS?


 5   A.      In the short term, the ratepayers will benefit by avoiding unnecessary rate increases. This

 6           is very important for ratepayers because multiple sources of significant rate increases will

 7           be coming in the next few years 26. Furthermore, continuing the transmission assets

 8           replacement under the Capital Maintenance and Reliability categories based on objective

 9           tests and monitoring will ensure that the transmission assets at the highest risk for failure

10           and where those failures would have the most significant impact will make the best use of

11           the transmission investment dollars in ensuring safe and reliable transmission system.

12           Also, the unnecessary replacement of healthy and performing transmission assets could be

13           prevented, thereby not diverting the resources and investments from where they are most

14           needed.

                           Qualifications of Michael P. Gorman


Q.   Please state your name and business address.
A.   Michael P. Gorman. My business address is 16690 Swingley Ridge Road, Suite 140,
     Chesterfield, MO 63017.


Q.   Please state your occupation.
A.   I am a consultant in the field of public utility regulation and a Managing Principal with the
     firm of Brubaker & Associates, Inc. (“BAI”), energy, economic and regulatory consultants.


Q.   Please summarize your educational background and work experience.
A.   In 1983 I received a Bachelor of Science Degree in Electrical Engineering from Southern
     Illinois University, and in 1986, I received a Master’s Degree in Business Administration
     with a concentration in Finance from the University of Illinois at Springfield. I have also
     completed several graduate level economics courses.


     In August of 1983, I accepted an analyst position with the Illinois Commerce Commission
     (“ICC”). In this position, I performed a variety of analyses for both formal and informal
     investigations before the ICC, including: marginal cost of energy, central dispatch, avoided
     cost of energy, annual system production costs, and working capital. In October of 1986,
     I was promoted to the position of Senior Analyst. In this position, I assumed the additional
     responsibilities of technical leader on projects, and my areas of responsibility were
     expanded to include utility financial modeling and financial analyses.


     In 1987, I was promoted to Director of the Financial Analysis Department. In this position,
     I was responsible for all financial analyses conducted by the Staff. Among other things, I
     conducted analyses and sponsored testimony before the ICC on rate of return, financial
     integrity, financial modeling and related issues. I also supervised the development of all
     Staff analyses and testimony on these same issues. In addition, I supervised the Staff's
     review and recommendations to the Commission concerning utility plans to issue debt and
     equity securities.

                                                                             Exhibit___(MPG-1)
                                                                                     Page 2 of 3
     In August of 1989, I accepted a position with Merrill-Lynch as a financial consultant. After
     receiving all required securities licenses, I worked with individual investors and small
     businesses in evaluating and selecting investments suitable to their requirements.


     In September of 1990, I accepted a position with Drazen-Brubaker & Associates, Inc.
     (“DBA”). In April 1995, the firm of Brubaker & Associates, Inc. was formed. It includes
     most of the former DBA principals and Staff. Since 1990, I have performed various
     analyses and sponsored testimony on cost of capital, cost/benefits of utility mergers and
     acquisitions, utility reorganizations, level of operating expenses and rate base, cost of
     service studies, and analyses relating to industrial jobs and economic development. I also
     participated in a study used to revise the financial policy for the municipal utility in Kansas
     City, Kansas.


     At BAI, I also have extensive experience working with large energy users to distribute and
     critically evaluate responses to requests for proposals (“RFPs”) for electric, steam, and gas
     energy supply from competitive energy suppliers. These analyses include the evaluation
     of gas supply and delivery charges, cogeneration and/or combined cycle unit feasibility
     studies, and the evaluation of third-party asset/supply management agreements. I have
     participated in rate cases on rate design and class cost of service for electric, natural gas,
     water and wastewater utilities. I have also analyzed commodity pricing indices and
     forward pricing methods for third party supply agreements, and have also conducted
     regional electric market price forecasts.


     In addition to our main office in St. Louis, the firm also has branch offices in Corpus
     Christi, Texas; Detroit, Michigan; Louisville, Kentucky and Phoenix, Arizona.


Q.   Have you ever testified before a regulatory body?
A.   Yes. I have sponsored testimony on cost of capital, revenue requirements, cost of service
     and other issues before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and numerous state
     regulatory commissions including: Alaska, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Colorado,
     Delaware, the District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa,

                                                                           Exhibit___(MPG-1)
                                                                                   Page 3 of 3
     Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota,
     Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New
     York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South
     Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia,
     Wisconsin, Wyoming, and before the provincial regulatory boards in Alberta, Nova Scotia,
     and Quebec, Canada. I have also sponsored testimony before the Board of Public Utilities
     in Kansas City, Kansas; presented rate setting position reports to the regulatory board of
     the municipal utility in Austin, Texas, and Salt River Project, Arizona, on behalf of
     industrial customers; and negotiated rate disputes for industrial customers of the Municipal
     Electric Authority of Georgia in the LaGrange, Georgia district.


Q.   Please describe any professional registrations or organizations to which you belong.
A.   I earned the designation of Chartered Financial Analyst (“CFA”) from the CFA Institute.
     The CFA charter was awarded after successfully completing three examinations which
     covered the subject areas of financial accounting, economics, fixed income and equity
     valuation and professional and ethical conduct. I am a member of the CFA Institute’s
     Financial Analyst Society.

Introduction and Summary
Q.PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND OCCUPATION.
A.My name is Lance D. Kaufman.  I am a consultant providing expert testimony before state public utility commissions in the Northwest, Southwest and Intermountain West and Georgia.
Q.PLEASE IDENTIFY THE PARTY ON WHOSE BEHALF YOU ARE TESTIFYING.
A.I am testifying on behalf of the Georgia Public Service Commission Public Interest Advocacy Staff (“Staff”).  
Q.Please summarise your background and professional experience.
A.I have a Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Oregon with field work in industrial organization and econometrics. I have worked in the utility industry for 10 years performing analysis and providing testimony on depreciation, cost of capital, rate spread and rate design, net power costs, cost allocations, decoupling mechanisms, load forecasting, and resource planning. I am a Certified Depreciation Professional. My Curriculum Vitae is provided in Exhibit LK-1.
Q.PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS.
A.I make the following recommendations:
Use the 2022 IRP economic lives of 2054 and 2058 as the terminal retirement dates for Hatch Units 1 and 2 respectively.
Remove the 25 percent contingency adder from the terminal net salvage of coal and gas production facilities.
Require the Company to file a decommissioning study of solar assets as part of its next rate case.
Calculate remaining lives using the survival curves identified in Exhibit LK-2 pages 20 through 22.
Overview of Depreciation Rates and Expense
Q.What is Depreciation Expense?
A.Depreciation is an expense that represents recovery of the Company’s capital investment over the expected life of the investment. Depreciation expense also accounts for the expected cost of removal (COR) and salvage value over the expected life of the investment.
Q.How does recovery of investment differ from return on investment?
A.Recovery of investment is the recovery of the original investment, while return on investment represents the financing cost on the asset. Assets are financed with a combination of debt and equity.
Q.How is depreciation expense calculated?
A.Depreciation expense is calculated by multiplying the gross plant balance in each Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) account or subaccount by a depreciation rate specific to that account or subaccount. Depreciation rates are approved by the Commission in each general rate case and typically are not changed between rate cases. Depreciation rate recommendations made to the Commission are usually supported by a depreciation study.
Q.What are GEORGIA POWER Company’s recommendations for depreciation rates and what are they based on?
A.Georgia Power Company’s (Company or Georgia Power) proposed depreciation rates are contained in Appendix Exhibit 2 of the Company’s filing. This appendix is a depreciation study performed on behalf of Georgia Power by the Alliance Consulting Group (“Alliance Study”). The Alliance Study includes a general discussion of depreciation at pages 6 through 20. I agree with this general discussion and refer the Commission to it for detail on how depreciation rates are calculated. However, I disagree with certain parameters and findings in the Alliance Study related to specific assets and plant accounts. In this testimony I identify the parameters that I disagree with, recommend alternate parameters, and provide the rates resulting from these alternate parameters. 
Q.What General issues do you raise in this testimony?
A.I address the terminal retirement date for Hatch plant, the decommissioning costs for coal and gas plants, and the survivor curves used to model future retirements.
Q.How should the Commission evaluate and resolve the disputed issues that you raise?
A.The Commission should weigh the evidence in the record that is specific to each plant or account and make a conclusion about the expected retirement outcomes based on that evidence. 
Q.How does chanGing a depreciation rate impact BoTH the Company and Customers?
A.The primary function of depreciation is to allocate costs to customers across time over the service life of the asset. Thus, an increase or decrease in depreciation rates does not have a direct impact on the total amount collected from customers or returned to the Company over time. The primary impact from changing a depreciation rate is the year in which the capital is fully recovered. A lower depreciation rate shifts the recovery of invested capital from the current time period to a future time period. A higher depreciation rate shifts the recovery of invested capital from a future time period to a current time period. 
Q.Why do your recommendations focus on the expected retirement outcomes?
A.A commonly accepted premise of fairness is that those who benefit from a cost should bear the cost. This concept is applied when using cost of service studies to support the allocation of costs across customers. The same concept is used to support the recovery of capital across time. Customers benefit from utility plant only as long as the plant is in service. Thus, the recovery of the investment in plant should be spread across time that plant is expected to be in service. Depreciation rates calculated based on expected retirement outcomes accomplish this goal.
Q.IS IT SOUND POLICY to collect extra expense in order to establish a buffer for unexpected retirements or cost of removal?
A.No, this is not sound policy for several reasons. Expected outcomes are outcomes that represent what is expected on average. While retirements occasionally exceed or fall short of expectations, these shortfalls and excesses are expected to balance out.  One property of a depreciation system is that it typically provides a mechanism for these shortfalls and excesses to accumulate and offset over time. Both the Alliance Study and my analysis adopt the Average Remaining Life Procedure. This procedure spreads excess and deficient depreciation reserves across the remaining lives of assets. In addition to the remaining life procedure, reserve transfers and regulatory asset accounting can be used to mitigate and address temporary excesses or shortfalls.
Because the expected outcome represents the outcome that is most likely to happen, collecting extra depreciation expense to establish a buffer beyond the expected outcome will over-allocate costs to current customers. This is unfair to current customers.
Q.The Alliance Study notes that informed judgment plays a role in studying depreciation. How do you recommend informed judgment be applied? 
A.The National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (“NARUC”) publication “Public Utility Depreciation Practices” offers the following guidance on the use of informed judgment:
The use of informed judgment can be a major factor in forecasting. A logical process of examining and prioritizing the usefulness of information must be employed, since there are many sources of data that must be considered and weighed by importance. For example, the following forces of retirement need to be considered: Do the past and current service life dispersions represent the future? Will scrap prices rise or fall? What will be the impact of future technological obsolescence? Will the company be in existence in the future? The analyst must rank the factors and decide the relative weight to apply to each. The final estimate might not resemble any one of the specific factors; however, the result would be a decision based upon a combination of the components.

The NARUC manual highlights that informed judgment is a logical process that employs specific information and factors. This is important because it means that, when informed judgment is applied, the information considered and the logic that was applied should be identifiable. In this testimony, when I apply informed judgment, I identify the factors that I considered and the logic that I apply in order to aid the Commission in determining whether my judgment is reasonable. 
Q.What Guidance can aid the Commission in weighing the merits of the informed judgment that you apply and that of the Company?
A.I recommend the Commission apply the results of academic research into the reliability of judgmental forecasts. This research offers five principles for reliable judgmental forecasting:
Organize and present information in a form that clearly emphasizes relevant information.
Limit the amount of information used in judgmental forecasting. Use a small number of particularly important cues.
Use mechanical methods to process information.
Combine several forecasts.
Require justification of forecasts.
I applied these principles in developing the recommendations in my testimony. However, I recommend the Commission place particular emphasis on the final principle of justification of forecasts. This principle is important to follow in a regulatory setting.
Q.How are depreciation rates calculated?
A.The depreciation expense for an account is an amount that, if collected over the average remaining life for the assents in the account and combined with current accumulated depreciation, will be equal to the amount that needs to be recovered, or the original investment in the assets less expected net salvage. Annual depreciation expense, or accrual, is expressed as a formula below.

The depreciation accrual rate is a rate that, when multiplied by the total investment or plant balance, will return the depreciation expense. This is expressed as a formula below.

Exhibit LK-2 contains the calculation of depreciation rates based on my recommendations. Working backwards through the calculations on Exhibit LK-2 page 1, the Accrual Rate-Staff Proposed (depreciation rate) column is the Annual Depreciation Amount divided by the Plant in Service. Thus, when the depreciation rate is multiplied by the Plant in Service it will result in the Annual Depreciation Amount. The Annual Depreciation Amount is the Amount to Be Recovered divided by the Remaining Life. The Amount to Be Recovered is the Plant in Service minus Net Salvage Amount minus Allocated Depreciation, and the Net Salvage Amount is the Amount to Be Recovered multiplied by the Net Salvage %.
Thus, the depreciation rate requires four inputs, Plant In Service, Allocated Depreciation (or Reserve), Net Salvage %, and Remaining Life, and the depreciation rate is calculated with the following formula:

Plant in Service and Reserve are typically undisputed values that are adopted from the utility’s accounting records. The primary focus of a depreciation study is the calculation of the net salvage rate and remaining life. 
Q.How do the issues you mentioned earlier regarding terminal retirement date, decommissioning costs, and Survivor Curves relate to the net salvage rate and remaining life?
A.The terminal retirement date affects the remaining life calculation for assets where an entire group of assets is scheduled to be retired collectively, such as generating units. The decommissioning cost is an input into the net salvage rate for assets that are decommissioned as part of terminal retirement. The survivor curves are statistical distributions that are used to calculate the remaining lives of assets.


Terminal Retirement Dates
Q.What Terminal Retirement Dates are proposed by the Company for Hatch Nuclear Plant depreciation rates?
A.The Company uses a terminal retirement date of 2038 for Hatch Common and Hatch Unit 2, and a terminal retirement date of 2034 for Hatch Unit 1 when calculating depreciation rates.
Q.What are the Company’s expected terminal retirement dates for the Hatch plant?
A.The Company currently expects to retire Hatch Unit 1 in 2054 and Unit 2 in 2058. In Docket No. 44160 the Company requested and received Commission approval for the capital and O&M costs that the Company will incur for the subsequent license renewal for Plant Hatch Units 1 and 2. The Company expects to submit an application for, and receive approval of, a license extension of this plant.
Q.How has the Commission treated depreciation lives for nuclear plants prior to final NUCLEAR REGULATORY COMMISSION (“NRC”) approval for past licence extensions?
A.The Commission has granted extended depreciable lives prior to final approval in the past. In the Company’s 2007 rate case docket, Docket No. 25060, the depreciable life for the currently operating Plant Vogtle Nuclear Units 1 and 2 was extended prior to NRC approval of the corresponding license extensions. 
Q.Does the Company agree that the Commission’s treatment of Vogtle’s depreciable life can reasonably be applied to Hatch?
A.The Company has agreed that if the facts and circumstances for the Hatch plant are similar to those of Vogtle, it is reasonable to apply a similar treatment of depreciable life to the Hatch plant.
Q.Are the facts and circumstances of Hatch simmilar to Votgle?
A.Yes.  While there are some differences between these two plants, these differences are immaterial in the context of setting depreciation rates. Depreciation rates reflect expectations about future plant retirements. While there is a small chance that the Hatch plant will not have its license extended, the expected outcome is a life extension, and thus depreciation rates should reflect this.
Q.What is the basis for your judgment that the expected outcome for the Hatch Plant is retirement in 2054 and 2058?
A.I considered that the Company currently expects to apply for and receive a license extension for such dates. Based on the information provided by the Company, it appears highly likely that the extension will occur. There is a small but unquantified chance that the Company does not receive the license or finds it economical to retire early despite the license extension. However, given the current national concerns regarding fuel security, energy diversity, and greenhouse gas emissions, this seems unlikely. There is also a small chance that the Company extends the life beyond 2058. I concluded that impact of these alternate outcomes offset each other, and a reasonable expectation is to rely on the expected outcome of retirement in 2054 and 2058.
Q.What is the impact of your recommendation?
A.Exhibit LK-2 pages 1 through 15 provides a comparison of my recommended rates with the Company’s filed depreciation study. My recommendation reduces depreciation expense under December 31, 2020 plant balance by approximately $128 million per year. The impact of my recommendations within the overall context of Staff’s case is provided in the Direct Testimony and Exhibits of Ralph Smith and Robert Trokey.


Decommissioning Costs
Q.What treatment has the Company requested for generation plant decommissioning costs?
A.The Company has requested that the results of its most recent decommissioning study be implemented when calculating depreciation rates.
Q.What is your response to the Company’s recommendation?
A.The Company’s study appears reasonable for hydro generation. However, decommissioning expense for coal and gas plants appear overstated while decommissioning expense for solar plants appear understated. I recommend that the contingency component of coal and gas plants be removed from depreciation rates and that the Company be required to submit a revised study of solar decommissioning costs in its next general rate case.

Of these plants, two plants, McDonough-Atkinson and Branch, have completed decommissioning and have similar size characteristics to the Company’s four remaining coal plants.

Q.Should contingency costs be included in depreciation rates?
A.No, depreciation rates should reflect expected outcomes rather than unexpected outcomes. Contingency costs are costs that are intended to account for unexpected outcomes.
Q.What is your recommendation regarding coal plant decommissioning?
A.I recommend that contingency cost be removed from the coal plant terminal retirement cost forecast.

Solar Plant
Q.Please Summarize your analYsIs of Solar plant decommissioning costs.
A.The Company has assumed no net decommissioning costs for its solar facilities. This assumption is not realistic as solar facilities are expected to have decommissioning costs. One solar developer has estimated solar decommissioning costs to range from $25,000 to $50,000 per MW. However, these estimates are not specific to the Company’s facilities. Although there is no basis for the Company’s assumption of no cost, I do not recommend an alternate rate because a formal study of the Company’s specific costs has not been performed. I recommend the Commission approve the Company’s proposed solar decommissioning expense, but also direct the Company to sponsor a solar decommissioning study of Company owned solar facilities and to incorporate these costs into its next depreciation study.


Remaining Lives
Q.How is an Account’s Expected Remaining Life Calculated?
A.Remaining life is determined by modeling when each asset in an account is expected to retire. Like humans, not all assets retire at the same age. The average age of human retirement in the United States is currently 61 years old, but some retire before or after that age. . Retirements of both people and assets follow a statistical distribution, and the shape of that distribution determines the average age of retirement. The figures below illustrate examples of different distributions, expressed as percent surviving. This figure expresses distributions as proportion surviving. In depreciation studies, retirement distributions are typically represented in this format and referred to as survivor curves.
Figure 1

 
Remaining life is the difference between current age and retirement age. For any given retirement distribution, remaining life is a function of current age. In the simplest example, suppose every person retires at age 61, and no person retires early or late. Under this distribution remaining life follows the function:

Different retirement distributions have different remaining life functions; however, each retirement distribution corresponds to a single remaining life function. Remaining life is thus dependent on the expected distribution of future retirements. 
Q.How is the distribution of future retirements determined?
A.The distribution of retirements is typically expressed as a distribution shape, an average age, and for some accounts a terminal retirement date. The Alliance Study estimates distribution shape and average age by visually matching historical retirements to various standardized survival curves. For example, for the account 392.21 Light Trucks the Alliance Study recommends the use of the L1.5 shaped Iowa curve and an average life of 6 years. This distribution produces a reasonable visual fit of the historic data, as seen below.
Figure 2: Company Proposed Survivor Curve for Account 392.2

The Alliance Study also notes that judgment was applied in modeling survivor curves. For some specific curves the Alliance Study’s recommended fit is, even on a visual basis, poor. I understand that for these curves the Alliance Study may be relying on the application of judgment to substantiate deviating from historic data. An example of a poor visual fit is provided below.
Figure 3: Company Proposed Survivor Curve for Account 397

I have alternate recommendations for some accounts where the Alliance Study recommends a curve that visually deviates from historic data. These alternate recommendations are based in part on a difference in judgment. The Alliance Study provides the following information regarding judgment:
Where there are multiple factors, activities, actions, property characteristics, statistical inconsistencies, property mix in accounts, or a multitude of other considerations that affect the analysis (potentially in various directions), judgment is used to take all of these considerations and synthesize them into a general direction or understanding of the characteristics of the property.  Individually, no one consideration in these cases may have a substantial impact on the analysis, but overall, the collective effect of these considerations may shed light on the use and characteristics of assets.  

The Alliance Study’s description of the use of judgment is problematic because it includes a long menu of factors and involves an ill-defined process of synthesis and is not transparent. This contradicts the principles of judgmental forecasting that fewer factors be considered and that forecasts be justified. The Alliance Study’s approach to judgment also conflicts with the NARUC depreciation guidance that judgment involve giving specific weight to specific factors.

Easements
Q.What are the characteristics of easements that affected your judgment?
A.Easements are not physical assets that degrade and fail over time. The Company’s easements have a theoretically unlimited life, but individual easements may be vacated if the Company no longer uses the easement. Thus, if an easement is never vacated, the easement will never be retired.
Q.What is your recommendation for Account 350 Transmission Easements and how does it compare to The Company’s recommendation
A.The figure below illustrates both Georgia Power and Staff’s proposed distributions for Account 350 Transmission Easements. 
Figure 4: Account 350 Transmission Easements

The Original Curve reflects the historic data. The solid blue line reflects the Company’s proposed square (SQ) survival curve with an average life of 85 years. The blue line with x represents the Staff proposal of an S6 curve and an average life of 120 years. The Company’s recommendation provides a poor visual fit after age 85 because the original survivor curve remains at 100 percent while the Company’s proposed survivor curve drops to zero percent, resulting in 100 percent error in every age after 85 years.
The Company offers the following rationale for these parameters: “Since the longest life in this functional group is 85 years, this study recommends retaining an 85-year life and SQ dispersion for this account.” While not explicitly stated, the underlying assumption is that all transmission easements will survive for the expected average life of the longest lived transmission asset (in this case transmission structures and improvements), and that all easements will be abandoned the year following the average life. 
The unreasonableness of this assumption is demonstrated by the Company’s grid investment program. As transmission assets are retired in the grid investment program, rather than vacating the corresponding easements, the Company is rebuilding transmission assets, thus extending the expected use of the transmission easements. There is no technology currently being contemplated that would lead to the wholesale abandonment of the Company’s easements.  While it is possible that the Company occasionally abandons transmission easements in the future, I expect that the majority of the Company’s easements will be retained as transmission lines are rebuilt rather than retired and vacated. While technological change could bring about a systematic retirement of transmission lines, no such change is likely to occur in the near future.
The historic data indicates 100 percent survival for throughout the entire age range, which is nearly 110 years. Thus, it is reasonable to expect that the actual average life will exceed 110 years by some amount. A square curve is an unreasonable shape for this asset because it is extremely unlikely that all transmission easements will be retired at a fixed age. Every retirement curve, other than a square curve, that fits the historic data predicts life in excess of 140 years. I recommend adopting the 120-S6 curve because this curve is consistent with historical data and the Company’s reinvestment in aging transmission but does not assume substantial life beyond the observed data. This recommendation also gives some weight to the Company’s forecast of an 85-year average life by shortening the life indicated by historical data, which suggests an average life of at least 140 years.
Q.What is your recommendation for the account 360 distribution easements?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 5: Account 360 Distribution Easements

As with the transmission easement account the Company proposes a square curve but with a shorter average life of 70 years. The Company’s proposed curve is a poor visual fit of the data after the age of 70. The Company makes this proposal “Based on lives for many assets in this function.” The rationale for the Company’s recommendation in this account suffers from the same flaws as transmission easements. Specifically, it is unlikely for distribution easements to be vacated after the retirement of the distribution assets associated with the easements. It is more reasonable to expect that the Company replaces retired distribution assets, extending the life of the distribution easement.
I recommend the 100-S6 curve be used for this account for similar reasons as Account 350. I recommend a lower average life for the distribution easement relative to transmission because my recommendation includes consideration of the Company’s forecast, and because the historic data includes some retirements.
Q.What is your recommendation for the account 389 General Plant Easements?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 6: Account 389 General Plant Easements

The Company recommends an SQ curve with a 60-year average life. The Company’s proposed curve is a poor fit of the data after age 30. The Company’s recommendation for this curve is different than its recommendation for the other easement accounts. The Alliance Study states “Since most of the assets in this account have retained the existing life, this study recommends retention of the existing 60-year life with an SQ dispersion.” The Company’s justification appears to be circular, as the reason that the assets have retained the existing life is that the study recommends retention of the existing life. 
Unlike transmission and distribution easements, the Company’s data shows material retirements of general plant easements. I recommend the use of an R2 curve with a 100-year average life. This results in a curve that visually fits the data when less weight is placed on the oldest historical retirements. My recommendation is based primarily on the Company’s historical retirements.
Structures and Improvements
Q.What common factors affect your analysis of structures and improvements accounts?
A.Structures and improvements accounts include building structures, individual components of structures such as roofs, lighting, and heating, and other property improvements such as fencing. Typically, the primary building structures account for most of the total value in these accounts. Certain building types and systems can, with proper maintenance, survive for hundreds of years or more. Other types of buildings with less durable materials or more integrated materials have can have lives from 50 to 100 years, and individual building components such as roofing and lighting typically range in expected life from several years to 40 or more years. Changing land value or land use typically drives the retirement of entire building systems rather than failure of the primary building structure. For accounts with terminal retirement dates, building structures are expected to survive.
Q.What is your recommendation for the account 331 Steam Structures and Improvements?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 7: account 331 Steam Structures and Improvements

The Company proposes an R2.5 curve with an average age of 100 years. This curve begins to deviate from the actual retirement data at an age of 20 years and exhibits substantial deviation for survival past 50 years. The Alliance Study offers no explanation for the basis of the proposed curves or the deviation from the historic data. The primary structures for this account house coal generation facilities and are unlikely to be retired prior to the terminal retirement dates for the corresponding units. Furthermore, many of these units are approaching retirement. As assets approach terminal retirement maintenance becomes more economical than replacement. Deteriorating building systems such as roofing and heating that would typically be replaced mid-life are more economical to repair towards a plant’s end of life because of the short duration over which replacement facilities would function. I recommend the use of an R2.5 curve with a 120-year average life. This recommendation is based on the factors described above and includes consideration of the Company’s analysis and expectations.  
Q.What is your recommendation for the account 352 Transmission Substation Structures and Improvements?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 8: Account 352 Transmission Substation Structures and Improvements

The Company proposes an R2.5 curve with an 85-year average life. The Company’s proposed curve is a poor fit of historic data for assets of 50 years old. The Company justifies its proposed curve based on the potential for the Grid Investment Program to retire some substation structures. However, the Grid Investment Program is only expected to affect 2.6 percent of substations over the next three years. Furthermore, brownfield substation investments will retain all structures except control houses, and control houses are expected to be more robust in the future.
I recommend an R2 survival curve with a 100-year average life be used for this account. This recommendation is based on a visual fit of the data, with less weight placed on the ages 70 through 100 to reflect the potential impact of the Grid Investment Program and the Company’s expectation that control houses will be more robust in the future. 
Q.What is your recommendation for the account 361 Distribution Substation Structures?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 9: Account 361 Distribution Substation Structures

The Company proposes an R2.5 survivor curve with an average life of 70 years. This curve results in a marginal deviation from the data for ages 20 through 40 and deviates materially from the historical data after age 50. The Company bases its recommendation on the potential impact of the Grid Investment Program and actuarial analysis. As I noted for Account 352 however, the Grid Investment Program affects only 2.6 percent of the Company’s substations and will therefore have a minimal impact on the average life. Furthermore, the Actuarial analysis does not support the Company’s recommended curve. Staff proposes a curve that has an improved fit for both the 20 to 40 age band and the 50 and later ages. Staff proposes an R1.5 curve with an 85-year average life. This recommendation provides an improved fit of the Company’s data and remains consistent with the Company’s expectations related to the Grid Investment Program and more robust control houses.
Q.What is your recommendation for the account 390 General Structures and Improvements?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 10: Account 390 General Structures and Improvements

The Company proposes an R1 survivor curve with an average life of 55 years. This curve deviates materially from the historical data between ages 40 and 90. The Company’s recommended curve is based on Company expectations regarding the lives of various building components ranging from 15 to 55 years and the main structures of the buildings surviving 60 to 80 years. As with the other structure accounts, I recommend basing the survivor curve for this account on historic data with less weight given to the oldest assets. I recommend an R0.5 curve with a 65-year average life. Unlike my recommendations for most other asset accounts, my recommendation for this account materially exceeds the actual percent surviving for later ages. I attribute this to a single abnormal retirement that is not representative of expected outcomes. My consistent treatment of placing less weight on tail or older aged portions of the historic survival curves is consistent with the Alliance Study which, quoting Depreciation Systems, states “Points at the end of the curve are often based on fewer exposures and may be given less weight than those points based on larger samples.” My recommendation for this account applies judgment that is consistent with the judgment used for my other recommendations. I consistently recommend curves that are fit to the Company’s historic data but that have lower weight placed on the oldest portions of the survivor curves.
Miscellaneous Accounts
Q.What is your recommendation for the account 332 Reservoirs, Dams, and Waterways?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 11: 332 Reservoirs, Dams, and Waterways

The Company proposes an R4 survivor curve with an average life of 100 years. This curve deviates materially from the historical data after 60 years of exposure. The Company provides no basis for its proposed curve or to justify the deviation from historic data. I recommend an R4 curve with an average life of 120 years. The majority of assets in this account are concrete structures or earthworks that will not be retired until the terminal retirement of corresponding hydro facility. Other hydro asset accounts have a similar length of history but display substantially greater retirements. This indicates that the retirement experience of the older assets in this account is reliable. 
I recommend an R4 curve with a 120-year average life be used for this account. This recommendation reflects consideration of the Company’s opinion regarding the appropriate shape of the retirement curve while also incorporating the extended average life suggested by actual retirement data and the fact that most assets in this account will survive to terminal retirement. I understand that the Company is undertaking a hydro modernization program to extend the lives of some hydro facilities. However, based on my review of the retirement units in this Account I do not expect the modernization to result in a material change in the Company’s actual survival curve because most of the value in these accounts will not be retired as part of the modernization. Furthermore, my recommended curve shows a substantially shorter life than the company’s historic data indicate in order to account for the potential of the modernization project.

Figure 12: Account 353 Station Equipment

Q.What is your recommendation for the account 392.3 Heavy Trucks?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 13: Account 392.3 Heavy Trucks

The Company proposes an L0 survivor curve with an average life of 9 years. This curve results in a marginal deviation from the data for ages 3 through 25. The Company’s recommendation is based on actuarial analysis and information gathered from Company personnel, who report that certain trucks are used on double shifts, potentially increasing mileage. I recommend the use of an L0 curve with a 10-year average life. Actuarial analysis supports an L0 with 10 years over one with 9 years, as can be seen by the improved fit across the entire exposure period. 

Q.What is your recommendation for the account 392.4 Trailers and ATVs?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 14: Account 392.4 Trailers and ATVs

The Company proposes an L1.5 survivor curve with an average life of 8 years. This curve deviates materially from the historical data after year 8. The Company justifies the recommendation based on the variety of assets in the account and actuarial analysis. However, this curve performs poorly at modeling the mixed asset nature of the account, which has short lived assets like ATVs and long-lived assets such as trailers.   While the Company’s recommended curve fits the short-lived assets well, the fit of the Company’s recommended curve is poor for trailers which is reflected in the deviation of the fit after age 8. I recommend the use of an L0 curve with an average life of 10 years. This curve sacrifices some fit of the early survival curve but achieves a large improvement in the fit of the longer-lived assets.
Q.What is your recommendation for the account 397 COmmunications Equipment?
A.The figure below compares the Company’s historic data with the Company’s proposed survivor curves and Staff’s recommended survivor curve.
Figure 15 Account 397 Communications Equipment

The Company proposes an L0 survivor curve with an average life of 20 years. This curve deviates materially from the historical data after year 20. The Company’s recommendation is based on an input from Company personnel and life analysis results. However, the Company personnel input is that approximately half of the accounts value will consist of fiber, microwaves towers, and antennae, which have expected lives of 40 years. As with the previous account 392.4, the Company’s proposed curve in this account fits short lived assets well, but at the cost of poorly fitting the retirement characteristics of long-lived assets such as fiber. I recommend the use of an O3 curve with a 30-year average life. This curve provides a reasonable fit of the short-lived assets in this account while still appropriately representing expectations for longer lived assets. 
Q.What is your assessment of the Depreciation parameters not discussed in this testimony?
A.I have reviewed the proposed remaining lives and net salvage rates for each account in this case that accumulates depreciation. I found the remaining parameters proposed by the Company to be reasonable and consistent with the data and expectations.
Q.DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR TESTIMONY?
A.Yes.
