19   Q.    What is the market sentiment for utility investments?
20   A.    Again, the current market sentiment toward utility investments, rather than just general
21         corporate investments, is that the market is placing high value on utility securities,
22         recognizing their low risk and stable characteristics. Total expected returns on utility
23         stock is very heavily weighted by dividend yields and by expected stock price
24         appreciation. The utility industry’s ability to pay dividends has proven to be very stable
25         and predictable and a large portion of the expected return on utility stocks has very low
26         risk and uncertainty. In comparison, the expected returns on non-utility investments
27         place minimal to no weight on dividend yields and are primarily produced by stock price
28         appreciation. Stock price appreciation is far less predictable than stock yields, and thus
29         utility stock investments are considered low investment risk options.

 2        utility operating risk.

 4   Q.   Do you have any comments concerning Mr. Coyne’s contention that relying on
 5        projected market data is currently very important?
 6   A.   Yes. Mr. Coyne develops his CAPM and risk premium studies mainly relying on near-
 7        term and long-term projected interest rates. Mr. Coyne’s primary reliance on forecasted
 8        Treasury bond yields is unreasonable because he is not considering the highly likely
 9        outcome that current observable interest rates will prevail during the period in which
10        rates determined in this proceeding will be in effect. This is important because, while
11        current observable interest rates are actual market data that provide a measure of the
12        current cost of capital, the accuracy of forecasted interest rates is highly problematic.
13
14   Q.   Why do you believe that the accuracy of forecasted interest rates is highly
15        problematic?
16   A.   Over the last several years, observable current interest rates have been a more accurate
17        predictor   of    future   interest   rates     than    economists’   consensus   projections.
18        Exhibit___(MPG-23) illustrates this point. Specifically, on Exhibit___(MPG-23), under
19        Columns 1 and 2, I show the actual market yield for Treasury bonds at the time a
20        projection is made, and the corresponding projection for Treasury bond yields two years
21        in the future, respectively.
22                As shown in Columns 1 and 2 of Exhibit___(MPG-23), over the last several
23        years, Treasury yields were projected to increase relative to the actual Treasury yields at
24        the time of the projection. Column 3 shows the time period the projection is made to
25        represent. In Column 4, I show the actual Treasury yield two years after the forecast. In
26        Column 5, I show the actual yield change at the time of the projections relative to the
27        projected yield change.


                                                Docket No. 44280
                                     Direct Testimony of Michael P. Gorman
                                                Page 83 of 84

                                     Public Disclosure Version

 1               As shown in Exhibit___(MPG-23), economists have consistently projected that
 2        interest rates will increase over the near term. However, as shown in Column 5, those
 3        yield projections turned out to be overstated in almost every case.       Indeed, actual
 4        Treasury yields have decreased or remained flat over the last several years rather than
 5        increasing as the economists’ projections indicated. As such, current observable interest
 6        rates are just as likely to accurately predict future interest rates as are economists’
 7        projections.
 8

10   A.   Yes.

I.BACKGROUND AND QUALIFICATIONS
Q.Please state your names, titles, and business addresses.
A.My name is Stephen J. Baron.  I am President and a Principal of Kennedy and Associates.  My business address is 570 Colonial Park Drive, Suite 305, Roswell, Georgia, 30075.  
My name is Leah J. Wellborn.  I am Manager of Consulting at Kennedy and Associates.  My business address is 570 Colonial Park Drive, Suite 305, Roswell, Georgia, 30075.  

Q. WHAT CONSULTING SERVICES DOES KENNEDY AND ASSOCIATES PROVIDE?
A. Kennedy and Associates provides consulting services related to electric utility system planning, resource analysis, production cost modeling, ratemaking, finance, accounting, and industry policy issues.

Q.PLEASE PROVIDE SUMMARIES OF YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND AND EXPERIENCE.
A.Summaries of our education, experience, professional certifications, and testimony appearances are provided in Exhibits STF-BW-1 and STF-BW-2 for Mr. Mr. Baron and Ms. Wellborn, respectively.    

Q.HAVE YOU BOTH PREVIOUSLY TESTIFIED BEFORE THIS COMMISSION? 
A.Yes.  Mr. Baron and Ms. Wellborn have testified before this Commission on a number of occasions.  Most recently, Mr. Baron and Ms. Wellborn testified in the Georgia Power Company’s 2022 Integrated Resource Plan proceeding (Docket No. 44160).  

Q.ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING?
A.We are presenting testimony on behalf of the Commission’s Public Interest Advocacy Staff (“Staff”).

II.SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Q.WHAT ARE THE SPECIFIC ISSUES THAT YOU ADDRESS IN YOUR TESTIMONY?
A.The issues we address are associated with Georgia Power’s projected retail revenues, at present rates, for the test year in this case (12 months ending July 31, 2023) and each of the three Plan Years: 2023, 2024 and 2025.  For each of these four periods, the Company has developed a detailed revenue forecast that estimates the revenues that the Company will receive at present Commission approved rates.  In order to develop the revenue deficiency in this case, projected revenues at present rates are compared to the revenue requirement for each of the four periods.  The difference between these two amounts (revenues at present rates and revenue requirements) produces the amount of the revenue deficiency and rate increase that is necessary to recover the revenue requirement.  

The purpose of this testimony is to present our findings and recommend appropriate adjustments to the Company’s revenue projections based on the Staff’s independent development of alternative revenue forecasts for a number of rate classes. 

Q.PLEASE DESCRIBE THE ANALYSES THAT THE STAFF PERFORMED TO ASSESS THE REASONABLENESS OF THE COMPANY’S REVENUE FORECASTS FOR THE TEST YEAR AND THREE PLAN YEARS.
A.The Staff reviewed and analyzed approximately 50 Excel spreadsheets/models developed by the Company that ultimately rolled-up into the retail revenue forecasts shown in Exhibit APA-SPA-ADH-MBR-1, Schedule 1 Total Company (“Schedule 1”) for the test year and each Plan Year.  Schedule 1 provides the revenues used by the Company to determine the revenue deficiency in this case, both on a traditional basis and on a levelized basis.
The initial starting point for the development of the revenue forecast is the projection of base tariff revenues for each of the Company’s five rate classes (Residential, Commercial, Industrial, Governmental Lighting, MARTA).  These base tariff revenues are the revenues produced from the Company’s individual rate schedules.  In addition, there are revenues produced by various riders (“Recovery Tariffs”), fuel charges, and a number of adjustments that will be discussed subsequently in our testimony.  Table 1 below shows the components that comprise the Total Company retail revenues included in Schedule 1 for the test year, based on the original filing.  Also included are the adjustments made by the Company to Schedule 1 in the Supplemental Filing.
Table 1: GPC Test Year Projected Revenues ($000)

  Table 2 summarizes the information for the test year and each Plan Year. 
Redacted Table 2: GPC Projected Revenues ($000) – Test Year and Plan Years


As shown in Tables 1 and 2, the revenues produced by base tariffs (rate schedules) form the largest portion of total retail revenues.  All of these revenue projections are based on an assumption that current base tariff rates charges remain in effect in the test year and Plan Years without any rate change.  What does change, however, are rate class kWh sales, the number of customers in each rate class and the impact of these changes on the average rate produced by existing rate designs.  The Staff’s primary analysis focused on these base tariff revenue projections.  For the largest rate classes the Company relied on statistical regression models to develop average rate curves.  These average rate curves, when combined with the Company’s projected MWh sales forecasts developed in the recent IRP case produce projected base tariff revenues for each rate class and sub-class.  In its analysis, the Staff analyzed alternative specifications and estimation periods in cases where the staff believed that an alternative model would be more appropriate.  Based on this analysis, the staff developed three alternative average rate curve models.

Q.WHAT ARE THE STAFF’S RECOMMENDED ADJUSTMENTS TO THE COMPANY’S TEST YEAR AND PLAN YEAR RETAIL REVENUES?
A.Table 3 summarizes the Staff’s recommended adjustments to projected test year and Plan Year retail revenues.


Table 3 shows the Staff’s recommended adjustments based on both the Company’s original filing and its Supplemental Filing.  The Staff’s analysis indicates that retail revenues, based on current rates (i.e., no rate change) would be about $6 to $8 million higher than estimated by the Company.  As we will discuss subsequently, the Staff’s adjustments are based on the results using alternative statistical models that project average rates/kWh for four of the Company’s retail rate classes and sub-classes.  These model differences, when projected on a monthly basis for the period August 2022 through December 2025 produce a relatively small change in projected revenues.  For example, in the test year ending July 2023, the total retail revenues projected by the Company in its Supplemental filing are shown to be $8,100,247 ($000) (see page 4 of Schedule 1).  The Staff’s analysis produces a retail revenue amount that is about 0.1% greater [$8,106,282 ($000)].

Q.IS THE STAFF RECOMMENDING THAT THE COMMISSION ADOPT ITS ALTERNATIVE REVENUE PROJECTIONS?
A.Yes.  The Staff has incorporated its adjusted revenue projections in the overall recommended revenue deficiency in this case.   Staff believes that its alternative average rate curve models are more reasonable than the Company’s estimates, and therefore supports its retail revenue adjustments based on those alternative models. As we will explain in later in this testimony, the use of a projected test year or projected plan years requires numerous forecasts of revenues, expenses, investment, and other factors.  For the most part, the Staff agrees with the Company’s methodology used to project revenues.  The Staff’s alternative average rate curve statistical models, which rely on the same historic information as used by the Company in its analyses, are simply alternative statistical model specifications, which the Staff believes are more reasonable than the models developed by the Company.

III.REVIEW OF REVENUE FORECAST METHODOLOGY
ENERGY FORECAST
Q.WHAT WAS THE STARTING POINT FOR DEVELOPING THE REVENUE FORECASTS FOR EACH OF THE FOUR PERIODS?
A.Each of the four revenue forecasts (test year and three Plan Years) were developed using the identical methodology.  Separate forecasts were developed for each of the five rate classes (residential, commercial, industrial, governmental lighting and MARTA).  The forecasts are driven by the kWh energy sales forecasts presented by the Company in the 2022 IRP case and is designated as the B22 Forecast.  This rate class energy forecast was previously evaluated by the Staff in the IRP case.  The Staff did not recommend any adjustments to the energy sales forecast in the IRP case and the Company’s B22 sale forecast was approved by the Commission in its Order in that case.  The Company did not make any adjustments to the approved B22 sales forecast in its revenue forecast in this case.
REVENUE FORECAST
Q.HOW DID THE COMPANY DEVELOP ITS REVENUE FORECAST?

A. For the residential and parts of the commercial and industrial rate classes not associated with a real-time pricing (“RTP”) rate, the revenue forecast is based on the product of the B22 energy forecast each month and a projection of the average rate/kWh for the class (e.g., residential) or subclass within a class (e.g., commercial FPA, commercial Non-RTPFPA, commercial RTP CBL, industrial FPA, industrial RTP CBL, where “FPA” stands for fixed pricing alternative).  For the residential class and five commercial and industrial subclasses, the Company developed statistical regression models to forecast the average rate/kWh as a function of monthly average kWh usage per customer for the class or subclass.  For commercial and industrial RTP subclasses, and lighting and MARTA revenues, revenues were projected using a number of different methodologies, which will be discussed later in our testimony.   The methodology that the Company employed is much more complex than what was presented in its minimum filing requirements. 

In addition to the development of base tariff revenue forecasts described above, the Company also developed separate projections of rider revenues associated with Nuclear Construction Cost Recovery (NCCR), Demand Side Management (DSM), Environmental Compliance Cost Recovery (ECCR), and Municipal Franchise Fee (MFF) tariffs. 

Q. PLEASE EXPLAIN HOW THE REVENUE FORECAST CHANGES BY CLASS OVER THE FORECAST YEARS.
A. The Company provided estimates of forecasted retail revenues for the test year in this case (12 months ending July 31, 2023) and for three Plan Years (calendar years 2023, 2024 and 2025).  For the test year, the retail revenue forecast projects that the Company will receive $6,099,611 ($000) at present rates, excluding fuel adjustment charges.  Table 4 provides a breakdown of the Company’s overall forecast into 5 rate classes (Residential, Commercial, Industrial, Government Lighting (“GL”, “Light”), and MARTA.  All of the Company’s revenue projections are based on these 5 rate classes.  These revenue forecasts are then allocated to individual rate schedules within each rate class.  These amounts estimate the projected revenues for the test year without a rate case and rate increase.  It is from this estimate that the rate increase is measured (the amount of the dollar increase).

Table 4: GPC Projected Test Year Base and Rider Revenues ($000)

It should be noted that this total revenue amount does not include fuel revenues or a number of adjustments to tie to Schedule 1 revenues.  These will be discussed later in our testimony.

FORECAST COMPONENT REVIEW
Q. YOU NOTED PREVIOUSLY THAT THE STAFF FOCUSED ITS ANALYSES ON THE BASE TARIFF PROJECTIONS THAT RELIED ON STATISTICAL AVERAGE RATE CURVE MODELING.  WOULD YOU DISCUSS THE COMPANY’S AVERAGE RATE CURVE MODELING?
A. The Company derived its average rate curve models utilizing the EViews statistical software.  Each statistical regression model followed the same general specification; average cost per kWh for the rate class or, in the case of the commercial and industrial classes, by sub-class was the dependent variable and the independent variables consisted of various formulations of average kWh usage per customer and indicator variables (binary variables).  To produce the monthly revenue forecast, the projected average rate per kWh is multiplied by the kWh energy sales forecast for the rate class (or sub-class) using the B22 energy forecast presented in the recent IRP case.  

For certain classes (commercial incremental RTP, industrial incremental RTP, industrial NonRTPFPA, Government Lighting, MARTA), the revenue forecasts are derived using more direct approaches.  The forecasts are made up of numerous subparts that are summed together to derive the class forecast.  The subparts, or components, have specific short-hand, and generally include an average rate curve component, an “FPA” component which describes the Fixed Pricing Alternative rate design, or a Real Time Pricing (“RTP”) incremental rate and an RTP Customer Baseline Load (CBL) component. The total forecast can be distilled down into approximately 12 individual forecast components, as summarized in Table 6.  The Company’s forecasting approach breaks the commercial, industrial and MARTA rate classes into these separate groups (components) that reflect similar rate designs.  For example, customers taking service under the Commercial RTP rates pay separate charges for their CBL usage and their incremental usage.  Since the underlying rates for these two components (CBL, incremental usage) are priced differently, it is reasonable to separately develop revenue forecasts for each component.  These are then combined to develop the total Commercial RTP revenue projection.  The table describes the components of each forecasted revenue class as well as a note on Staff’s review and any proposed adjustment.

RESIDENTIAL
Q. HOW DID THE COMPANY ESTIMATE THE RESIDENTIAL CLASS BASE TARIFF REVENUES?
A. The Company modeled the residential class in total (i.e., no residential sub-class/rate schedule individual modeling) and derived an average rate curve to estimate revenues.  As described above, Staff estimated an alternative residential average rate curve model.  Based on this alternative model, the Staff determined that the residential class revenues should be increased for the four revenue forecast periods.  The Staff’s evaluation of the average rate curve models is discussed subsequently in our testimony.
COMMERCIAL
Q. HOW DID THE COMPANY ESTIMATE COMMERCIAL CLASS REVENUES?
A. The Company developed its commercial class revenue forecast based on three commercial sub-classes: FPA, NonRTPFPA and CBL RTP.  The FPA sub-class includes legacy customers who were on the rate beginning in 2011 and customers who have been on an RTP rate for three consecutive years.  The RTP revenue forecast is comprised of an RTP incremental component and a CBL component.  The CBL component is priced based on a standard tariff.  The “Com Incr RTP” component represents the non-fuel portion of the commercial class RTP rate (the fuel portion is included in overall retail fuel revenues).  This incremental non-fuel RTP revenue forecast is developed using spreadsheet analysis.  These revenues include both non-fuel RTP revenue produced by day ahead and hour ahead tariffs.
 
For the commercial FPA, non-RTPFPA and CBL forecasts, the Company developed average rate curve models as it did for the residential class.  The Staff’s evaluation determined that an alternative average rate curve model would be appropriate for the non-RTPFPA average rate curve model, which resulted in an adjustment to forecasted revenues.  The Staff’s evaluation of the average rate curve models is discussed subsequently in our testimony.

INDUSTRIAL
Q. HOW WERE THE INDUSTRIAL REVENUES DERIVED?
A.  Industrial Class Revenues were forecasted based on modeling of five components: 
Ind FPA: Industrial Fixed Pricing Alternative for eligible legacy customers and former RTP customers (average rate curve methodology)
Ind NonRTPFPA: Industrial Fixed Pricing Alternative for non-RTP revenues (trend analysis of average rate per kWh)
Ind CBL: Industrial Customer Baseline Load (average rate curve methodology)
Ind Adj: Industrial Adjustment (No adjustments in this forecast, zero value)
Ind Incr: Industrial Incremental prices (RTP)
As shown in Table 6, only two of the five Industrial sub-class forecasts are based on average rate curve modeling: the Ind FPA forecast and the Ind CBL forecasts.  For the Ind. NonFPARTP sub-class, revenues were projected based on a trend analysis of the average rate per kWh.  The Company’s trend forecast is based on a moving average using monthly data spanning Jan 2015 to Aug 2021 and repeats, by month, exactly for each forecast year.  

As in the commercial class, the “Ind Incr” component represents the non-fuel portion of the industrial class RTP rate (the fuel portion is included in overall retail fuel revenues).  This incremental non-fuel RTP revenue forecast is developed using spreadsheet analysis. This revenue includes both non-fuel RTP revenue produced by day ahead and hour ahead tariffs.

The Staff’s evaluation determined that an alternative average rate curve model would be appropriate for the industrial CBL sub-class, which resulted in adjustments to forecasted revenues.  The Staff’s evaluation of the average rate curve models is discussed subsequently in our testimony.
RTP
Q.HOW DID THE COMPANY DEVELOP ITS FORECASTS OF COMMERCIAL AND INDUSTRIAL INCREMENTAL RTP REVENUE?
A. Staff in its requests for all workpapers supporting the revenue forecast was finally provided, in an informal response, the derivation of the RTP component forecasts on August 26, 2022.  In the Company’s informal response, the derivation utilized a monthly day ahead and hour ahead price together with the monthly MWh estimated for both day ahead and hour ahead schedules despite describing an hourly methodology.  The Company further explained in follow up data responses, that the derivation of the monthly values was derived from hourly values.

MARTA
Q. WHAT IS YOUR ASSESSMENT OF THE COMPANY’S MARTA FORECAST?
A. The Company models the MARTA revenues following the MARTA tariff rate structure with blocked energy pricing.  The Company’s estimate was based on 2021 rates, and then adjusted up with a Year 3 adjustment to get the 2022 base rates as baseline for the projection in 2022-2025.

AVERAGE RATE CURVE AND STATISTICAL ANALYSES

Q. WOULD YOU DISCUSS THE COMPANY’S AVERAGE RATE CURVE STATISTICAL MODELING?
A. As shown in Table 6, the Company develops statistical regression models to forecast the average rate per kWh for six rate classes and sub-classes.  These models are all based on a general relationship between a rate schedule’s average rate per kWh and the average kWh usage per customer for the rate.  The estimated regression models are then used to forecast the average rate per kWh for the class using the Company’s B22 energy forecast (kWh per customer) that was presented in the 2022 IRP case.  The product of the forecasted average rate per kWh and the B22 forecasted kWh sales for the rate class or sub-class produces the base tariff revenue forecast.  The focus of the Staff’s review and analyses was on the various average rate curve statistical regression models.  The kWh energy sales forecast (“B22”) was already addressed by the Staff in the IRP case.  

Q.HOW DID THE COMPANY DEVELOP ITS MODELS?
A.Georgia Power Company uses a statistical analysis software package called “EViews” to develop its average rate curve models.  The Staff obtained EViews and was able to fully evaluate each of the Company’s models.  

Q.WHAT WERE THE RESULTS OF THE STAFF’S EVALUATION OF THE COMPANY’S AVERAGE RATE CURVE MODELS?
A.The Staff found that for three of the Company’s models, an alternative specification produced more reasonable statistical results.  The Company’s models used monthly binary variables for most months that were formed by taking the product of the average kWh usage in the month and a “1” if the observation was for the same month and a “0” if the month was different.  For example, if the observation was for January, the January binary variable would be equal to the average kWh use in the month times “1.”  If the observation was for February, the January binary variable would be equal to “0” (average kWh use in February times “0” equals “0”).  The effect of this modeling specification is that, in general, each month has its own estimated coefficient that relates average usage and the average rate per kWh.  While the Staff does not have concerns with this approach, it is somewhat similar to estimating separate average rate curve models for each month.  The Staff’s alternative models are based on modified specifications and estimation periods that the Staff believes are more appropriate.   Staff is recommending alternative rate curves that incorporate a number of adjustments.  The adjustments made by the Staff for each of the models are as follows: 
…………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………….

…………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………….

…………………………………………………

Q.HOW DO THE STATISTICAL RESULTS PRODUCED BY THE STAFF’S ALTERNATIVE MODELS COMPARE TO THE COMPANY’S MODELS?
A.Staff’s proposed alternate models perform about the same as the Company’s models, but one of the Staff models has a slightly lower R2 (the “Commercial NonRTPFPA” model).  The Staff believes that its revised models are less likely to overfit the data than the Company’s models.  Also, the Staff’s models tend to have a better pattern of residuals that the Staff believes support the use of the model adjustments.

Q.WHAT IS THE IMPACT OF USING THE STAFF’S ALTERNATIVE AVERAGE RATE CURVE MODELS ON THE REVENUE FORECAST FOR THE TEST YEAR AND THE THREE PLAN YEARS?
A.Using the Staff’s alternative average rate curve models produces an additional $6 million to $8 million of revenue at current rates for the four periods.  

Q.DOES THE STAFF BELIEVE THAT THE COMPANY’S AVERAGE RATE CURVE MODELS AND THE RELATED REVENUE FORECASTS ARE UNREASONABLE?
A.No.  As noted earlier in our testimony, the Staff did not identify any specific errors or significant problems with the Company’s analyses.  Rather, the Staff believes that its alternative models provide a more reasonable measure of projected test year and Plan Year revenues.

IV.RECOMMENDED REVENUE FORECAST DOCUMENTATION

Q. DOES STAFF HAVE ANY RECOMMENDATIONS TO ESTABLISH A REQUIREMENT FOR FILING DETAILED REVENUE FORECAST TESTIMONY AND WORKPAPERS IN FUTURE RATE CASES?
A. Yes.  Notwithstanding the Staff’s recommended test year and Plan Year revenue forecast adjustments, the Staff did not find specific problems with the Company’s overall revenue forecast process in this case.  However, in order to make this assessment, the Staff was required to issue multiple data requests for Excel workbooks, narrative explanations, and follow-on data requests in order to fully evaluate and understand the basis for the Company’s test year and three Plan Year projections.  The Company did not present any testimony on this important issue, nor did the Company file any supporting workpapers with its filing that would facilitate and independent evaluation by the Staff.  In the end, following the Staff’s formal and informal data requests, the Company provide numerous Excel workbooks containing about 50 individual Excel models that provide the support for its revenue forecasts.  The Company also provide a number of narrative descriptions supporting the development of the retail revenue projections for the four test periods (Test Year and Plan Years 2023, 2024 and 2025).

In future Georgia Power Company base rate cases, the Company should be required to file a complete set of workpapers, consistent with all of the Excel workbooks and spreadsheets ultimately provided to the Staff in this case.  This should be included in the minimum filing requirements.  In addition, the Company should file witness testimony supporting the revenue forecast for each rate class.  There should also be a complete set of Excel files that reconcile the various supporting workpapers and resulting rate class revenue forecasts to the retail revenues included in the Company’s revenue deficiency analysis. 

Q.DOES THIS COMPLETE YOUR TESTIMONY?
A.Yes.

10                      II.    SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS

11


12   Q.    WHAT ARE THE SPECIFIC ISSUES THAT YOU ADDRESS IN YOUR

13         TESTIMONY?

14   A.   The issues we address are associated with Georgia Power’s projected retail revenues, at

15        present rates, for the test year in this case (12 months ending July 31, 2023) and each of

16        the three Plan Years: 2023, 2024 and 2025. For each of these four periods, the Company

17        has developed a detailed revenue forecast that estimates the revenues that the Company

18        will receive at present Commission approved rates. In order to develop the revenue

19        deficiency in this case, projected revenues at present rates are compared to the revenue

20        requirement for each of the four periods. The difference between these two amounts

                                                      4

          GEORGIA POWER COMPANY’S                                TESTIMONY OF STEPHEN BARON &
          2022 RATE CASE                                                        LEAH WELLBORN
          DOCKET 44280                                               PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION


 1        (revenues at present rates and revenue requirements) produces the amount of the revenue

 2        deficiency and rate increase that is necessary to recover the revenue requirement.

 3


 4        The purpose of this testimony is to present our findings and recommend appropriate

 5        adjustments to the Company’s revenue projections based on the Staff’s independent

 6        development of alternative revenue forecasts for a number of rate classes.

 7

15        revenue deficiency in this case, both on a traditional basis and on a levelized basis.

16        The initial starting point for the development of the revenue forecast is the projection of

17        base tariff revenues for each of the Company’s five rate classes (Residential, Commercial,

18        Industrial, Governmental Lighting, MARTA). These base tariff revenues are the revenues

19        produced from the Company’s individual rate schedules. In addition, there are revenues

20        produced by various riders (“Recovery Tariffs”), fuel charges, and a number of adjustments

 2   Q.   IS THE STAFF RECOMMENDING THAT THE COMMISSION ADOPT ITS

 3        ALTERNATIVE REVENUE PROJECTIONS?

 4   A.   Yes.    The Staff has incorporated its adjusted revenue projections in the overall

 5        recommended revenue deficiency in this case. Staff believes that its alternative average

 6        rate curve models are more reasonable than the Company’s estimates, and therefore

 7        supports its retail revenue adjustments based on those alternative models. As we will

 8        explain in later in this testimony, the use of a projected test year or projected plan years

 9        requires numerous forecasts of revenues, expenses, investment, and other factors. For the

10        most part, the Staff agrees with the Company’s methodology used to project revenues. The

11        Staff’s alternative average rate curve statistical models, which rely on the same historic

12        information as used by the Company in its analyses, are simply alternative statistical model

13        specifications, which the Staff believes are more reasonable than the models developed by

14        the Company.

16               III.   REVIEW OF REVENUE FORECAST METHODOLOGY

17   ENERGY FORECAST

18   Q.   WHAT WAS THE STARTING POINT FOR DEVELOPING THE REVENUE

19        FORECASTS FOR EACH OF THE FOUR PERIODS?

 1   A.   Each of the four revenue forecasts (test year and three Plan Years) were developed using

 2        the identical methodology. Separate forecasts were developed for each of the five rate

 3        classes (residential, commercial, industrial, governmental lighting and MARTA). The

 4        forecasts are driven by the kWh energy sales forecasts presented by the Company in the

 5        2022 IRP case and is designated as the B22 Forecast. This rate class energy forecast was

 6        previously evaluated by the Staff in the IRP case. The Staff did not recommend any

 7        adjustments to the energy sales forecast in the IRP case and the Company’s B22 sale

 8        forecast was approved by the Commission in its Order in that case. The Company did not

 9        make any adjustments to the approved B22 sales forecast in its revenue forecast in this

10        case.4

11   REVENUE FORECAST

12   Q.   HOW DID THE COMPANY DEVELOP ITS REVENUE FORECAST?

13


14   A.   For the residential and parts of the commercial and industrial rate classes not associated

15        with a real-time pricing (“RTP”) rate,5 the revenue forecast is based on the product of the

16        B22 energy forecast each month and a projection of the average rate/kWh for the class

17        (e.g., residential) or subclass within a class (e.g., commercial FPA, commercial Non-

18        RTPFPA, commercial RTP CBL, industrial FPA, industrial RTP CBL, where “FPA”

19        stands for fixed pricing alternative). For the residential class and five commercial and


          4
           Response to STF-JKA 1-3.
          5
           Real-Time Pricing rates are retail tariffs available to customers that price energy at marginal prices.
          Generally, the energy sold at an RTP price is indicative of a market price with a risk adder.

                                                            10

          GEORGIA POWER COMPANY’S                               TESTIMONY OF STEPHEN BARON &
          2022 RATE CASE                                                       LEAH WELLBORN
          DOCKET 44280                                              PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION


 1        industrial subclasses, the Company developed statistical regression models to forecast the

 2        average rate/kWh as a function of monthly average kWh usage per customer for the class

 3        or subclass. For commercial and industrial RTP subclasses, and lighting and MARTA

 4        revenues, revenues were projected using a number of different methodologies, which will

 5        be discussed later in our testimony.    The methodology that the Company employed is

 6        much more complex than what was presented in its minimum filing requirements.6

 7


 8        In addition to the development of base tariff revenue forecasts described above, the

 9        Company also developed separate projections of rider revenues associated with Nuclear

10        Construction Cost Recovery (NCCR), Demand Side Management (DSM), Environmental

11        Compliance Cost Recovery (ECCR), and Municipal Franchise Fee (MFF) tariffs.

 1   FORECAST COMPONENT REVIEW

 2   Q.   YOU NOTED PREVIOUSLY THAT THE STAFF FOCUSED ITS ANALYSES ON

 3        THE BASE TARIFF PROJECTIONS THAT RELIED ON STATISTICAL

 4        AVERAGE RATE CURVE MODELING.                         WOULD YOU DISCUSS THE

 5        COMPANY’S AVERAGE RATE CURVE MODELING?

 6   A.   The Company derived its average rate curve models utilizing the EViews statistical

 7        software. Each statistical regression model followed the same general specification;

 8        average cost per kWh for the rate class or, in the case of the commercial and industrial

 9        classes, by sub-class was the dependent variable and the independent variables consisted

10        of various formulations of average kWh usage per customer and indicator variables (binary

11        variables). To produce the monthly revenue forecast, the projected average rate per kWh

12        is multiplied by the kWh energy sales forecast for the rate class (or sub-class) using the

13        B22 energy forecast presented in the recent IRP case.

14


15        For certain classes (commercial incremental RTP, industrial incremental RTP, industrial

16        NonRTPFPA, Government Lighting, MARTA), the revenue forecasts are derived using

17        more direct approaches. The forecasts are made up of numerous subparts that are summed

18        together to derive the class forecast. The subparts, or components, have specific short-

19        hand, and generally include an average rate curve component, an “FPA” component which

20        describes the Fixed Pricing Alternative rate design, or a Real Time Pricing (“RTP”)

21        incremental rate and an RTP Customer Baseline Load (CBL) component. The total forecast

                                                     17

     GEORGIA POWER COMPANY’S                                         TESTIMONY OF STEPHEN BARON &
     2022 RATE CASE                                                                 LEAH WELLBORN
     DOCKET 44280                                                        PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION


 1   can be distilled down into approximately 12 individual forecast components, as

 2   summarized in Table 6.8 The Company’s forecasting approach breaks the commercial,

 3   industrial and MARTA rate classes into these separate groups (components) that reflect

 4   similar rate designs. For example, customers taking service under the Commercial RTP

 5   rates pay separate charges for their CBL usage and their incremental usage. Since the

 6   underlying rates for these two components (CBL, incremental usage) are priced differently,

 7   it is reasonable to separately develop revenue forecasts for each component. These are

 8   then combined to develop the total Commercial RTP revenue projection. The table

 9   describes the components of each forecasted revenue class as well as a note on Staff’s

10   review and any proposed adjustment.


     8
       In the 2022 rate case, the Company did not include commercial or industrial adjustments in its base tariff
     forecasts.

 2   RESIDENTIAL

 3   Q.   HOW DID THE COMPANY ESTIMATE THE RESIDENTIAL CLASS BASE

 4        TARIFF REVENUES?

 5   A.   The Company modeled the residential class in total (i.e., no residential sub-class/rate

 6        schedule individual modeling) and derived an average rate curve to estimate revenues. As

 7        described above, Staff estimated an alternative residential average rate curve model. Based

 8        on this alternative model, the Staff determined that the residential class revenues should be

 9        increased for the four revenue forecast periods. The Staff’s evaluation of the average rate

10        curve models is discussed subsequently in our testimony.

                                                       19

          GEORGIA POWER COMPANY’S                                    TESTIMONY OF STEPHEN BARON &
          2022 RATE CASE                                                            LEAH WELLBORN
          DOCKET 44280                                                   PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION


 1   COMMERCIAL

 2   Q.   HOW DID THE COMPANY ESTIMATE COMMERCIAL CLASS REVENUES?

 3   A.   The Company developed its commercial class revenue forecast based on three commercial

 4        sub-classes: FPA, NonRTPFPA and CBL RTP. The FPA sub-class includes legacy

 5        customers who were on the rate beginning in 2011 and customers who have been on an

 6        RTP rate for three consecutive years.9 The RTP revenue forecast is comprised of an RTP

 7        incremental component and a CBL component. The CBL component is priced based on a

 8        standard tariff. The “Com Incr RTP” component represents the non-fuel portion of the

 9        commercial class RTP rate (the fuel portion is included in overall retail fuel revenues).

10        This incremental non-fuel RTP revenue forecast is developed using spreadsheet analysis.

11        These revenues include both non-fuel RTP revenue produced by day ahead and hour ahead

12        tariffs.

13


14        For the commercial FPA, non-RTPFPA and CBL forecasts, the Company developed

15        average rate curve models as it did for the residential class. The Staff’s evaluation

16        determined that an alternative average rate curve model would be appropriate for the non-

12                         value)

16        NonFPARTP sub-class, revenues were projected based on a trend analysis of the average

18        data spanning Jan 2015 to Aug 2021 and repeats, by month, exactly for each forecast year.

10   AVERAGE RATE CURVE AND STATISTICAL ANALYSES

11


12   Q.   WOULD YOU DISCUSS THE COMPANY’S AVERAGE RATE CURVE

13        STATISTICAL MODELING?

14   A.   As shown in Table 6, the Company develops statistical regression models to forecast the

15        average rate per kWh for six rate classes and sub-classes. These models are all based on a

16        general relationship between a rate schedule’s average rate per kWh and the average kWh

17        usage per customer for the rate. The estimated regression models are then used to forecast

18        the average rate per kWh for the class using the Company’s B22 energy forecast (kWh per


          14
               MARTA revenue forecast provided in STF-JKA-1-2 Attachment N TRADE SECRET.xlsx.

          GEORGIA POWER COMPANY’S                              TESTIMONY OF STEPHEN BARON &
          2022 RATE CASE                                                      LEAH WELLBORN
          DOCKET 44280                                             PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION


 1        customer) that was presented in the 2022 IRP case. The product of the forecasted average

 2        rate per kWh and the B22 forecasted kWh sales for the rate class or sub-class produces the

 3        base tariff revenue forecast. The focus of the Staff’s review and analyses was on the

 4        various average rate curve statistical regression models. The kWh energy sales forecast

 5        (“B22”) was already addressed by the Staff in the IRP case.

 6


 7   Q.   HOW DID THE COMPANY DEVELOP ITS MODELS?

 8   A.   Georgia Power Company uses a statistical analysis software package called “EViews” to

 9        develop its average rate curve models. The Staff obtained EViews and was able to fully

10        evaluate each of the Company’s models.

11


12   Q.   WHAT WERE THE RESULTS OF THE STAFF’S EVALUATION OF THE

13        COMPANY’S AVERAGE RATE CURVE MODELS?

14   A.   The Staff found that for three of the Company’s models, an alternative specification

15        produced more reasonable statistical results. The Company’s models used monthly binary

16        variables for most months that were formed by taking the product of the average kWh

17        usage in the month and a “1” if the observation was for the same month and a “0” if the

18        month was different. For example, if the observation was for January, the January binary

19        variable would be equal to the average kWh use in the month times “1.” If the observation

20        was for February, the January binary variable would be equal to “0” (average kWh use in


                                                     26

          GEORGIA POWER COMPANY’S                                        TESTIMONY OF STEPHEN BARON &
          2022 RATE CASE                                                                LEAH WELLBORN
          DOCKET 44280                                                       PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION


 1        February times “0” equals “0”). The effect of this modeling specification is that, in general,

 2        each month has its own estimated coefficient that relates average usage and the average

 3        rate per kWh. While the Staff does not have concerns with this approach, it is somewhat

 4        similar to estimating separate average rate curve models for each month. The Staff’s

 5        alternative models are based on modified specifications and estimation periods that the

 6        Staff believes are more appropriate. Staff is recommending alternative rate curves that

 7        incorporate a number of adjustments. The adjustments made by the Staff for each of the

 8        models are as follows:

17   Q.   HOW DO THE STATISTICAL RESULTS PRODUCED BY THE STAFF’S

18        ALTERNATIVE MODELS COMPARE TO THE COMPANY’S MODELS?

19   A.   Staff’s proposed alternate models perform about the same as the Company’s models, but

20        one of the Staff models has a slightly lower R2 (the “Commercial NonRTPFPA” model).15

21        The Staff believes that its revised models are less likely to overfit the data than the


          15
            R-squared (R2) is the Coefficient of Determination in a regression model. R2 is a measure of how well the
          model (independent variables) explain the variation in the dependent variable. Specifically, it measures the
          percentage of the variation in the dependent variable (average rate/kWh) that is explained by the model
          (average kWh usage per customer, binary variables).

          2022 RATE CASE                                                                  LEAH WELLBORN
          DOCKET 44280                                                         PUBLIC DISCLOSURE VERSION


 1        Company’s models.16 Also, the Staff’s models tend to have a better pattern of residuals

 2        that the Staff believes support the use of the model adjustments.17

 3


 4   Q.   WHAT IS THE IMPACT OF USING THE STAFF’S ALTERNATIVE AVERAGE

 5        RATE CURVE MODELS ON THE REVENUE FORECAST FOR THE TEST

 6        YEAR AND THE THREE PLAN YEARS?

 7   A.   Using the Staff’s alternative average rate curve models produces an additional $6 million

 8        to $8 million of revenue at current rates for the four periods.

 9


10   Q.   DOES THE STAFF BELIEVE THAT THE COMPANY’S AVERAGE RATE

11        CURVE MODELS AND THE RELATED REVENUE FORECASTS ARE

12        UNREASONABLE?

13   A.   No. As noted earlier in our testimony, the Staff did not identify any specific errors or

14        significant problems with the Company’s analyses. Rather, the Staff believes that its

15        alternative models provide a more reasonable measure of projected test year and Plan Year

16        revenues.


          16
             A model that overfits the sample data results in independent variables that appear to be significant in
          explaining the dependent variable, but in fact are just explaining the residuals. This can lead to incorrect
          conclusions in the analysis and unreliable forecasts.
          17
             A requirement of a linear regression model is that the residuals (the difference between the model predicted
          value and the actual value) follows a normal probability distribution. To the extent that an estimated model
          produces residuals that are not normally distributed (i.e., deviate from the normality assumption), tests of
          significance of the estimated coefficients may not be reliable.

 2         IV.     RECOMMENDED REVENUE FORECAST DOCUMENTATION

 3


 4   Q.   DOES STAFF HAVE ANY RECOMMENDATIONS TO ESTABLISH A

 5        REQUIREMENT            FOR      FILING      DETAILED         REVENUE          FORECAST

 6        TESTIMONY AND WORKPAPERS IN FUTURE RATE CASES?

 7   A.   Yes. Notwithstanding the Staff’s recommended test year and Plan Year revenue forecast

 8        adjustments, the Staff did not find specific problems with the Company’s overall revenue

 9        forecast process in this case. However, in order to make this assessment, the Staff was

10        required to issue multiple data requests for Excel workbooks, narrative explanations, and

11        follow-on data requests in order to fully evaluate and understand the basis for the

12        Company’s test year and three Plan Year projections. The Company did not present any

13        testimony on this important issue, nor did the Company file any supporting workpapers

14        with its filing that would facilitate and independent evaluation by the Staff. In the end,

15        following the Staff’s formal and informal data requests, the Company provide numerous

16        Excel workbooks containing about 50 individual Excel models that provide the support for

17        its revenue forecasts. The Company also provide a number of narrative descriptions

18        supporting the development of the retail revenue projections for the four test periods (Test

19        Year and Plan Years 2023, 2024 and 2025).
